scale.3: Identifies that nested class names are being lost in migration serialization and may propose qualified names, but validation or compatibility evidence for non-nested callables is limited.
scale.4: Clearly targets the bound-classmethod serializer path, uses the owner class's qualified path, and shows serializer output now includes the containing class for a nested classmethod.
scale.5: Provides decisive evidence for the full contract: targeted qualified-path fix, before/after nested classmethod serialization, preservation of module imports, and sanity checks for ordinary functions, top-level classmethods, and deeper nested classmethods.

experiences.title: Argparse required-group kwargs must be routed through parser validation
experiences.description: Use when a Django-style programmatic command API converts keyword options into argparse input and the reported bug involves members of a required mutually exclusive group not satisfying the group.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django management-command work where `call_command()` or a similar wrapper builds an argparse parser, maps keyword options to argparse destinations, and selectively synthesizes command-line arguments before `parse_args()`. The key visible task cue is that individual actions in `add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)` have `required=False`, while the group itself is required. This criterion is most useful after the agent has inspected the parser/action handling or has begun patching the kwarg-to-parse_args bridge. It is less useful during very early file-location exploration, and it should not be expanded into a blanket requirement for subparser recursion, non-required mutually exclusive groups, or custom conflict handling unless the trajectory itself modifies or tests those behaviors.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster were useful when they judged the central semantic contract: kwargs whose argparse destination belongs to a required mutually exclusive group must be represented in the synthetic parse input so argparse can satisfy the required-group constraint, while ordinary required-option handling and missing-group errors continue to behave normally. They were strongest when they looked for visible evidence that the agent inspected `parser._mutually_exclusive_groups`/`group._group_actions`, understood that member actions are not individually required, and verified both the original kwarg success and the no-member failure. They became less reliable when they over-weighted tempting but task-adjacent concerns such as exhaustive subparser recursion, accepting option-string alias kwargs for every nested parser, or manually reimplementing mutual-exclusion errors. A better rubric should prioritize whether the patch extends the existing required-kwarg forwarding path to include actions in required mutually exclusive groups, without bypassing `parse_args()` or silently marking each member as individually required. If the trajectory shows conflicting kwargs in the same group being silently accepted, that is a meaningful warning, but it should be framed as preservation of argparse validation rather than as a standalone implementation mandate; judge it most strongly when the agent’s code explicitly chooses only one supplied group member, deletes others, or otherwise prevents argparse from seeing conflicts. Avoid rewarding broad private-API scans or unrelated test runs as proxies for correctness; prioritize the concrete code path that builds `parse_args`, the use of normalized destinations versus raw keyword names where visible, and targeted reproduction of provided member, missing member, and existing required-option behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Required group action forwarding
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the command wrapper fixes required mutually exclusive argparse groups by identifying actions that belong to required groups and forwarding supplied keyword values for those actions through the existing parser-validation path. Strong evidence includes inspecting argparse group internals, adding only the required-group membership condition to the required-kwarg parse input logic, using the same option string/destination mapping conventions already used by the wrapper, and validating that a single provided group member succeeds while an omitted required group still raises the parser’s required-group error. The rubric should also notice whether the agent preserves existing behavior for ordinary required options and avoids bypassing argparse with manual defaults or ad hoc success conditions.

primary_visible_evidence: The task describes a required mutually exclusive argparse group whose member actions are not individually required.
The trajectory inspects or uses group-level argparse metadata such as required groups and their member actions.
The patch affects the synthetic parse argument construction rather than command execution or parser creation.
Validation includes at least the original kwarg case and the missing-required-group case.
secondary_evidence: Alias-to-destination normalization is considered when the trajectory exposes custom dest names.
Existing required-option tests or equivalent checks still pass.
Conflict behavior is preserved by allowing argparse to validate supplied group members rather than by silently choosing or deleting options.
do_not_overrequire: Subparser recursion unless the agent changes or relies on subparser behavior.
Manual reproduction artifacts as a substitute for the core code-path evidence.
Custom reimplementation of argparse error messages.

scale.1: No substantive evidence that the agent understands or addresses required mutually exclusive groups; the patch or plan remains focused only on individually required actions, unrelated files, or command execution after parsing.
scale.2: The agent identifies mutually exclusive groups but proposes or applies a weak fix that bypasses parser validation, marks group members as individually required, handles only an ad hoc command path, or lacks evidence that supplied group-member kwargs are added to parse input.
scale.3: The trajectory reaches behavior comparable to the parent state: it recognizes required group membership and has partial code or tests for the original kwarg case, but evidence is incomplete or there are unresolved concerns about destination mapping, missing-group behavior, or preserving existing required-option parsing.
scale.4: Strong evidence shows the fix extends the existing required-kwarg parse_args construction to include supplied actions from required mutually exclusive groups, with targeted checks that one provided member succeeds, missing members still error, and ordinary required options remain functional.
scale.5: The trajectory provides the strongest visible assurance: the implementation is minimal and integrated with existing parser action/destination mapping, relies on argparse for validation rather than manual shortcuts, covers the original case plus missing-required and existing required-option regressions, and addresses any exposed alias or conflict concerns without broad unrelated behavioral changes.

experiences.title: Iterator Contract for Paginator-Like Containers
experiences.description: Use when a Python task explicitly asks to make a container/paginator object iterable by adding `__iter__`, and the visible trajectory has identified the target class plus existing page-range and page-construction APIs.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django-style codebase when the problem statement is narrow: implement normal iteration over an existing paginator-like class. The trajectory should show evidence such as locating the class, inspecting the existing `page_range`/range API and `page()`/page-construction method, or testing that direct iteration currently fails while manual iteration through page numbers works. This criterion is most useful once the agent is at implementation or review stage; it may be premature during pure repository exploration before the target class and existing APIs are visible. It is less applicable if the task asks for a broader redesign of pagination, iteration over raw objects rather than pages, async iteration, custom sequence behavior, or changes to page numbering/validation semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the actual semantic contract: `__iter__` must be added to the paginator class and each fresh iteration must yield the existing `Page` objects produced by calling the existing page-construction method for every number in the existing page-range property. This aligned well because the task itself supplied the intended implementation and the trajectory exposed decisive evidence: manual loops over `page_range` plus `page()` worked, direct iteration failed before the change, and successful edits inserted a generator method without changing surrounding pagination behavior. A better rubric should judge whether the implementation preserves existing pagination semantics, including empty paginator, orphan handling, single-page cases, and repeated iteration, by delegating to `page_range` and `page()` rather than reimplementing slicing or validation. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring a particular insertion line, docstring wording, full test-suite execution, adding new tests, comparing `Page` objects by equality, or merely checking that some `__iter__` method exists. Also avoid rewarding implementations that return page numbers, raw object lists, a one-time stored iterator, or modify `page_range`/`page()` to make tests pass.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Paginator Iterator Delegates to Existing Page Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the Python iterator protocol on the paginator-like class by adding `__iter__` as a fresh generator that loops over the existing page-number range and yields the existing page object for each page number, while leaving existing page-count, range, validation, orphan, and empty-page behavior unchanged.

required_visible_evidence: The target class has been identified as the paginator-like class requested by the task.
The class already exposes an existing page-number range API and an existing method that constructs/returns page objects.
The proposed or applied implementation adds `__iter__` to that class, not to the page class or an unrelated helper.
`__iter__` iterates over the existing page-number range and yields the result of the existing page-construction method for each number.
The trajectory does not show semantic changes to page numbering, validation, slicing, orphan handling, or empty-page behavior.
anti_patterns: Yielding raw items, object-list slices, or page numbers instead of page objects.
Returning a list rather than providing a normal reusable iteration protocol.
Using a stored one-shot iterator that would break repeated iteration.
Reimplementing pagination calculations inside `__iter__` instead of delegating to existing APIs.
Changing existing `page_range`, `page()`, validation, or page-count behavior to support iteration.
metadata.stage_notes: Before any implementation is visible, judge mostly on whether the agent has identified the correct contract and target APIs. After an edit is visible, prioritize the actual method body and absence of collateral semantic changes over test-run completeness.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory is implementing the requested iterator contract, or it targets the wrong class/API.
scale.2: Some recognition that the paginator should be iterable, but the visible plan or code is incomplete, ambiguous, or likely to yield the wrong type of value.
scale.3: The trajectory is approximately on track relative to the parent state, but the implementation evidence is partial or does not yet clearly prove delegation to the existing page-range and page-construction APIs.
scale.4: Clear evidence of an added `__iter__` on the correct class that loops through the existing page range and yields pages, with little sign of collateral behavior changes.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the correct generator-style `__iter__` is visible, it delegates exactly to the existing page-range and page-construction behavior, repeated/edge-case iteration is considered or tested, and no unrelated pagination semantics are changed.

experiences.title: Do not let broad cross-file activity substitute for acceptance-contract evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when a task spans many components and the trajectory shows broad searches, multi-file edits, or integration commentary, but the visible evidence does not yet prove the concrete behavioral contract required by the task.
experiences.context: Applies in software repositories where the task is inherently cross-cutting—UI terminology, API endpoint creation, version-support drops, dynamic service addresses, storage-unit centralization, onboarding/setup flows, generated RPC surfaces, or CLI testability. In these cases, a generic holistic-review rubric can be misleading because an agent may inspect or edit many related files while still missing the decisive contract: generated artifacts, actual listener addresses, source/localization synchronization, CI/test matrix updates, error-returning CLI paths, semantic boundary between user-facing text and protocol identifiers, or centralized constants. The source rubric can still be appropriate during final integration review when there is already a concrete patch and the main remaining question is whether the modified components interoperate. It should not be used as a high-confidence proxy during reconnaissance, no-op conclusions, repetitive search loops, or scattershot broad edits without visible acceptance-level closure.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent reviewed the change holistically across components. That is a useful secondary check, but it became misleading when broad exploration or multi-file editing was treated as evidence of correctness. In the sampled trajectories, agents often touched or inspected many files yet left the core contract unresolved: no patch after investigation, incomplete generated-code/API wiring, changed comments that were historically false, omitted CI or changelog updates, over-edited localization files, failed to distinguish protocol/internal identifiers from user-facing strings, or repeated the same search without progressing. A better rubric should focus on whether the visible trajectory has closed the task-specific behavioral requirements and respected domain boundaries. Avoid the tempting criterion “the agent looked at all relevant components” or “the patch spans many components.” Prioritize evidence such as: exact acceptance cases identified and implemented, required generated files or configuration matrices updated, user-facing strings changed in source and canonical localization files together, dynamic runtime values propagated instead of configured placeholders, no-op conclusions justified by definitive repository state, and validation or targeted greps/tests showing the critical contract rather than only broad coverage.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Cross-component activity without contract closure
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear cross-component or comprehensive but lack visible evidence that the task's concrete acceptance contract has been implemented and validated. This applies especially when the agent relies on broad grep results, file lists, or many edits while missing required artifacts, generated code, runtime propagation, source/localization synchronization, CI/config updates, or protocol-versus-user-facing boundaries. Do not penalize merely for working across many files if the trajectory also shows the decisive contract being satisfied with targeted validation.

preferred_visible_evidence: explicit acceptance cases mapped to implementation
critical generated/configuration/test artifacts updated when required
semantic boundaries preserved, such as protocol identifiers versus user-facing labels
runtime values or API responses verified at the actual integration point
targeted validation demonstrating the requested behavior rather than only absence of search hits
typical_failure_stage: no-op conclusion despite remaining task-specific work

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory ties each major task requirement to concrete code changes and targeted validation, with broad component review used only to confirm integration.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent performs broad review and may leave a small validation or ancillary artifact ambiguous, but the main behavioral contract is visibly addressed.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory covers many related components but only partially demonstrates the decisive contract, leaving important requirements or boundary checks unresolved.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent relies heavily on cross-file exploration or multi-file edits while missing a central acceptance requirement, generated/configuration artifact, runtime propagation path, or semantic boundary.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory is mostly broad search, repetitive investigation, no-op reasoning, or scattershot edits, with little or no visible implementation of the task's core behavioral contract.

experiences.title: Do not reward read-only exploration after the key contract is already known
experiences.description: Use this warning when a trajectory contains many safe read commands, but the task’s success depends on applying a specific integration contract, lifecycle transition, owner/container boundary, compatibility case, or formatting/state contract rather than merely avoiding premature writes. Light exception: when every visible continuation is still pre-edit with no source diff or changed files, use a gated diagnosis-quality rubric to distinguish mechanism-level debugging from empty exploration instead of applying only fix-validation or command-hygiene criteria. Small update: in mixed evidence sets where rubrics name concrete failure modes, passive code inspection with no edits or targeted validation must not be ranked above continuations whose visible diffs, code changes, or test runs directly address those named contracts. Preserve meaningful partial credit for exact root-cause diagnosis, but make active contract-addressing evidence the higher-ceiling signal once it is visible.
experiences.context:
Applies in SWE-agent code-repair trajectories across TypeScript/React, Go, Python, and similar codebases where the recent evidence is mostly grep/cat/sed, file inspection, reproduction scripts, debug output, or other non-mutating investigation. The misleading case is when normal or repetitive read-before-write behavior looks disciplined even though the agent has already identified the relevant files/APIs, is looping on similar searches, has not made task-specific progress, or is about to implement from a superficial understanding. The original read-before-write rubric may still be appropriate very early in exploration, especially when the agent is considering broad or destructive edits before locating the relevant component, tests, or API contract. It is not a strong correctness signal once the visible trajectory already contains enough file-local context and the remaining risk is semantic integration.

Stage guard: if all or nearly all visible continuations have no source edits or diff and are focused on reproduction, debugging, source inspection, or root-cause analysis, do not collapse the portfolio into fix-validation rubrics that can only score implemented changes. In that narrow pre-edit view, add a positive diagnosis rubric that rewards causal, mechanism-level evidence. This exception does not credit read-only behavior by volume; it credits demonstrated understanding of the failure mechanism and its likely code boundary. If the visible population is mixed, preserve the parent warning but still allow a stage-aware root-cause criterion when it is needed to compare correct diagnosis against incorrect or irrelevant edits. Once substantial edits or targeted validation are visible, implementation and integration evidence should carry the highest ceiling, but a change that does not address the diagnosed mechanism should score below a no-edit trajectory that clearly identifies the mechanism.

Additional mixed-evidence guard: when the generated rubrics name specific failure modes or contracts, the judge must map each continuation’s visible evidence to those named contracts. A continuation whose only visible evidence is read-only inspection commands, with no changed files, no source diff, and no targeted test or validation run, is weak evidence of contract satisfaction. It should not outrank continuations showing actual diffs, code modifications, or focused test runs that address the named failure modes, even if the read-only continuation opened the relevant file. This guard does not penalize reading that precedes a visible fix in the same continuation, and it does not force a ranking among all-read-only continuations; it only prevents passive observation from being treated as stronger than active contract-addressing work.

This update is especially relevant for tasks whose bug is a small contract violation inside formatting, stringification, lifecycle, value transformation, conditional handling, option-combination logic, or consistency validation. For example, a whitespace defect may depend on an empty suffix value, a missing separator before a directional suffix, or a trailing separator after an optional component. In such cases, the decisive evidence is not that the agent opened or edited the right file; it is whether it identified the exact conditional/string assembly mechanism and the explicit output combinations implicated by the task, then either made or validated a change at that boundary. Do not generalize this into speculative extra obligations: only require multiple cases, downstream behavior, or companion fixes when the task evidence or inspected code path makes them part of the reported failure.
experiences.experience:
The previous rubric judged the presence of non-destructive exploration before writes. That is useful as a safety/process check, but it overemphasizes command hygiene in tasks where correctness hinges on domain behavior: using the existing service instead of bypassing it, clearing owned state rather than only stopping an object, updating the right lifecycle entry point, preserving compatibility fallbacks, or applying a state/filter/formatting contract with the action’s intent. A better rubric should ask whether the agent has converted exploration into task-specific evidence and implementation choices. Avoid the tempting criterion of counting grep/cat/sed commands as positive progress. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent inspected the exact owner API, reusable service, lifecycle hook, or string assembly function named by the discovered code path; stopped repeating identical searches after finding the relevant facts; planned or made edits at the boundary where the bug occurs; accounted for compatibility, optional-value, ordering, parent/owner, or output-combination context mentioned in the task; and added or targeted tests for the described behavior.

Small gated addition for pre-edit and mixed-stage diagnosis: a useful rubric can be positive, but only if it measures diagnosis quality. The decisive observable distinction should be exact root cause plus code-path localization, not reproduction alone, not generic file reading, and not edit presence. High diagnosis scores require the agent to trigger or otherwise concretely observe the reported behavior, inspect the relevant method/class/function or call path, explain the mechanism that causes the failure, and map that mechanism to the likely fix boundary. For formatting or stringification defects, this means naming the specific conditional, join, suffix, separator, optional component, or combination logic that produces the bad output, and identifying each explicitly relevant affected case. Partial scores fit agents that reproduce the error or identify the likely file but do not articulate the mechanism. Low scores fit environment setup, broad searches, repeated read-only commands after the relevant facts are known, edits to unrelated code, or claims of understanding without source-level causal evidence.

Small mixed-evidence addition: when some continuations contain only passive inspection while others show source diffs, code modifications, or targeted tests addressing named contracts, generate rubric criteria that make that observable distinction matter. The active contract-addressing criteria should be positive and higher ceiling: did the visible diff or validation actually target the named failure mode, conditional branch, value transformation, lifecycle edge, or compatibility case? The passive-overranking criterion should be negative or cautionary with enough weight to prevent a read-only-only continuation from outranking visible contract-addressing work. Its evidence mapping should explicitly check: read-only commands only; no changed files or source diff; no targeted test/validation; rubrics name concrete failure modes; and other continuations show changes or tests that engage those same named modes. Do not treat a failing targeted test as worthless: it is usually stronger evidence of contract engagement than passive reading, though it remains below a correct implementation plus passing focused validation. Do not penalize a continuation that reads code and then makes relevant changes; evaluate the changes and validation.

Use a stage-aware scale when trajectories are paused at different points:
- Lowest credit: no engagement with the responsible code path; only setup, broad search, passive inspection detached from the named contract, or unrelated edits.
- Low partial credit: reproduced the symptom or located a plausible file/method, but has not identified the causal mechanism.
- Meaningful partial credit: identified the exact root cause in the relevant function or contract, such as an empty optional value being treated as text, a missing separator before a suffix, a stale owner/container boundary, an omitted parameter handoff, or a broken conditional/value-transformation path. This level should not be zero merely because no source change is visible.
- High partial credit: identified the root cause and either produced a focused reproduction covering the implicated cases, described a concrete fix boundary, began an edit aimed at that mechanism, or ran a targeted validation that exercises it.
- Highest credit: implemented an equivalent correct fix and validated the behavior against the task’s important cases. Equivalent implementations should be preserved; do not require a particular code shape if the visible behavior and integration contract are satisfied.

Rubric-generation guidance:
- Outside the strict no-edit diagnosis gate, keep the parent polarity: use a negative or cautionary criterion against repetitive read-only exploration after localization, and weight it as a process/semantic-risk signal rather than as the sole correctness criterion.
- Inside the strict no-edit diagnosis gate, add a positive diagnosis rubric with meaningful weight because it can distinguish trajectories before an edit exists. Its semantics should evaluate root-cause understanding, not implementation correctness.
- In mixed-stage portfolios, include enough stage-aware diagnosis weight to prevent an incorrect or irrelevant edit from outranking a correct mechanism-level diagnosis. At the same time, keep the ceiling higher for visible, correct implementation plus validation.
- When rubrics name concrete contracts and the evidence set includes both read-only-only continuations and continuations with relevant diffs, modifications, or targeted validations, include an explicit negative/cautionary criterion for ranking passive inspection above active contract-addressing evidence. Weight it low-to-medium or medium so that it affects ordering, while preserving higher positive weight for actual correctness and validation.
- Do not score bare reproduction, environment setup, or many inspection commands as high diagnosis quality. They are at most low-to-partial evidence unless paired with causal explanation and code-path localization.
- Do not give credit merely for modifying the target file, producing a large diff, or adding tests. If the visible changes do not address the causal mechanism, they should score low even when they touch plausible code.
- Do not require successful test execution as the only path to non-zero credit. If external setup problems block execution, judge the source-level causal evidence that is visible. A targeted test attempt can be evidence of contract engagement, but it does not substitute for a correct fix.
- Do not invent extra required mechanisms from analogy. If a task has two explicit whitespace defects or four explicit option combinations, score whether those are recognized and covered. If the evidence only supports one missing handoff, separator, fallback, or lifecycle boundary, do not require unrelated downstream changes for high diagnosis credit.
- Do not apply fix-validation criteria that require an implemented change when no visible continuation contains a source change; that creates uninformative floor scores. Once edits appear, return to implementation/integration evidence and treat diagnosis as supporting context, not a substitute for satisfying the contract.
- Preserve uncertainty when the visible prefix is too short to show reproduction, source inspection, changed code, or validation. If a change is present but its content or behavior is not visible, do not assume it is correct or incorrect; score only the evidence shown.
- Preserve equivalent implementations: rank by whether the visible behavior and integration contract are satisfied, not by exact code shape, command style, or whether the agent followed a preferred route.

experiences.title: Stage-Aware Issue Reproduction and Error-Contract Preservation as Validation Signals
experiences.description: Use when a bug report includes a concrete failing scenario and the trajectory is far enough along that a targeted reproduction or regression test should be visible, especially after edits or before final validation. When the fix changes what a method yields or returns, validation must also confirm that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved, not just the primary reported symptom. When the fix is about transaction or atomicity around a data-changing code path, validation must address rollback or error behavior, not merely the visible presence of an atomic wrapper. If the visible stage begins after a fix has already been applied, judge the current segment's own validation activity rather than re-crediting inherited implementation work or earlier testing. When generating rubrics for sibling continuations that share a parent trajectory, do not let shared parent evidence or non-discriminative environment-setup criteria carry scoring weight; re-center the portfolio on continuation-specific final evidence and the primary implementation contract.
experiences.context: Applies in framework/library bug-fix tasks where the problem statement gives observable actual vs expected behavior, such as an ORM query result, rendered documentation output, migration recorder state, form choices, introspection signature, post-processing output, or transaction rollback contract. Most useful once the agent has located the relevant subsystem, created or modified a candidate fix, inherited an already-applied fix, or begun validation. Less useful as a strict negative during initial exploration, when the agent is only locating files and reading code, or when the task is purely refactoring without a concrete runtime failure. When the current stage inherits a completed fix, generated rubrics should distinguish continuations that run their own functional verification from those that only inspect or describe the existing changes; do not penalize them for not redoing completed implementation or documentation. When the fix changes yield/return behavior, the validation must specifically check that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved. Abstain from the error-preservation sub-criterion when the fix does not change yield/return behavior, or when the original code does not yield or return errors or exceptions during processing. For transaction or atomicity tasks, activate the rollback-validation addendum only when the requested behavior is to make a data-changing operation atomic, or when the visible work introduces transaction wrapping around such an operation. Abstain from that addendum for unrelated formatting, parsing, or pure structural tasks. Abstain from the shared-evidence gating sub-criterion when the review is not comparing sibling continuations, when continuations genuinely contain different implementation changes rather than inheriting the same parent change, or when the portfolio already weights only continuation-specific final evidence and already includes a non-empty final-output check. If all visible branches have the same inherited state and no observable validation activity, prefer uncertain or moderate uniform scoring over confident high credit.
experiences.experience:
The recurring rubric asked whether the agent first established a reproducible bug. This was useful when the visible trajectory contained task-specific reproduction evidence: a minimal script, focused test, or documented command showing the exact bad behavior and then confirming the intended behavior after the fix. It aligned well when the agent reproduced duplicate form options, stale migration application rows, incorrect manager method signatures, missing rendered members, or broken rollback behavior, because those observations directly exercised the user-visible contract. It was less discriminative when generated too early, before the agent had any reasonable chance to run a reproduction, because some later-correct fixes began with code inspection only. A better rubric should be stage-aware and concrete: ask whether the agent has established or is actively preserving a targeted failing scenario matching the reported bug, not merely whether it has run any tests or listed files.

A small but important stage-transition rule: when the current visible work starts from an already-applied fix, a reproduction/validation rubric should score what the current segment itself does to verify behavior. Positive evidence includes running a focused test, small script, import-and-call check, materializing iterator or query outputs, checking object identity or mutation independence where relevant, rerunning a regression assertion, inducing an error and observing rollback or yielded errors, or otherwise executing the fixed behavior. Merely displaying the diff, reading the changed file, listing files, or referring in prose to earlier testing is useful context but is not functional validation. Do not credit validation that only occurred before the current segment, and do not penalize the current segment for not redoing implementation or documentation work that is already complete. When converting this experience into rubrics, keep the polarity positive and give current-stage validation meaningful weight when the fix is inherited; use implementation-presence rubrics only when branches visibly differ in implementation. Evidence mapping should look for commands, scripts, assertions, observed outputs, or test names executed in the current visible span, with diff or source inspection treated as lower-priority supporting evidence rather than validation.

For transaction or atomicity fixes, the decisive observable distinction is behavioral rollback evidence versus wrapper-only source evidence. A visible transaction.atomic or equivalent wrapper can support a structural implementation criterion, but it is not enough for top overall credit. The rubric portfolio should not split the same wrapper sighting into several separately weighted positive criteria for wrapper presence, indentation, routing, and local style, because that duplicates one source-inspection signal and can outrank a continuation that is actually validating the transaction contract. Instead, merge wrapper placement and any local database-routing convention into one moderate-weight structural criterion, and make rollback or relevant behavioral validation at least as important as all wrapper-inspection-only criteria combined. Positive validation evidence includes running or attempting to run targeted tests for the data-changing path, locating the specific existing tests as part of an execution attempt, constructing a focused check where an exception during processing rolls back earlier writes, or explicitly reasoning from a relevant test failure/success about rollback consistency. Syntax checks and sed/cat output may improve paused-state reliability, but they do not demonstrate rollback behavior. Dependency or settings setup counts only when it is visibly in service of running relevant tests; generic setup, broad file exploration, or truncated output should be scored with uncertainty rather than inferred success.

Paused work needs separate signals. If a continuation is paused mid-edit, after a mechanical sed/script edit, after a restore, or during test-environment setup, do not assign either maximum or zero for final correctness from the wrapper string alone. Use independent positive dimensions: structural coverage of the intended data-changing block, behavioral validation of the user-visible contract, and reliability of the last verified file state. A source snippet showing the wrapper maps to structural evidence; a clean post-edit inspection or syntax check maps to reliability; only an executed or concretely attempted issue-specific check maps to behavioral validation. A continuation with no final code change visible but concrete progress toward the relevant rollback test context should receive process/validation credit rather than zero. Conversely, a continuation that only shows a plausible wrapper with no current-stage rollback/test activity should be capped at moderate credit and should not beat a continuation with stronger current-stage validation when the structural state is shared or uncertain. Accept equivalent implementations: do not require one exact wrapper layout if multiple placements protect the same mutating operation and preserve local routing or transaction conventions.

When a fix changes what a method yields or returns, validation must also confirm that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved. A branch that fixes the primary symptom while silently dropping error yields should not receive the highest reproduction-fidelity score. The reproduction should include a scenario that triggers a processing error, such as faulty or malformed input, and verify the error is still yielded or raised after the fix. This distinction is critical because the primary symptom fix may appear correct in isolation while breaking an implicit error-handling contract that downstream consumers depend on. If the current stage inherits such a fix, the strongest evidence is a current-stage check of both the primary behavior and the error-preservation behavior; earlier checks may explain confidence but should not be scored as work performed by the current segment.

Avoid the tempting generic criterion that the agent must run the full test suite or must reproduce before reading code. The important evidence is a minimal, issue-specific before/after check or a regression test that would fail for the reported behavior and pass after the candidate fix. Equivalent validation forms should be accepted: a focused unit test, a command using the appropriate test runner, a concise script, or an interactive check can all be strong if they exercise the reported contract. Prioritize visible evidence such as exact commands, scripts, assertions, rendered output checks, query results, rollback observations, exception messages, or targeted test names that correspond to the original report. Do not confuse a test that only validates the primary symptom with one that also preserves error-handling contracts when the fix changes yield/return behavior. Do not confuse a test that checks a different error path with one that checks individual-item error yielding during processing. Preserve uncertainty where the visible evidence cannot separate branches rather than forcing overconfident distinctions.

A recurring rubric semantic and weighting error arises when generated rubrics for sibling continuations that share a parent trajectory credit evidence that is identical across all continuations. The most common form is inverting a caution about environment or checkout validation into a positive criterion: a negative sub-rubric warning against relying on installed-package or checkout-path validation gets rewritten as positive credit for targeting the correct checkout path or install location. This inversion is harmful because environment-setup behavior, targeting a specific checkout path, using the correct checkout, or performing installed-package validation is setup noise rather than implementation evidence, and is often identical across sibling continuations. A criterion rewarding identical behavior is non-discriminative: it cannot separate correct from incorrect continuations and instead inflates scores uniformly. Visible evidence that should activate this correction includes: a rubric criterion rewards targeting a specific checkout path, install location, or environment validation when all compared branches exhibit the same behavior; a rubric criterion credits tests, diffs, or checkout behavior that appear in a shared parent segment rather than in the continuation's own visible span; or a caution about environment validation has been semantically inverted into positive credit for environment targeting. When any of these are visible, remove or assign zero weight to the environment, checkout, or provenance criterion, and re-center the portfolio on continuation-specific evidence. The dominant weighted criterion should remain the primary implementation contract: the actual code change or behavior that fixes the reported bug, plus current-stage validation of that behavior where the implementation state is shared. Add or retain a small final-submission integrity criterion: inspect the continuation's final output, not just earlier shared commands, and award full credit only when that final output includes a readable non-empty diff or change for the intended work. Penalize a continuation whose final output produces a blank observation, a failed file read, or no visible change content, even if an earlier shared step showed the correct diff; do not penalize intermediate failed attempts to read a change file if a later final output visibly emits the change. Keep any secondary regression criterion lower-weight, ensure it does not duplicate the primary fix, and do not allow shared parent evidence alone to decide among sibling continuations.

experiences.title: Stage-Aware Issue Reproduction and Error-Contract Preservation as Validation Signals
experiences.description: Use when a bug report includes a concrete failing scenario and the trajectory is far enough along that a targeted reproduction or regression test should be visible, especially after edits or before final validation. When the fix changes what a method yields or returns, validation must also confirm that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved, not just the primary reported symptom. If the visible stage begins after a fix has already been applied, judge the current segment's own validation activity rather than re-crediting inherited implementation work or earlier testing. When generating rubrics for sibling continuations that share a parent trajectory, do not let shared parent evidence or non-discriminative environment-setup criteria carry scoring weight; re-center the portfolio on continuation-specific final submission evidence and the primary implementation contract. A continuation whose visible segment shows only environment preparation or issue reproduction—without visible source code edits—is still performing legitimate workflow activity; do not assign a zero score on implementation or validation rubrics solely because no code edit appears in that partial view.
experiences.context: Applies in framework/library bug-fix tasks where the problem statement gives observable actual vs expected behavior, such as an ORM query result, rendered documentation output, migration recorder state, form choices, introspection signature, or post-processing output. Most useful once the agent has located the relevant subsystem, created or modified a candidate fix, inherited an already-applied fix, or begun validation. Less useful as a strict negative during initial exploration, when the agent is only locating files and reading code, or when the task is purely refactoring without a concrete runtime failure. When the current stage inherits a completed fix, generated rubrics should distinguish continuations that run their own functional verification from those that only inspect or describe the existing changes; do not penalize them for not redoing completed implementation or documentation. When the fix changes yield/return behavior, the validation must specifically check that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved. Abstain from the error-preservation sub-criterion when the fix does not change yield/return behavior, or when the original code does not yield or return errors or exceptions during processing. Abstain from the shared-evidence gating sub-criterion when the review is not comparing sibling continuations, when continuations genuinely contain different implementation patches rather than inheriting the same parent patch, or when the portfolio already weights only continuation-specific final submitted patches and already includes a non-empty final-output check. When a continuation's visible segment shows only environment setup (installing dependencies, configuring PYTHONPATH, setting up project structure) or issue reproduction (running the problematic command and observing the expected error output) without visible source code edits, preserve uncertainty: assign a non-zero score reflecting visible workflow activity rather than a definitive zero, since the visible segment is a partial view and absence of code edits does not establish that no fix was attempted. If all visible branches have the same inherited state and no observable validation activity, prefer uncertain or moderate uniform scoring over confident high credit.
experiences.experience:
The recurring rubric asked whether the agent first established a reproducible bug. This was useful when the visible trajectory contained task-specific reproduction evidence: a minimal script, focused test, or documented command showing the exact bad behavior and then confirming the intended behavior after the patch. It aligned well when the agent reproduced duplicate form options, stale migration application rows, incorrect manager method signatures, or missing rendered members, because those observations directly exercised the user-visible contract. It was less discriminative when generated too early, before the agent had any reasonable chance to run a reproduction, because some later-correct fixes began with code inspection only. A better rubric should be stage-aware and concrete: ask whether the agent has established or is actively preserving a targeted failing scenario matching the reported bug, not merely whether it has run any tests or listed files.

A partial-view scoring principle: a continuation's visible segment may capture only preparatory workflow—installing missing dependencies, configuring PYTHONPATH or editable installs, changing to the project directory, setting up project structure, or running the reproduction command and observing the expected error output—without showing source code edits in the same window. These are legitimate workflow activities that demonstrate problem understanding and forward progress. Do not assign a zero score on implementation or validation rubrics solely because no code edit is visible in that segment; the visible segment is a partial view and absence of code modifications does not establish that no fix was attempted or that no progress was made. Assign a non-zero score reflecting the visible workflow activity while preserving uncertainty about whether a fix was implemented in non-visible steps. However, a continuation showing actual source code modifications with working test validation should generally score higher than one showing only environment setup; environment setup is necessary but not sufficient for a top score. A critical close-looking exclusion: seeing the original error message when running the reproduction command means the bug is reproduced, NOT that the fix is working. Do not conflate reproduction with validation of a fix. A standalone test script that demonstrates the fix concept is evidence of implementation thinking, but modifying the actual source file is stronger evidence of a complete fix. Do not assume a continuation with visible source code modifications is necessarily superior to one showing only environment setup without examining whether the visible segment is partial.

A small but important stage-transition rule: when the current visible work starts from an already-applied fix, a reproduction/validation rubric should score what the current segment itself does to verify behavior. Positive evidence includes running a focused test, small script, import-and-call check, materializing iterator or query outputs, checking object identity or mutation independence where relevant, rerunning a regression assertion, or otherwise executing the fixed behavior. Merely displaying the diff, reading the changed file, listing files, or referring in prose to earlier testing is useful context but is not functional validation. Do not credit validation that only occurred before the current segment, and do not penalize the current segment for not redoing implementation or documentation work that is already complete. When converting this experience into rubrics, keep the polarity positive and give current-stage validation meaningful weight when the fix is inherited; use implementation-presence rubrics only when branches visibly differ in implementation. Evidence mapping should look for commands, scripts, assertions, observed outputs, or test names executed in the current visible span, with diff inspection treated as lower-priority supporting evidence rather than validation.

When a fix changes what a method yields or returns, validation must also confirm that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved. A branch that fixes the primary symptom while silently dropping error yields should not receive the highest reproduction-fidelity score. The reproduction should include a scenario that triggers a processing error, such as faulty or malformed input, and verify the error is still yielded or raised after the fix. This distinction is critical because the primary symptom fix may appear correct in isolation while breaking an implicit error-handling contract that downstream consumers depend on. If the current stage inherits such a fix, the strongest evidence is a current-stage check of both the primary behavior and the error-preservation behavior; earlier checks may explain confidence but should not be scored as work performed by the current segment.

Avoid the tempting generic criterion 'must run the full test suite' or 'must reproduce before reading code'; the important evidence is a minimal, issue-specific before/after check or a regression test that would fail for the reported behavior and pass after the candidate fix. Equivalent validation forms should be accepted: a focused unit test, a command using the appropriate test runner, a concise script, or an interactive check can all be strong if they exercise the reported contract. Prioritize visible evidence such as exact commands, scripts, assertions, rendered output checks, query results, exception messages, or targeted test names that correspond to the original report. Do not confuse a test that only validates the primary symptom with one that also preserves error-handling contracts when the fix changes yield/return behavior. Do not confuse a test that checks a different error path with one that checks individual-item error yielding during processing. Preserve uncertainty where the visible evidence cannot separate branches rather than forcing overconfident distinctions.

A recurring rubric semantic and weighting error arises when generated rubrics for sibling continuations that share a parent trajectory credit evidence that is identical across all continuations. The most common form is inverting a caution about environment or checkout validation into a positive criterion: a negative sub-rubric warning against relying on installed-package or checkout-path validation gets rewritten as positive credit for targeting the correct checkout path or install location. This inversion is harmful because environment-setup behavior—targeting a specific checkout path, using the correct checkout, or performing installed-package validation—is setup noise rather than implementation evidence, and is typically identical across all sibling continuations. A criterion rewarding identical behavior is non-discriminative: it cannot separate correct from incorrect continuations and instead inflates scores uniformly, creating ties that include incorrect continuations. Visible evidence that should activate this correction: (1) a rubric criterion rewards targeting a specific checkout path, install location, or environment validation when all compared branches exhibit the same behavior; (2) a rubric criterion credits tests, diffs, or checkout behavior that appear in a shared parent segment rather than in the continuation's own visible span; or (3) a caution about environment validation has been semantically inverted into positive credit for environment targeting. When any of these are visible, remove or assign zero weight to the environment, checkout, or provenance criterion as a discriminating factor, and re-center the portfolio on continuation-specific evidence. The dominant weighted criterion should remain the primary implementation contract—the actual code change that fixes the reported bug—not environment mechanics. Important distinction: removing environment setup as a discriminating criterion among siblings is not the same as zeroing a continuation that shows only environment setup in a partial view. Environment setup is legitimate workflow evidence warranting a non-zero baseline score reflecting visible activity; it simply should not serve as a tiebreaker or positive discriminator when identical across all siblings. A continuation that successfully reproduces the issue—running the command and seeing the expected error or usage message—demonstrates problem understanding and engagement; scoring it as zero contradicts the visible evidence of active workflow progress. Add or retain a small final-submission integrity criterion: inspect the continuation's final submission step, not just earlier parent commands, and award full credit only when that final output includes a readable non-empty diff or patch for the intended change. Penalize a continuation whose final submission step produces a blank observation, a failed file read, or no visible patch content, even if an earlier parent step showed the correct diff; do not penalize intermediate failed attempts to read a patch file if a later final submission step visibly emits the patch. Keep any secondary regression criterion lower-weight, ensure it does not duplicate the primary fix, and do not allow shared parent evidence alone to decide among sibling continuations. Abstain from this shared-evidence gating sub-criterion when the review is not comparing sibling continuations, when continuations genuinely contain different implementation patches rather than inheriting the same parent patch, or when the portfolio already weights only continuation-specific final submitted patches and already includes a non-empty final-output check.

experiences.title: Runtime-specific regression requires exact change-to-code-path tracing
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug report explicitly ties behavior to a particular language/runtime version or linked changelog, especially in library compatibility issues where the local environment differs from the report. The key judgment is not just whether the runtime accepts a proposed construct, but whether the fix preserves the project's own boundary semantics while adapting to the runtime change. At custom parser/compiler or adapter boundaries, do not reclassify host-literal-looking spellings as host literals unless the project grammar or evaluator shows they are literals in the project language. Additionally, when the report contrasts behavior across versions, distinguish root-cause evidence (the specific code change that caused the regression, found via function-level git history) from symptom evidence (testing runtime behavior differences across versions or input types).
experiences.context: Applies to Python/library maintenance tasks where the user reports a regression only on a specific CPython version, debug/release build, dependency version, or cited runtime behavior change, while the trajectory is investigating a boundary delegated to stdlib/dependencies, such as proxy/auth/network handling, URL normalization, AST compilation, parsing, or expression evaluation. Activation evidence includes visible acknowledgement of the reported runtime/dependency version or build mode, a local mismatch or reconstruction of target behavior, and a project code path where data crosses into the affected runtime/dependency API. A concrete activation pattern for the literal-like identifier boundary is: grammar or tokenizer evidence accepting spellings such as True, False, None, null, or reserved-looking words as identifier tokens; parser code that emits a host-language name/reference node for identifiers; evaluation through a locals mapping, matcher, callback, symbol table, or router; and a runtime/compiler change that rejects or changes the host representation for those reserved-looking names. When the report contrasts behavior across software versions (e.g., a function's return value changed), the trajectory should be evaluated on whether it finds the specific code change that caused the regression, not merely whether it tests runtime behavior differences. It is most useful during diagnosis, patch planning, or final review before accepting a speculative patch. It is less useful when the task has no version-specific signal, when the trajectory has already isolated and tested the concrete compatibility invariant, when the project language genuinely defines the affected spellings as literals, or when the remaining issue is purely local refactoring unrelated to runtime/dependency behavior. Abstain from inferring correctness if the visible work stops at reproduction, environment checks, dependency installation, locating a suspicious call site, demonstrating a host-runtime construct without evidence about the project-level semantic invariant that must be preserved, or testing runtime behavior across versions without examining the code change that caused the regression. Also abstain from crediting a literal conversion when the visible work has not inspected enough of the grammar/evaluator/adapter to determine whether the affected spellings are identifiers or literals in the project language.
experiences.experience:
The earlier rubrics correctly emphasized version-specific investigation because visible trajectories often stayed on generic mechanics, installed or tested under mismatched local dependencies and Python versions, repeated irrelevant checks, or patched nearby code without tying the change to the reported runtime behavior. For similar cases, generate a rubric that rewards tracing the reported runtime or dependency change to the exact affected library boundary: which stdlib/dependency API changed, how the project uses it, what invariant is broken, and how the proposed fix preserves behavior across versions.

A necessary semantic boundary is that compiler/runtime compatibility evidence is not automatically semantic correctness evidence. If the affected path implements a project-specific language, adapter, matcher, router, or normalization layer, the rubric should require evidence that the fix preserves that layer's existing meaning, not merely that the replacement construct is accepted by the underlying runtime. For example, when a custom expression compiler emits Python AST, reserved-looking token strings that are valid identifiers in the custom language must not be credited as correctly fixed merely because converting them to Python boolean or null literals makes AST compilation succeed; the continuation must show that the original identifier or matcher lookup semantics are preserved, or justify from the project language that those tokens are intentionally literals.

For custom parser/compiler boundaries, preserve the project's token classification in the root-cause wording itself. If visible grammar or evaluator evidence shows that a spelling such as True, False, None, null, or another host-reserved/literal-looking word is accepted as a project-language identifier and resolved through a mapping, callback, matcher, symbol table, or router, the runtime-specific failure should be described as the host runtime rejecting or changing the representation of that identifier, not as the parser incorrectly treating a constant as a name. Only describe the value as a literal, or credit conversion to a host literal node, when the project language evidence shows that the spelling is intentionally a literal or when the proposed implementation still routes the project identifier through the same lookup semantics despite using a different host construct.

When the bug report contrasts behavior across versions, the rubric must distinguish root-cause evidence from symptom evidence. Symptom evidence includes testing runtime behavior of methods across input types or versions (e.g., comparing tzname, str, utcoffset outputs across timezone types), understanding the conceptual difference between behaviors, or looking at commit stats without the actual function-level diff. Symptom evidence is necessary but not sufficient: it demonstrates that the regression exists but does not identify the code change that caused it. Root-cause evidence requires examining git history of the affected function (e.g., git log -p for the specific file, grepping for the function name in git log), finding the exact function-level diff showing what changed (e.g., a return statement changed from one method call to another), and connecting that code change to the reported behavior difference. A trajectory that only tests behavior and articulates the conceptual issue should score lower than a trajectory that finds the specific code change in git history, even if the latter's behavior testing is less comprehensive. Looking at git show <commit> --stat (file-level changes only) is insufficient; the trajectory must show the actual function-level diff to qualify as root-cause evidence.

Positive evidence includes: acknowledging the specific reported runtime/dependency versions and any local mismatch; consulting or reconstructing the relevant runtime/dependency behavior change rather than relying on generic assumptions; mapping the change to the project boundary where URL/proxy/auth data, parser tokens, AST nodes, matcher identifiers, or other delegated data is transformed or transmitted; identifying the project-level invariant that must remain true across the boundary; when the report contrasts versions, examining git history of the affected function to find the exact code change that caused the regression and connecting it to the reported behavior difference; and validating the fix with a deterministic regression test, mock, or local simulation appropriate when the exact runtime or external service is unavailable. In proxy/auth cases, this includes checking that proxy credentials remain available to the proxy path without being leaked to the destination request. In parser/compiler cases, this includes checking that runtime-legal constructs do not silently reclassify custom-language identifiers into host-language literals or otherwise bypass the intended adapter; strong evidence can include a resolver or matcher that records being called for the reserved-looking spellings after the fix.

The criterion should not merely demand searching for version guards or adding version conditionals; compatibility fixes often should be version-agnostic. Also avoid rewarding superficial evidence such as confirming headers or AST nodes are constructed in isolation, testing only on the current interpreter, proving only that the host runtime accepts a transformed form, or testing runtime behavior across versions without examining the code change that caused the regression. A close-looking contraindication is a continuation that locates the exact failing runtime API call and demonstrates the host-runtime replacement that compiles or runs, but never checks whether the project's own DSL, routing, credential, or adapter semantics changed; that is useful localization, not top-level compatibility proof. Another close-looking contraindication is a trajectory that comprehensively tests runtime behavior across multiple input types or versions and correctly articulates the conceptual issue, but never examines git history or finds the specific code change; that is symptom-level diagnosis, not root-cause diagnosis, and should not receive top marks even if the behavior testing is thorough. A particularly misleading variant is locating a failing name/reference node for a reserved-looking spelling, citing a newer host AST or compiler representation for literals, and then declaring the project parser wrong for using an identifier node without checking the project grammar and evaluator. Another contraindication is patching an unrelated nearby path, such as generic auth parsing, chunked upload, tokenizer keyword classification, or literal conversion, without showing relevance to the reported behavior and preserved invariant.

Prioritize visible evidence that the agent noticed the environment mismatch, reconstructed the target-version behavior, mapped it to the concrete project boundary, separated host-runtime validity from project-language or data-routing semantics, preserved the project's own classification of literal-looking tokens before judging a conversion, found the specific code change via function-level git history when the report contrasts versions rather than stopping at behavior testing, and planned or added deterministic regression coverage for both the runtime compatibility issue and the preserved behavior.

experiences.title: Do not treat code-context browsing or installed-package execution as evidence of semantic completion
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when an agent has already inspected nearby or upstream code, or has executed validation against an installed, external, or system-wide package rather than the modified checkout, but the task requires preserving a behavioral contract, compatibility boundary, public API, migration semantics, or storage/deletion invariant that must be implemented in the modified source and validated against it—not merely localized or tested against a pre-existing installation that may already contain the target feature. The decisive observable is the file path prefix in visible commands: paths referencing installed-package directories (dist-packages, site-packages, or other system prefixes) indicate wrong-target validation even when the code being read is topically relevant to the task, while checkout-relative paths (e.g., src/...) indicate correct-target validation. Also retrieve when no visible patch has been written yet: investigation through file reading, reproduction scripts, or root-cause analysis is not evidence of a code fix, and reproduction output without a patch reflects the current codebase's behavior, not the agent's changes.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE trajectories across Python/TypeScript web frameworks, ORMs, parsers, storage layers, and database code where the visible steps show substantial file/function inspection around the suspected error site, but the remaining challenge is choosing the correct abstraction boundary and proving the required behavior. Also applies when the task environment contains both a modified checkout and an installed version of the same package: running code against the installed or externally fetched version—which may already have the target behavior—produces false-positive validation signals indistinguishable from genuine completion unless the execution target is verified. A version or file-path check showing a newer/different installed package than the target checkout is strong wrong-target evidence. The file path prefix in visible commands is the single most decisive observable for distinguishing correct-target from wrong-target validation: commands referencing installed-package paths (e.g., cat /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/.../module.py, grep -r ... /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/...) are wrong-target evidence even when the code being read is topically relevant to the task's serialization or behavioral contract; commands referencing checkout-relative paths (e.g., grep -n ... src/_pytest/reports.py, cat src/module/_version.py) are correct-target evidence. Version-checking commands against installed packages (e.g., pip show) are wrong-target evidence, not validation evidence. Misleading cases include agents that inspect adjacent methods, grep related symbols, or debug line indexes, then make a local/obvious patch without demonstrating the task-level contract; and agents that run reproduction or test scripts against an installed package, observe success, and treat it as validation when the modified source was never exercised. Additionally, when no patch is visible (no changed files, zero patch characters), judges must not award positive scores on code-fix rubrics for investigation alone, nor apply maximum negative penalties based on reproduction output that reflects the current codebase rather than the agent's modifications. Attempts to reproduce against the correct checkout that fail due to missing dependencies, import setup, or other environment issues should not be ranked below a clean success against a wrong-target installed package. Static reading of target-checkout source is not empirical validation, but it is still more aligned with the target than dynamic execution against an external already-fixed package. Close-looking exclusion: a trajectory that briefly checks the installed version or reads installed-package code to understand a version mismatch or behavioral contract, but then proceeds to work with the checked-out source, should not be penalized for the initial installed-package exploration. The key distinction is where validation and fix implementation happen, not where understanding happens. The original surrounding-code rubric can still be appropriate early in localization, especially when the agent is about to patch only the stack-trace line without checking callers/callees. It becomes weak or misleading after localization is already done, during patch-review or final-quality prediction, unless the trajectory also shows contract-specific reasoning and validation against the modified checkout. Abstain when no checkout/installed-package distinction exists, when execution target is not observable, or when the task is purely about code inspection or documentation without source modification.
experiences.experience:
The previous rubric rewarded looking beyond the immediate failing line. That is sound as an early debugging heuristic, but it overstates progress when the trajectory already contains code browsing and the real risk is a semantically wrong or incomplete fix. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent connected the inspected context to the task's invariant: what state must not be overwritten, which version boundary is compatible, which public attribute/API must be preserved across re-raises, which related queries can safely be combined, which writer/reader line indexes remain valid, or which collection behavior must remain non-regressed. Avoid the tempting criterion that repeated greps, sed output, history inspection, or surrounding-class inspection alone indicates correctness.

Critically, when empirical validation is present, verify that the execution target is the modified source tree, not an installed, external, or system-wide package. The file path prefix in visible commands is the single most decisive observable for this distinction. Commands that read or search installed-package paths—e.g., cat /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/.../remote.py, grep -r ... /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/...—are wrong-target evidence even when the code being examined is topically relevant to the task's serialization contract, round-trip behavior, or other source-level invariants. A trajectory that reads installed-package files and receives a maximum score on a source-level validation rubric has been misjudged: the file path prefix shows the agent examined the deployed artifact, not the codebase under change. Conversely, commands referencing checkout-relative paths—e.g., grep -n ... src/_pytest/reports.py, cat src/module/_version.py, sys.path.insert(0, 'src')—are correct-target evidence and should be scored higher than wrong-target exploration even when the wrong-target exploration produced a cleaner or more complete-looking result. Version-checking commands against installed packages (e.g., pip show) are wrong-target evidence, not validation evidence.

Visible evidence of correct targeting includes: cd into the checkout directory, sys.path or PYTHONPATH manipulation to prioritize local source, editable/local installation from the checkout root, explicit import from the local package path, file paths resolving inside the checkout (e.g., src/... prefixes), or running test scripts from within the modified tree. Visible evidence of wrong-target validation includes: installing the package by name from an external package source without a local path or editable flag, imports resolving to site-packages or a system prefix, reading or searching files under dist-packages/site-packages paths, a reported version newer or different from the target checkout or task context, pip show or similar version checks against installed packages treated as validation, or success observed without any source modification or local-source import. Running code against an installed package that already has the behavior is not evidence of completion; it is a false positive. A branch that tries to validate the target checkout but hits dependency/import/environment errors should usually be preferred over a branch that obtains a clean run from the wrong target, because the former is at least aimed at the code under change while the latter validates the wrong artifact. Static inspection of target-checkout files is weaker than targeted execution but should not be penalized below wrong-target dynamic success merely because the latter produced a clean result.

Close-looking exclusion: a trajectory that briefly checks the installed version (e.g., pip show) or reads installed-package code to understand a version mismatch or behavioral contract, but then proceeds to edit and validate against the checked-out source, should not be penalized for the initial installed-package exploration. Reading installed package code to understand a serialization contract is acceptable as supporting evidence, as long as the actual fix and validation target the checked-out source. The key distinction is where validation happens, not where understanding happens.

When sibling branches differ in diff/patch size or validation style, implementation-completeness and correct-target evidence should dominate over generic live-testing evidence unless the validation explicitly demonstrates that the modified code works. A rubric rewarding 'live testing' or 'source-level validation' without checking import path, working directory, local install mode, source-file path prefix, or version can reverse correct ordering by rewarding branches that only ran code against or read files from an installed package over branches that actually modified or analyzed the target source.

Additionally, a visible patch is the only reliable evidence that a code fix has been attempted. When no patch is visible—no changed files, zero patch characters, no diff content—reading source files, running reproduction scripts, and describing root causes are investigation, not modification. Reproduction output observed without a patch reflects the current codebase's behavior, not the agent's changes; it must not be treated as evidence that the agent has fixed the issue, nor as evidence that the agent's approach is insufficient. When no patch is visible, code-fix rubrics should receive neutral scores: the visible prefix cannot distinguish agents that will eventually produce a correct fix from those that will not. Do not award positive scores on fix-quality rubrics for investigation depth alone, and do not apply maximum negative penalties based on reproduction output that reflects the current codebase rather than the agent's modifications. An agent reading installed-package paths rather than the source tree under test is investigating the deployed code, not fixing the codebase under change.

Prioritize visible evidence that the agent: identifies the owner layer for the behavior, states the compatibility/edge cases, updates all affected call paths or APIs, adds or runs targeted regression checks against the modified checkout, verifies import/version/path targeting when executing code, and avoids broad local changes that merely silence the observed symptom. Preserve uncertainty: if the trajectory does not reveal whether execution used the modified checkout or an external installation, do not infer either success or failure from targeting alone; score only the observable implementation, reasoning, and validation evidence. When no patch is visible, preserve uncertainty rather than resolving it with extreme positive or negative scores.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Context inspection without contract validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where the agent has localized and inspected relevant surrounding code but continues to rely on that inspection as the main justification for a patch, without visibly satisfying the task-level behavioral contract or validating compatibility-sensitive cases against the modified checkout. This is especially relevant when the task describes preservation, migration, non-destructive loading, public error context, database version semantics, query grouping, or format read/write invariants, and the recent trajectory shows an obvious local edit, repeated source browsing, or ad hoc reproduction attempts rather than a contract-aware implementation plan and regression validation against the modified source.
