When no patch is visible, investigation alone should not receive positive scores on fix-quality rubrics; preserve uncertainty with neutral scores.

visible evidence to check: agent has already inspected nearby/upstream code or related classes
task requires a semantic invariant beyond fixing the immediate stack-trace line
patch plan or edits are localized to the first suspicious site without addressing all ownership/call-path boundaries
no targeted test or reproduction validates the stated invariant and compatibility cases against the modified checkout
recent steps show repetitive greps/debug prints or environment setup instead of closing the semantic gap
no visible patch has been written (changed_files empty, current_patch_chars is 0) — investigation is not modification

file path prefixes in visible commands reference installed-package directories (dist-packages, site-packages) rather than checkout-relative paths (src/...) — reading topically-relevant code from installed paths is still wrong-target investigation
metadata.source rubric boundary: Surrounding-code inspection remains useful only as an early localization rubric, not as a strong predictor once the unresolved question is semantic correctness. When no patch is visible, do not infer fix quality from investigation alone. The file path prefix in visible commands distinguishes whether investigation targets the checked-out source or the deployed artifact.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory both inspected context and tied the patch to the required invariant with targeted validation against the modified checkout or clear coverage of affected call paths.
scale.2: Minor evidence: some contract reasoning is present, but one secondary compatibility or validation point remains weak.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent inspected the right area and made plausible local changes, but validation and ownership-boundary reasoning are incomplete. When no patch is visible, this level applies: investigation is present but fix quality is unknown.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mostly consists of browsing or local symptom fixing, with little proof that the task-level invariant, public API, or compatibility behavior is preserved.
scale.5: Severe evidence: despite extensive surrounding-code inspection, the agent repeats searches or makes a narrow/fragile patch that ignores explicit preservation, migration, public-context, grouping, or read/write requirements and lacks meaningful regression validation. Do not apply this level when no patch is visible and the only evidence is investigation; preserve uncertainty instead.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrong-target installed-package validation as false-positive completion signal
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Strongly penalize trajectories where the agent runs reproduction scripts, tests, or validation code against an installed, external, or system-wide package rather than the modified checkout, especially when the installed version may already contain the target behavior. A clean run against the wrong target is not strongest evidence of bug verification or completion; it is misleading evidence and should be scored lower than an attempt to validate the correct checkout, even if the correct-target attempt encounters dependency, import, or environment errors. The file path prefix in visible commands is the decisive observable: reading or searching files under installed-package paths (e.g., /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/...) is wrong-target evidence even when the code being examined is topically relevant to the task's serialization contract or behavioral invariant. Version-checking commands against installed packages (e.g., pip show) are wrong-target evidence, not validation evidence. When sibling branches differ in implementation or validation evidence, correct-target implementation and validation should dominate unless the successful execution explicitly demonstrates that the modified code was exercised. When no patch is visible, reproduction output reflects the current codebase's behavior, not the agent's changes; do not treat successful reproduction as evidence of a fix, nor apply maximum negative penalties based on reproduction output that does not reflect the agent's modifications.

visible evidence to check: agent installs the package by name from an external package source without a local path or editable/local checkout mode
imports resolve to site-packages, a system prefix, or another path outside the modified checkout

experiences.title: Do not treat code-context browsing or installed-package execution as evidence of semantic completion
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when an agent has already inspected nearby or upstream code, or has executed validation against an installed, external, or system-wide package rather than the modified checkout, but the task requires preserving a behavioral contract, compatibility boundary, public API, migration semantics, or storage/deletion invariant that must be implemented in the modified source and validated against it—not merely localized or tested against a pre-existing installation that may already contain the target feature. Also retrieve when no visible patch has been written yet: investigation through file reading, reproduction scripts, or root-cause analysis is not evidence of a code fix, and reproduction output without a patch reflects the current codebase's behavior, not the agent's changes. Additionally retrieve when an agent discovers that an installed package shadows the testbed source on sys.path and takes corrective action—this is high-value diagnostic work that unblocks all subsequent correct-target validation and should be credited above running tests to green without a source patch.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE trajectories across Python/TypeScript web frameworks, ORMs, parsers, storage layers, and database code where the visible steps show substantial file/function inspection around the suspected error site, but the remaining challenge is choosing the correct abstraction boundary and proving the required behavior. Also applies when the task environment contains both a modified checkout and an installed version of the same package: running code against the installed or externally fetched version—which may already have the target behavior—produces false-positive validation signals indistinguishable from genuine completion unless the execution target is verified. A version or file-path check showing a newer/different installed package than the target checkout is strong wrong-target evidence. Misleading cases include agents that inspect adjacent methods, grep related symbols, or debug line indexes, then make a local/obvious patch without demonstrating the task-level contract; agents that run reproduction or test scripts against an installed package, observe success, and treat it as validation when the modified source was never exercised; and agents that run tests to green against the correct checkout but without any source patch, presenting existing-behavior pass output as progress. Additionally applies when an agent discovers package-location shadowing (e.g., via __file__ inspection, pip show, or PYTHONPATH checks) and corrects it (uninstall, path manipulation): this diagnostic work explains why other branches' test results may be misleading and unblocks all subsequent source-level development. When no patch is visible (no changed files, zero patch characters), judges must not award positive scores on code-fix rubrics for investigation alone, nor apply maximum negative penalties based on reproduction output that reflects the current codebase rather than the agent's modifications. However, environment-shadowing diagnosis and correction should be credited as high-value diagnostic work regardless of patch status, because it unblocks correct-target validation for all subsequent steps. Attempts to reproduce against the correct checkout that fail due to missing dependencies, import setup, or other environment issues should not be ranked below a clean success against a wrong-target installed package. Static reading of target-checkout source is not empirical validation, but it is still more aligned with the target than dynamic execution against an external already-fixed package. The original surrounding-code rubric can still be appropriate early in localization, especially when the agent is about to patch only the stack-trace line without checking callers/callees. It becomes weak or misleading after localization is already done, during patch-review or final-quality prediction, unless the trajectory also shows contract-specific reasoning and validation against the modified checkout. Abstain when no checkout/installed-package distinction exists, when execution target is not observable, or when the task is purely about code inspection or documentation without source modification.
experiences.experience:
The previous rubric rewarded looking beyond the immediate failing line. That is sound as an early debugging heuristic, but it overstates progress when the trajectory already contains code browsing and the real risk is a semantically wrong or incomplete fix. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent connected the inspected context to the task's invariant: what state must not be overwritten, which version boundary is compatible, which public attribute/API must be preserved across re-raises, which related queries can safely be combined, which writer/reader line indexes remain valid, or which collection behavior must remain non-regressed. Avoid the tempting criterion that repeated greps, sed output, history inspection, or surrounding-class inspection alone indicates correctness.

Critically, when empirical validation is present, verify that the execution target is the modified source tree, not an installed, external, or system-wide package. Visible evidence of correct targeting includes: cd into the checkout directory, sys.path or PYTHONPATH manipulation to prioritize local source, editable/local installation from the checkout root, explicit import from the local package path, file paths resolving inside the checkout, or running test scripts from within the modified tree. Visible evidence of wrong-target validation includes: installing the package by name from an external package source without a local path or editable flag, imports resolving to site-packages or a system prefix, a reported version newer or different from the target checkout or task context, or success observed without any source modification or local-source import. Running code against an installed package that already has the behavior is not evidence of completion; it is a false positive. A branch that tries to validate the target checkout but hits dependency/import/environment errors should usually be preferred over a branch that obtains a clean run from the wrong target, because the former is at least aimed at the code under change while the latter validates the wrong artifact. Static inspection of target-checkout files is weaker than targeted execution but should not be penalized below wrong-target dynamic success merely because the latter produced a clean result.

When sibling branches differ in diff/patch size or validation style, implementation-completeness and correct-target evidence should dominate over generic live-testing evidence unless the validation explicitly demonstrates that the modified code works. A rubric rewarding 'live testing' without checking import path, working directory, local install mode, source-file path, or version can reverse correct ordering by rewarding branches that only ran code against an installed package over branches that actually modified or analyzed the target source.

Additionally, a visible patch is the only reliable evidence that a code fix has been attempted. When no patch is visible—no changed files, zero patch characters, no diff content—reading source files, running reproduction scripts, and describing root causes are investigation, not modification. Reproduction output observed without a patch reflects the current codebase's behavior, not the agent's changes; it must not be treated as evidence that the agent has fixed the issue, nor as evidence that the agent's approach is insufficient. Running tests to green without a source patch, even against the correct checkout, is at best neutral—it validates existing behavior, not a fix. When no patch is visible, code-fix rubrics should receive neutral scores: the visible prefix cannot distinguish agents that will eventually produce a correct fix from those that will not. Do not award positive scores on fix-quality rubrics for investigation depth alone, and do not apply maximum negative penalties based on reproduction output that reflects the current codebase rather than the agent's modifications.

However, environment-shadowing diagnosis is a distinct positive signal that must be credited even without a source patch. When an agent discovers that an installed package shadows the testbed source on sys.path—via __file__ or __code__.co_filename inspection, pip show output, PYTHONPATH or sys.path checks—and takes corrective action such as pip uninstall, path manipulation, or explicit recognition that test results may be invalid, this is high-value diagnostic work that unblocks all subsequent correct-target validation. A continuation that diagnoses and corrects shadowing should be ranked above one that runs tests to green without a source patch, because the former unblocks all future work while the latter only validates existing behavior. The key discriminator is whether the agent has identified and addressed the root cause of wrong-target execution, not merely observed test output. Fixing an unrelated import error (e.g., a collections.abc migration) and then running pre-existing tests to green is environment hygiene, not issue resolution—especially when no target file was changed. But discovering that the installed package shadows the testbed and uninstalling it is critical root-cause diagnosis that explains why other continuations' test results may be misleading.

Prioritize visible evidence that the agent: identifies the owner layer for the behavior, states the compatibility/edge cases, updates all affected call paths or APIs, adds or runs targeted regression checks against the modified checkout, verifies import/version/path targeting when executing code, avoids broad local changes that merely silence the observed symptom, and—when encountering misleading test results—investigates whether package shadowing is the cause and takes corrective action. Preserve uncertainty: if the trajectory does not reveal whether execution used the modified checkout or an external installation, do not infer either success or failure from targeting alone; score only the observable implementation, reasoning, and validation evidence. When no patch is visible, preserve uncertainty rather than resolving it with extreme positive or negative scores—except that environment-shadowing diagnosis and correction should be credited as a positive signal regardless of patch status.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Context inspection without contract validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where the agent has localized and inspected relevant surrounding code but continues to rely on that inspection as the main justification for a patch, without visibly satisfying the task-level behavioral contract or validating compatibility-sensitive cases against the modified checkout. This is especially relevant when the task describes preservation, migration, non-destructive loading, public error context, database version semantics, query grouping, or format read/write invariants, and the recent trajectory shows an obvious local edit, repeated source browsing, or ad hoc reproduction attempts rather than a contract-aware implementation plan and regression validation against the modified source. When no patch is visible, investigation alone should not receive positive scores on fix-quality rubrics; preserve uncertainty with neutral scores. Running tests to green without a source patch, even against the correct checkout, is at best neutral—it validates existing behavior, not a fix—and should not be ranked above environment-shadowing diagnosis and correction.
