When no patch is visible at either the summary or command level, preserve uncertainty rather than resolving it with extreme positive or negative scores.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Context inspection without contract validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where the agent has localized and inspected relevant surrounding code but continues to rely on that inspection as the main justification for a patch, without visibly satisfying the task-level behavioral contract or validating compatibility-sensitive cases against the modified checkout. This is especially relevant when the task describes preservation, migration, non-destructive loading, public error context, database version semantics, query grouping, or format read/write invariants, and the recent trajectory shows an obvious local edit, repeated source browsing, or ad hoc reproduction attempts rather than a contract-aware implementation plan and regression validation against the modified source. When no patch is visible at either the summary or command level, investigation alone should not receive positive scores on fix-quality rubrics; preserve uncertainty with neutral scores. Patch visibility must be checked at the command and output level: file-modification commands (sed -i, python write scripts) with confirming output may not appear in changed_files or diff_stat summaries.

visible evidence to check: agent has already inspected nearby/upstream code or related classes
task requires a semantic invariant beyond fixing the immediate stack-trace line
patch plan or edits are localized to the first suspicious site without addressing all ownership/call-path boundaries
no targeted test or reproduction validates the stated invariant and compatibility cases against the modified checkout
recent steps show repetitive greps/debug prints or environment setup instead of closing the semantic gap

no visible patch at summary level (changed_files empty, current_patch_chars is 0) — but also check command level for sed -i, python write scripts, or other file-modification commands with confirming output
file-modification commands may not appear in changed_files or diff_stat summaries — read trajectory commands and outputs to detect actual patching
metadata.source rubric boundary: Surrounding-code inspection remains useful only as an early localization rubric, not as a strong predictor once the unresolved question is semantic correctness. When no patch is visible at either summary or command level, do not infer fix quality from investigation alone.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory both inspected context and tied the patch to the required invariant with targeted validation against the modified checkout or clear coverage of affected call paths.
scale.2: Minor evidence: some contract reasoning is present, but one secondary compatibility or validation point remains weak.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent inspected the right area and made plausible local changes, but validation and ownership-boundary reasoning are incomplete. When no patch is visible at either summary or command level, this level applies: investigation is present but fix quality is unknown.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mostly consists of browsing or local symptom fixing, with little proof that the task-level invariant, public API, or compatibility behavior is preserved.
scale.5: Severe evidence: despite extensive surrounding-code inspection, the agent repeats searches or makes a narrow/fragile patch that ignores explicit preservation, migration, public-context, grouping, or read/write requirements and lacks meaningful regression validation. Do not apply this level when no patch is visible at either summary or command level and the only evidence is investigation; preserve uncertainty instead.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrong-target installed-package validation as false-positive completion signal
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Strongly penalize trajectories where the agent runs reproduction scripts, tests, or validation code against an installed, external, or system-wide package rather than the modified checkout, especially when the installed version may already contain the target behavior. A clean run against the wrong target is not strongest evidence of bug verification or completion; it is misleading evidence and should be scored lower than an attempt to validate the correct checkout, even if the correct-target attempt encounters dependency, import, or environment errors. When sibling branches differ in implementation or validation evidence, correct-target implementation and validation should dominate unless the successful execution explicitly demonstrates that the modified code was exercised. When no patch is visible at either summary or command level, reproduction output reflects the current codebase's behavior, not the agent's changes; do not treat successful reproduction as evidence of a fix, nor apply maximum negative penalties based on reproduction output that does not reflect the agent's modifications. Additionally, even when validation targets the correct checkout, the testbed may already produce the target behavior for some inputs without any patch, so correct-looking test output alone is not sufficient evidence of a fix—patch visibility at the command level is the primary signal.

visible evidence to check: agent installs the package by name from an external package source without a local path or editable/local checkout mode
imports resolve to site-packages, a system prefix, or another path outside the modified checkout
a version check reports a version newer than, different from, or incompatible with the target checkout or task context
success is observed without verifying that the modified source was imported or executed
diff/patch is zero or minimal at summary level while validation success comes only from the installed/external package
a sibling branch that targets the checkout but has setup errors is being ranked below a wrong-target clean run
reproduction output when no patch is visible reflects the current codebase, not the agent's changes — do not infer fix quality from it
agent reads from installed-package paths rather than the source tree under test — this investigates the deployed code, not the codebase to be fixed
testbed may already produce target behavior for some inputs without any patch — even correct-target test output can be a false positive when no patch is visible
test scripts may encode wrong expectations — test output showing unexpected forms does not necessarily mean a visible patch is incorrect
metadata.contraindication: Do not apply when no checkout/installed-package distinction exists, when validation explicitly targets the modified checkout via working directory, local/editable install, sys.path/PYTHONPATH, local import path, or source-file path, or when the execution target is genuinely unobservable.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: validation explicitly targets the modified checkout, or no empirical validation was attempted so wrong-target execution does not apply.
scale.2: Minor evidence: validation targeting is somewhat ambiguous, but there is some visible evidence of local checkout use.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: validation ran and targeting is unclear, or execution mixed local and installed sources without proving the modified code was exercised. When no patch is visible, reproduction output reflects the current codebase; do not escalate beyond this level based on reproduction alone. Even with correct targeting, if the testbed may already produce the target behavior without a patch, do not treat correct-looking output as strong completion evidence.
scale.4: Clear evidence: validation ran against an installed/external/system package, success was treated as completion evidence, and no local-source targeting was verified.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory obtains clean success from an installed/external package that appears newer, different, or already fixed, while the modified checkout is not exercised; this should rank below correct-target attempts even when those attempts hit setup errors.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Target-checkout reproduction and validation evidence
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Reward empirical reproduction or regression validation only when visible evidence shows the modified checkout is the execution target and a patch has been written. Correct-target setup attempts retain value even if they fail for dependency, import, or environment reasons, because they demonstrate attention to validating the code under change rather than an external already-fixed package. Static source exploration of the target checkout is weaker than successful execution but is still aligned with the target and should not be outweighed by wrong-target dynamic success. When no patch is visible at either summary or command level, reproduction output reflects the current codebase's behavior, not the agent's changes; do not award strong validation credit for reproduction alone without a visible patch. Patch visibility must be checked at the command and output level: file-modification commands (sed -i, python write scripts) with confirming output may not appear in changed_files or diff_stat summaries. Even with correct targeting and a visible patch, test output can be misleading if the testbed already produces the target behavior for some inputs or if test scripts encode wrong expectations; a branch with a visible patch should not be scored zero merely because a test run shows unexpected output.

visible evidence to check: working directory is the modified checkout or test scripts are launched from inside it
PYTHONPATH/sys.path prioritizes the checkout source directory
editable or local installation is run from the checkout root
imports or source-file paths resolve inside the checkout
reported version matches the target checkout or task context
failed execution is due to setup/dependency/import errors after attempting to target the checkout rather than because an external package was used

a visible patch exists at summary level (changed_files non-empty, current_patch_chars > 0) OR at command level (sed -i, python write scripts with confirming output like 'modified successfully') before reproduction output is treated as validation of the agent's changes
file-modification commands may not appear in changed_files or diff_stat summaries — read trajectory commands and outputs to detect actual patching
testbed may already produce target behavior for some inputs without any patch — correct-looking test output alone is not sufficient evidence of a fix
test scripts may encode wrong expectations — unexpected test output does not necessarily invalidate a visible patch
metadata.uncertainty boundary: If visible evidence does not reveal the execution target, do not award strong target-checkout validation credit; score the rest of the trajectory on observable implementation and reasoning. When no patch is visible at either summary or command level, reproduction output reflects the current codebase, not the agent's changes; preserve uncertainty with neutral scores rather than inferring fix quality. When a patch is visible but post-patch validation is absent or ambiguous, preserve uncertainty about whether the fix works.

scale.1: No target-checkout validation evidence: no reproduction/validation is attempted, the execution target is unobservable, or no patch is visible at either summary or command level so reproduction output reflects the current codebase rather than the agent's changes.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent appears to intend local validation but targeting proof is incomplete, or no patch is visible yet but investigation targets the correct checkout.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: local targeting is plausible or partially shown, but validation fails before exercising the key behavior or lacks version/path confirmation. A visible patch exists at command level but post-patch validation is ambiguous or uses potentially wrong expectations, leaving fix correctness uncertain.
scale.4: Strong evidence: reproduction or tests visibly run against the modified checkout and cover the main behavior, with a visible patch at summary or command level, though some secondary compatibility cases remain untested.
scale.5: Very strong evidence: targeted reproduction/regression checks visibly run against the modified checkout, import/version/path evidence is clear, a visible patch at summary or command level exercises the changed code, and the checked behavior maps directly to the task-level invariant. Post-patch validation confirms the expected behavior and covers edge cases.

experiences.title: Task-Relevant Objective Verification After Risky Edits
experiences.description: Retrieve when an agent has already made code changes—especially broad refactors, API migrations, generated rewrites, fragile search/replace edits, or other modification-heavy work—and the next useful rubric should judge whether it grounded completion in visible patch content plus meaningful pass/fail validation, read the results, and corrected or credibly isolated failures before stopping.
experiences.context: Applies in software-repair trajectories across Go, Python, TypeScript/React, and similar codebases when visible work has moved beyond exploration into implementation or final review. It is most relevant after multi-file edits, removed/renamed APIs, import/type-sensitive changes, parser/formatter behavior changes, build-system/version updates, or any trajectory with failed sed/script edits, wholesale rewrites, suspicious diffs, or claims that a change is complete. It is less applicable during pure investigation before a patch exists, and it should not replace a semantic task-specific rubric when the visible patch is small and clearly addresses the issue. The criterion should distinguish strong task-relevant validation from weak proxies: agent self-assessment, grep-only cleanup, syntax-only checks, or a narrow compile of one file may be useful evidence but should not be treated as proof that the intended behavior, integration, or changed code is correct. When the visible record does not show the patch or the test outcome clearly, preserve uncertainty rather than assuming success or failure.
experiences.experience:
The recurring useful rubric in these cases asks whether the agent grounded its final confidence in observable evidence: visible changed content that plausibly implements the intended modification, followed by task-relevant objective validation with a clear pass/fail result, and iteration on any relevant failures. This is valuable when the trajectory shows risky edits because lack of validation leaves observable hazards such as stale imports, malformed loops, untested API signature changes, untouched call sites, accidental broad diffs, or failed commands that were not followed by a corrective run.

A better rubric should make the evidence hierarchy explicit. Strong positive evidence includes a visible diff or file content showing the relevant change, plus unit tests, targeted integration tests, typecheck/build, lint/format, or an executable reproduction that directly exercises the reported behavior or affected integration points. A project’s real test runner reporting a clear pass for relevant tests is strong validation evidence, even if separate exploratory commands or custom scripts also failed for setup, path, or dependency reasons. Those failed attempts should reduce confidence only when they are the only validation or when their output directly demonstrates the changed behavior is broken.

Weak or insufficient evidence includes the agent saying the patch looks correct, an empty or absent diff despite claims of success, grep-only searches for old names, syntax-only checks that would also pass with no behavioral change, custom scripts that never reach the code under test, test commands aimed at non-existent or unrelated paths, or failed validation whose output is ignored. Syntax and compile checks can support a score but should not justify maximum credit by themselves after a behavioral or integration-sensitive edit. Conversely, do not assign the lowest score when there is visible passing output from a relevant real test runner; map that as positive evidence while preserving any remaining uncertainty about patch content or coverage.

When generating or applying a rubric from this experience, keep the polarity positive and weight the decisive distinction toward confirmed patch-and-validation evidence rather than confidence statements. Maximum credit should normally require both visible implementation evidence and relevant passing validation, or a clearly justified equivalent when direct tests are impractical. Middle scores should capture partial evidence: visible patch with only syntax checks, relevant tests attempted but inconclusive, or passing tests with ambiguous patch visibility. Low scores should be reserved for no visible implementation evidence and no successful relevant validation, especially when completion rests on self-assessment. Do not over-apply this as a universal demand to run the entire suite in early exploration or when no implementation has been attempted. Prioritize visible command output, exit status, whether the check matches the task behavior and changed files, whether subsequent edits respond to observed results, and whether uncertainty is explicitly preserved when the evidence is incomplete.

experiences.title: Contract-Level Behavioral Test Evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an agent claims validation through added tests, changed expected outputs, or ad hoc scripts for a behavior-specific bug or feature; judge whether those tests assert the actual user-visible contract — including the exact set of produced values when the fix changes what is yielded or returned — rather than merely exercising code paths, confirming aggregate statistics match, using inspection methods that require error-prone manual resolution, or relying on self-reported success and submission status without examining the actual scope of visible test commands. An agent that submits after only the basic reported reproduction case passes has not demonstrated the full contract when the task requires edge-case or chain-semantic coverage.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent trajectories across Python, Go, and TypeScript repositories after the agent has identified a fix and is using tests or manual scripts as confidence evidence. It is most relevant for tasks involving parsing metadata, fallback ordering, event-driven UI updates, set/membership semantics, deterministic selection, API parameter precedence, signal or callback registration, yield/return logic, or multi-step lookup chains where a patch can look plausible while missing a boundary condition. It is less decisive during early exploration, when no implementation exists yet, or for very small localized source fixes whose correctness is directly visible from the changed line and no durable test has been added. Do not retrieve it merely because no formal test was run; absence of tests alone is not a reliable flaw for simple one-line compatibility fixes. Do retrieve it when tests are present but may be superficial, omitted from the submitted diff, only check that code runs, update expectations to match an incorrect intermediate representation, rely on aggregate statistics (e.g., matching copied/processed counts) that can be satisfied by wrong fixes which skip or duplicate items, use inspection methods that require manual intermediate resolution (e.g., iterating raw internal data structures needing dereferencing or key matching) where false negatives or false positives can occur, or cover only the basic reported reproduction case while the contract requires edge-case or chain-semantic coverage. Abstain from the aggregate-statistics criterion when the fix does not modify what is produced (yielded, returned, emitted output), or when the exact output cannot be observed from the visible prefix and only aggregate statistics are available. Abstain from the methodology-quality criterion when no validation or inspection activity is visible in the trajectory prefix. Abstain from the simple-case-only criterion when the task's contract does not extend beyond the reported reproduction case.
experiences.experience: The prior rubric judged whether validation was meaningful. It was useful when visible test activity revealed whether the agent understood the behavioral contract: strong evidence came from tests that exercised the exact reported scenario, asserted the final observable result, and included important branches such as missing data, fallback paths, resize/update events, explicit override versus default behavior, or deterministic ordering. It correctly flagged trajectories where the agent relied on smoke scripts, repeated commands, changed expected values without checking the real semantic object, or added tests that did not cover the required fallback/edge case. However, it can be misleading if used as a blanket requirement: a tiny, obvious formatting or parameter-default fix may be correct even with weak or no committed tests. A better retrieved rubric should focus on the quality and relevance of the validation evidence, not on the mere presence, count, or passing status of tests. Avoid the tempting criterion 'tests pass, therefore patch is good' or 'no tests, therefore patch is bad.' Prioritize visible evidence that tests would fail on the original bug, assert the user-facing contract exactly, cover the boundary cases named in the task, and are actually part of the patch or otherwise reproducible from the trajectory. When a fix modifies what is produced (yielded, returned, emitted output), matching aggregate statistics — such as 'N files copied, N post-processed' or 'N items returned' — can be a false proxy: a wrong fix that skips or omits items can still produce matching counts. The discriminating evidence is whether each expected item appears exactly once in the output with its correct final value, not whether aggregate counts match. Prefer evidence that enumerates the exact output set (e.g., listing each yielded item with its final value) over evidence that only checks aggregate counts or command success. This distinction is critical because wrong fixes that eliminate duplicates by skipping yields, or that omit failing items, can produce the same aggregate counts as correct fixes that process each item exactly once. Additionally, when an agent uses an inspection method that requires manual intermediate resolution — iterating raw internal data structures that need dereferencing, key matching, or format conversion — the validation output can be actively misleading. False negatives (printing 'not found' or 'not connected' when the behavior is correct) or false positives (appearing to confirm a fix while checking the wrong thing) can arise from error-prone manual steps. The discriminating evidence is whether the agent used a method or API that directly resolves the semantic question — a purpose-built inspection function that returns resolved, specific results — rather than one requiring manual dereferencing or key matching that agents frequently get wrong. Do not treat raw internal-structure iteration as equivalent to purpose-built inspection APIs when the former requires manual steps that produce misleading output. This methodology-quality dimension is distinct from both 'tests pass therefore good' and 'aggregate counts match therefore good': even when an agent appears to inspect the right thing, the wrong inspection method can yield evidence that looks thorough while being actively wrong. Furthermore, an agent's self-reported success message, patch diff presence, or submission status must not be treated as primary evidence of contract completion. The judge must read the actual test commands visible in the trajectory and assess their scope: if they only cover the basic reported reproduction case while the task's contract requires edge-case, chain-semantic, or cross-component coverage, the score must reflect incomplete contract coverage regardless of the agent's confidence statement. A continuation that submits after only the simple case passes should not be ranked above continuations that show active investigation of edge cases or existing test-suite failures, even if the latter have not yet submitted. The discriminating evidence is the scope and results of visible test commands — whether they cover the full contract or only the simple case — not the agent's declaration of success. This dimension is distinct from the aggregate-statistics and inspection-methodology dimensions: even when tests appear to pass and the agent claims completion, the test scope may be insufficient if it omits the edge cases the contract requires. A single rubric evaluating contract coverage, inspection methodology quality, and test-scope adequacy is more discriminative than multiple rubrics that each check whether validation was attempted.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Meaningful Contract Validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the agent's validation evidence demonstrates the intended behavioral contract, not just code execution, aggregate statistics, inspection methods that produce misleading results, or self-reported success without adequate test scope. High-quality evidence includes committed or clearly described tests/manual checks that reproduce the reported issue, assert the exact user-visible expected result, cover named edge cases and fallback/update paths, use a method or API that directly resolves the semantic question rather than requiring error-prone manual intermediate steps, and would distinguish the proposed fix from common wrong implementations. When the fix modifies what is produced (yielded, returned, emitted output), the evidence should enumerate the exact output set — each item appearing exactly once with its correct final value — rather than relying on aggregate counts that can be satisfied by wrong fixes which skip or duplicate items. When the task's contract extends beyond the simple reported case, the evidence should cover the full scope including edge cases, chain semantics, or cross-component propagation, not just the basic reproduction. This rubric should be applied relative to the current trajectory: look only at visible task requirements, test diffs, commands run, outputs observed, and whether validation artifacts are included or durable. Do not use the agent's self-reported success message, patch diff presence, or submission status as primary signals of contract completion; prioritize the scope and results of visible test commands.

prioritize_evidence: tests or scripts reproduce the specific reported behavior
assertions check exact semantic outputs or state changes, not merely absence of crashes
when the fix changes what is produced, assertions enumerate the exact output set — each item appears exactly once with its correct final value — not just matching aggregate counts

validation uses a method or API that directly resolves the semantic question rather than requiring error-prone manual intermediate steps (e.g., raw internal-structure iteration with manual dereferencing or key matching)

coverage includes task-specified boundaries such as fallback order, missing data, update events, deterministic selection, membership semantics, signal or callback registration, explicit override behavior, or chain-semantic edge cases beyond the simple reported case
test commands cover the full contract scope, not just the basic reported reproduction case, when the task requires edge-case or chain-semantic coverage
validation artifacts are committed or clearly part of the final patch when appropriate
test output confirms the relevant tests actually ran rather than being skipped or unmatched
deprioritize_evidence: test count or broad suite pass status without relevant assertions
aggregate statistics (e.g., matching copied/processed counts) that can be satisfied by wrong fixes which skip or duplicate items, when the fix changes what is produced
inspection methods that require manual resolution steps where false negatives or false positives can occur, producing misleading evidence that appears thorough
raw internal-structure iteration treated as equivalent to purpose-built inspection APIs when the former requires manual dereferencing or key matching
agent's self-reported success message, patch diff presence, or submission status without examining the actual scope of visible test commands
test commands that only cover the basic reported reproduction case when the task's contract requires edge-case, chain-semantic, or cross-component coverage
manual scripts that only print values or check a superficial substring
updated expected values that mirror the implementation without checking the requested behavior
absence of tests for a trivial source-level fix whose correctness is directly inspectable
dependency installation or test infrastructure setup as validation evidence
metadata.applicability_stage: post-implementation or final-review stage, especially when the agent cites validation as confidence
metadata.abstain_when: the fix does not modify what is produced (yielded, returned, output), or the exact output cannot be observed from the visible prefix and only aggregate statistics are available; or when no validation or inspection activity is visible in the trajectory prefix; or when the task's contract does not extend beyond the simple reported reproduction case

scale.1: No meaningful behavioral validation is visible, or the agent only ran commands that do not exercise the reported scenario; any tests are absent, skipped, unrelated, or merely confirm the code imports/runs.
scale.2: Weak validation exists but is superficial: it checks a narrow implementation detail, printed output, a happy path, or aggregate statistics that could be satisfied by wrong fixes, while omitting the core behavior or task-specified boundaries; or it uses an inspection method that requires error-prone manual intermediate steps (e.g., raw internal-structure iteration with manual dereferencing) and produces misleading results such as false negatives or false positives; or it covers only the basic reported reproduction case and claims success without testing the edge cases or chain semantics the contract requires.
scale.3: Validation is comparable to the parent trajectory: some relevant behavior is exercised, but important edge cases, fallback/update semantics, exact assertions, exact output enumeration, or chain-semantic coverage are incomplete or not clearly committed; or the inspection method used is ambiguous — output is truncated, the API is unclear, or the method requires manual steps whose correctness cannot be verified from the visible prefix.
scale.4: Strong validation directly covers the reported scenario and at least one important boundary condition, with assertions on observable behavior (including exact output enumeration when the fix changes what is produced), uses a method or API that directly resolves the semantic question rather than requiring error-prone manual intermediate steps, and shows evidence that the relevant tests ran.
scale.5: Excellent validation would fail on the original bug and distinguishes the fix from likely wrong implementations; it asserts the exact user contract, includes all task-critical branches and edge cases beyond the simple reported case, enumerates the exact output set when the fix changes what is produced, uses a purpose-built inspection method that directly resolves the semantic question with comprehensive configuration coverage, is durable in the patch, and the trajectory shows the targeted tests actually executed.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Simple-Case Submission Without Edge-Case or Chain-Semantic Coverage
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize agents that claim completion and submit after validating only the basic reported reproduction case while the task's behavioral contract requires preserving semantics for more complex cases such as nested lookups, mixed array-index and object-key paths, cross-component propagation, or other edge cases beyond the simple scenario. The judge must read the actual test commands visible in the trajectory and assess their scope, not just the final success or submission message. An agent that submits after only the simple case passes should not be ranked above agents that show active investigation of the edge cases or existing test-suite failures, even if the latter have not yet submitted. Do not use the agent's self-reported success, the presence of a patch diff, or submission status as primary signals of contract completion.

visible_evidence_to_check: test commands only cover the basic reported case from the issue description
no edge-case, chain-semantic, or nested-path tests visible in the trajectory
no existing test-suite execution visible
agent declares success or complete and submits without edge-case evidence
other trajectories in the same batch show edge-case or chain tests failing or being debugged
preferred_evidence: edge-case or chain-specific test commands and their results
existing test-suite execution showing pass or fail status
awareness of path semantics or multi-step lookup behavior in code comments or reasoning
debugging output showing the simple fix breaks nested or edge-case paths
do_not_use_as_primary_signal: agent confidence statement or success message
patch diff presence alone without test scope evidence
submission or finished status without examining test coverage
metadata.close_looking_exclusion: Do not penalize an agent that is still in progress and has not yet reached edge-case testing, as long as it has not falsely claimed completion. The flaw is claiming completion with only simple-case evidence, not merely being early in the trajectory. Also do not penalize an agent that shows edge-case tests passing alongside the simple case.
metadata.abstention_boundary: If the visible prefix is too short to determine whether edge-case testing was performed or whether the agent is still progressing toward it, do not assume either coverage or its absence; score at mid-scale and note the uncertainty. Also abstain when the task's contract does not extend beyond the simple reported reproduction case.

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the agent validates both the simple case and the edge cases or chain semantics required by the contract, or the visible prefix is too short to assess and the judge abstains.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent tests the simple case and mentions edge cases but does not run edge-case-specific tests before submitting.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent tests only the simple reported case, claims success, and submits, with no visible edge-case or test-suite validation despite the contract requiring it.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent submits with high confidence after only the basic reproduction passes, while the contract explicitly requires edge-case or chain-semantic coverage, and other trajectories show the simple fix breaks edge-case semantics.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the agent's simple-case fix is known to break edge cases, yet it declares the fix complete and submits, and the judge ranks it above trajectories actively debugging the edge-case breakage.

experiences.title: Descriptor detection alone is not enough for class-property autodoc fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Sphinx autodoc trajectories involving `@classmethod @property` members, especially when the agent focuses on raw descriptor detection, `__func__` unwrapping, Python-version descriptor behavior, or any single diagnostic branch of the autodoc pipeline. The rubric must require multiple resolving branches as conjunctive visible evidence so that satisfying one branch alone cannot tie at the maximum.
experiences.context: Applies in the Sphinx autodoc/autosummary environment for a bug where class members decorated as `@classmethod` over `@property` are omitted or documented with the wrong docstring. A common misleading rubric rewards the agent for noticing that the raw class dictionary contains `classmethod(<property ...>)` and that the wrapped property is reachable through `.__func__`. That observation is useful during early investigation and can be a valid progress criterion before edits exist. It becomes insufficient or misleading at implementation/final-review stages, because successful documentation requires the full autodoc pipeline to preserve the raw descriptor, select the property documenter, import/replace the object with the underlying property for documentation, retrieve the original property docstring using the correct class/member context, emit the class-property marker in the directive, and avoid unrelated compatibility edits. A recurring failure mode is that a rubric's top scale is satisfied by a single correct diagnostic insight — e.g., descriptor detection or `__func__` unwrapping — while the trajectory never touches the documenter pipeline or confirms generated output, letting incomplete trajectories tie at the maximum with only one resolving branch. The original detection-focused idea may still apply when the visible trajectory has only explored root cause; it should not be used as a primary correctness predictor once the agent has edited helper predicates, documenter logic, or version checks without demonstrating end-to-end generated documentation.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often asked whether the trajectory detected `classmethod` or `staticmethod` wrapping a `property` and extracted metadata from `.__func__`/`fget`. That criterion was too narrow: agents could satisfy it while still leaving autodoc to call normal `getattr()`, use the returned value's docstring, fail to set a classmethod/property directive option, omit inherited-docstring lookup through the owning class and member name, or make broad helper/version changes unrelated to the reported behavior. For this task shape, avoid a tempting criterion that treats `inspect.isproperty(classmethod_obj)` or generic descriptor unwrapping as the fix. Also avoid rewarding Python version checks or `staticmethod` expansion unless the trajectory ties them to the requested behavior and tests. A better rubric must require multiple resolving branches as conjunctive visible evidence: (1) raw descriptor preservation from the defining class via class-dictionary or MRO lookup rather than evaluated attribute access; (2) classification as a property only for `classmethod` wrapping a property, with the property documenter handling import/object replacement; (3) correct docstring/abstract/type-hint retrieval from the property/fget using the owning class and member name; (4) emission and domain support for a class-property marker in the directive; and (5) validation through actual autodoc output or targeted regression tests showing the expected docstring. No single branch should be sufficient to reach the top scale: a trajectory that demonstrates descriptor detection and some documenter logic but lacks output confirmation, or that confirms output without touching the documenter pipeline, should land in the middle of the scale, not at the maximum. This prevents incomplete trajectories from tying at the top with only one resolving branch. Abstention boundary: preserve uncertainty (do not assign the maximum) when the visible prefix shows only partial branches — e.g., detection without documenter code examination, documenter edits without rendered-output confirmation, or a regression test that does not distinguish the property getter's docstring from the returned object's docstring.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete end-to-end class-property autodoc handling
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that stop at or primarily implement a single resolving branch for `@classmethod @property` members without showing that the complete autodoc path documents the original property correctly. The rubric requires multiple resolving branches conjunctively: descriptor preservation, property documenter import/replacement, docstring retrieval, class-property directive output, and generated documentation confirmation. No single branch — not descriptor detection, not `__func__` unwrapping, not version checks, not standalone output inspection — should be sufficient to reach the top scale (score 1 = no flaw). This flaw is present when visible evidence shows the agent only expands property/classmethod detection, unwraps `.__func__` locally, patches unrelated Python-version compatibility, or confirms output without touching the documenter pipeline, while lacking evidence across the remaining branches.

metadata.environment: Sphinx autodoc/autosummary; Python descriptor behavior for classmethod wrapping property
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Crediting any single diagnostic branch — descriptor detection, `__func__` unwrapping, `isproperty` broadening, version checks, or standalone output inspection — as sufficient evidence without the full conjunctive set of resolving branches
preferred_visible_evidence: raw class-dictionary descriptor or defining-class MRO lookup is used instead of evaluated attribute access (branch 1)
property documenter handles import/object replacement and records classmethod status (branch 2)
docstring lookup uses the owning class and member name and reaches the underlying property/getter (branch 3)
generated directive/domain output can represent a class property, including abstract variants when relevant (branch 4)
targeted test or documentation build confirms the class property appears with the intended docstring (branch 5)
multiple branches are visible conjunctively, not just one in isolation

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory demonstrates all five resolving branches — descriptor preservation, property documenter import/unwrapping, docstring retrieval, class-property directive output, and generated documentation content confirmed via test or build output. No single branch alone reaches this level.
scale.2: Minor evidence of incompleteness: four of five branches are addressed, but one secondary aspect such as directive display or abstract/property metadata remains only lightly evidenced. The trajectory is clearly more than a single diagnostic branch but is not fully conjunctive.
scale.3: Moderate incompleteness: the trajectory handles two or three branches — typically detection and some documenter logic — but visible evidence is missing for either correct docstring retrieval, class-property directive support, or an actual autodoc output/regression test. A single diagnostic insight plus one implementation step lands here, not at the top.
scale.4: Clear incompleteness: the trajectory mainly changes one branch — helper predicates or local unwrapping logic — and does not show that member discovery/import avoids evaluated attribute access or that generated documentation uses the original property docstring. Satisfying descriptor detection alone lands here at best.
scale.5: Most severe incompleteness: the trajectory rewards or implements unrelated version/staticmethod/helper changes, or the visible output still shows the returned object's docstring/metadata instead of the class-property getter's documentation. No resolving branch is meaningfully demonstrated.

experiences.title: Do not reward read-only exploration, fallback behavior, or test-activity masking patch destruction after the key contract is already known
experiences.description: Use this warning when a trajectory contains many safe read commands, but the task's success depends on applying a specific integration contract, lifecycle transition, owner/container boundary, or compatibility case rather than merely avoiding premature writes. Also use this warning when the rubric portfolio risks displacing a directly stated implementation contract by rewarding the fallback or alternative behavior the task explicitly says to replace. Also use this warning when a continuation reverts or destroys an already-applied implementation patch (e.g., restoring a backup copy, checking out the original file) and the rubric portfolio risks masking that destruction by rewarding test-exploration, diagnostic output, or pattern-matching criteria. Light exception: when every visible continuation is still pre-patch with no source diff or changed files, use a gated diagnosis-quality rubric to distinguish mechanism-level debugging and correct-contract identification from empty exploration or pursuit of the old/fallback behavior instead of applying only fix-validation or command-hygiene criteria.
experiences.context:
Applies in SWE-agent code-repair trajectories across TypeScript/React, Go, Python, and similar codebases where the recent evidence is mostly grep/cat/sed, file inspection, reproduction scripts, debug output, or other non-mutating investigation. The misleading case is when normal or repetitive read-before-write behavior looks disciplined even though the agent has already identified the relevant files/APIs, is looping on similar searches, has not made task-specific progress, or is about to implement from a superficial understanding. The original read-before-write rubric may still be appropriate very early in exploration, especially when the agent is considering broad or destructive edits before locating the relevant component, tests, or API contract. It is not a strong correctness signal once the visible trajectory already contains enough file-local context and the remaining risk is semantic integration.

A second misleading case arises when the task statement directly specifies an implementation contract—e.g., a method should return an existing value instead of generating a derived one—and the rubric portfolio displaces that contract by rewarding the old/fallback behavior or by broadening into adjacent concerns. This is especially dangerous because the fallback behavior may look plausible and well-tested, yet it is precisely what the task asks to remove.

A third misleading case arises in the validation phase after an implementation patch has been applied: a continuation may revert the patch by restoring a backup copy or checking out the original file, destroying the implementation contract entirely. If the rubric portfolio includes test-validation or pattern-matching criteria, it may score this patch-reverting continuation alongside or above continuations that preserve the patch and take constructive steps such as configuring the environment to enable test execution. This is especially dangerous because test-exploration activity and diagnostic output look like progress, yet the implementation has been destroyed. Patch destruction is an all-or-nothing negative signal: no volume of test activity, diagnostic output, or pattern-matching compensates for reverting the implementation.

Stage guard: if all or nearly all visible continuations have no source edits or diff and are focused on reproduction, debugging, source inspection, or root-cause analysis, do not collapse the portfolio into fix-validation rubrics that can only score implemented changes. In that narrow pre-patch view, add a positive diagnosis rubric that rewards causal, mechanism-level evidence and correct-contract identification. This exception does not reward read-only behavior by volume; it rewards demonstrated understanding of the failure mechanism, its likely code boundary, and the specific replacement the task requires. If any continuation has begun implementing a source change, or if the visible population is mixed, preserve the parent warning and prefer rubrics that can evaluate task-specific implementation/integration evidence while giving only appropriate partial credit for diagnosis.
experiences.experience:
The previous rubric judged the presence of non-destructive exploration before writes. That is useful as a safety/process check, but it overemphasizes command hygiene in tasks where correctness hinges on domain behavior: using the existing service instead of bypassing it, clearing owned state rather than only stopping an object, updating the right lifecycle entry point, preserving compatibility fallbacks, or applying a state/filter contract with the action's intent. A better rubric should ask whether the agent has converted exploration into task-specific evidence and implementation choices. Avoid the tempting criterion of counting grep/cat/sed commands as positive progress. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent inspected the exact owner API or reusable service named by the discovered code path; stopped repeating identical searches after finding the relevant facts; planned or made edits at the lifecycle boundary where the bug occurs; accounted for compatibility or parent/owner context mentioned in the task; and added or targeted tests for the described behavior.

Recurring rubric error to prohibit: when the task directly states an implementation contract—replace behavior A with behavior B—the rubric portfolio must not displace that contract by rewarding A (the fallback/old behavior) or by broadening into adjacent but unrelated concerns. Visible evidence that should activate this correction: the task text names a specific method, property, or code path and says it should use a different value or path; the rubric portfolio includes criteria that give credit to the old/fallback behavior, to preserving generated or derived values the task says to remove, or to adjacent but unrelated concerns; and candidates that implement the correct replacement are not distinguished from or are scored below candidates that keep the old behavior. The correction is to align the implementation rubric narrowly on the stated replacement, explicitly prohibit credit for the old/fallback behavior, and ensure the trajectory-evidence rubric rewards identification of the correct contract over pursuit of the fallback. The rubric should accept any implementation that achieves the stated contract, not just one exact code pattern, while still prohibiting the old/fallback behavior.

Second recurring rubric error to prohibit: when a continuation reverts or destroys an already-applied implementation patch—by restoring a backup copy, checking out the original file, or otherwise undoing the source change—the rubric portfolio must not mask that destruction by rewarding test-exploration, diagnostic output, or pattern-matching criteria. Patch destruction is a critical negative signal that must dominate the score regardless of preceding or surrounding test activity. Visible evidence that should activate this correction: a continuation contains an explicit reversion command (e.g., copying a backup file over the source, checking out the modified file from version control); the rubric portfolio includes criteria that give credit for test diagnostics, query capture, or pattern-matching without checking whether the patch is still intact; and candidates that preserve the patch and take constructive environment-setup steps are scored below candidates that revert the patch but show partial test output. The correction is to treat patch destruction as a floor-level negative signal, explicitly prohibit test-activity or diagnostic-output criteria from compensating for patch destruction, and ensure that constructive environment-setup actions preserving the patch are credited at least as highly as partial test diagnostics. A continuation that reverts the patch must receive the lowest score regardless of any test-exploration or diagnostic activity in preceding steps. A continuation that takes constructive environment-setup steps to enable test infrastructure while preserving the patch should not be outranked by continuations showing only partial test diagnostics.

Small gated addition for pre-patch diagnosis rounds: when no continuation has produced a source change, a useful rubric can be positive rather than negative, but only if it measures diagnosis quality and contract identification. The decisive observable distinction should be: reproduction plus causal tracing plus localization to the responsible code path plus identification of the correct replacement, not reproduction alone and not generic file reading. High scores require the agent to trigger the reported behavior, inspect the relevant method/class/function or call path, explain the mechanism that causes the failure, and map that mechanism to the likely fix boundary and the specific replacement the task requires. Partial scores fit agents that reproduce the error or identify the likely file but do not articulate the mechanism or the correct replacement. Low scores fit environment setup, broad searches, repeated read-only commands after the relevant facts are known, pursuit of the old/fallback behavior, or claims of understanding without source-level causal evidence.

Rubric-generation guidance:
- Outside the strict no-patch diagnosis gate, keep the parent polarity: use a negative or cautionary criterion against repetitive read-only exploration after localization, and weight it as a process/semantic-risk signal rather than as the sole correctness criterion.
- Inside the strict no-patch diagnosis gate, add a positive diagnosis rubric with meaningful weight, because it can distinguish trajectories before an edit exists. Its semantics should evaluate root-cause understanding and correct-contract identification, not patch correctness.
- Do not score bare reproduction, environment setup, or many inspection commands as high diagnosis quality. They are at most low-to-partial evidence unless paired with causal explanation and code-path localization.
- Do not apply fix-validation criteria that require an implemented change when no visible continuation contains a source change; that creates uninformative floor scores. Once edits appear, return to implementation/integration evidence and treat diagnosis as supporting context, not a substitute for satisfying the contract.
- When the task directly states an implementation contract (replace A with B), do not let any rubric reward A or treat A as a required or acceptable behavior. Align the implementation rubric narrowly on B and explicitly prohibit credit for A. If the rubric portfolio contains criteria that reward the old/fallback behavior or broaden into adjacent concerns, reduce their weight or remove them.
- When a continuation reverts or destroys an already-applied implementation patch, score it at the lowest level regardless of any test-exploration, diagnostic output, or pattern-matching activity. Patch destruction is an all-or-nothing negative signal that must dominate all other criteria. No volume of test activity compensates for destroying the patch.
- Do not let test-validation criteria, diagnostic output volume, or pattern-matching in preceding steps compensate for patch destruction in the continuation being scored. Partial test output without a valid, preserved patch is diagnostic activity without implementation—do not reward it as if the implementation contract is satisfied.
- Credit constructive environment-setup actions (e.g., installing the project in editable mode to enable test execution) that preserve the implementation patch at least as highly as partial test diagnostics, because they represent progress toward full resolution while maintaining the implementation contract.
- When the visible prefix shows only test-exploration commands without clear evidence of whether the implementation patch is preserved or reverted, preserve uncertainty about the implementation contract. Do not infer patch preservation from test activity alone, and do not infer patch destruction without an explicit reversion command. Score based on observable patch state and constructive environment actions, not on test-output volume or pattern-matching in parent trajectories.
- When continuations are pre-patch, allocate substantial weight (roughly 40–55%) to the trajectory-evidence rubric so the evaluator can distinguish candidates that identified the correct contract from those still pursuing the old/fallback behavior. If completed diffs are present, reduce the trajectory-evidence weight and let the implementation rubric dominate.
- Preserve uncertainty when the visible prefix is too short to show reproduction, source inspection, or attempted implementation.

Abstention boundary: Do not apply the contract-displacement correction if the task does not directly state a specific implementation contract (i.e., it does not name a method, property, or code path and a required replacement). Do not apply the pre-patch diagnosis gate if visible continuations already contain complete code patches that can be judged directly by the implementation contract rubric. Do not apply if the task concerns broad refactoring or style where no single stated contract is being displaced. Do not apply the patch-destruction correction if no visible continuation contains an explicit reversion command or if the patch state cannot be determined from observable evidence.

experiences.title: Stage-Aware Issue Reproduction and Error-Contract Preservation as Validation Signals
experiences.description: Use when a bug report includes a concrete failing scenario and the trajectory is far enough along that a targeted reproduction or regression test should be visible, especially after edits or before final validation. When the fix changes what a method yields or returns, validation must also confirm that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved, not just the primary reported symptom. If the visible stage begins after a fix has already been applied, judge the current segment's own validation activity rather than re-crediting inherited implementation work or earlier testing. When generating rubrics for sibling continuations that share a parent trajectory, do not let shared parent evidence or non-discriminative environment-setup criteria carry scoring weight; re-center the portfolio on continuation-specific final submission evidence and the primary implementation contract. Also prevent overlapping testing rubrics from collectively rewarding broad proxy test-running more than issue-specific verification: the decisive distinction is whether validation exercises the exact behavior or edge contract the fix is meant to correct, not how many generic commands were run.
experiences.context: Applies in framework/library bug-fix tasks where the problem statement gives observable actual vs expected behavior, such as an ORM query result, rendered documentation output, migration recorder state, form choices, introspection signature, command-line error behavior, parser behavior, or post-processing output. Most useful once the agent has located the relevant subsystem, created or modified a candidate fix, inherited an already-applied fix, or begun validation. Less useful as a strict negative during initial exploration, when the agent is only locating files and reading code, or when the task is purely refactoring without a concrete runtime failure. When the current stage inherits a completed fix, generated rubrics should distinguish continuations that run their own functional verification from those that only inspect or describe the existing changes; do not penalize them for not redoing completed implementation or documentation. When the fix changes yield/return behavior, the validation must specifically check that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved. Abstain from the error-preservation sub-criterion when the fix does not change yield/return behavior, or when the original code does not yield or return errors or exceptions during processing. Abstain from the shared-evidence gating sub-criterion when the review is not comparing sibling continuations, when continuations genuinely contain different implementation patches rather than inheriting the same parent patch, or when the portfolio already weights only continuation-specific final submitted patches and already includes a non-empty final-output check. Apply the redundant-validation correction only when two or more candidate rubrics reward the same underlying testing activity, such that broad non-targeted testing can accumulate repeated credit while a focused check of the reported behavior receives less total credit. Do not apply that correction when validation rubrics measure genuinely distinct stages or dimensions, such as pre-fix reproduction versus post-fix confirmation, implementation correctness versus regression coverage, or unrelated compatibility risks. If all visible branches have the same inherited state and no observable validation activity, or if the evidence cannot distinguish targeted from broad validation, prefer uncertain or moderate uniform scoring over confident high credit.
experiences.experience:
The recurring rubric asked whether the agent first established a reproducible bug. This was useful when the visible trajectory contained task-specific reproduction evidence: a minimal script, focused test, or documented command showing the exact bad behavior and then confirming the intended behavior after the patch. It aligned well when the observations directly exercised the user-visible contract, such as duplicate options, stale recorded state, incorrect method signatures, missing rendered members, wrong parser error behavior, or malformed post-processing output. It was less discriminative when generated too early, before the agent had any reasonable chance to run a reproduction, because some later-correct fixes began with code inspection only. A better rubric should be stage-aware and concrete: ask whether the agent has established or is actively preserving a targeted failing scenario matching the reported bug, not merely whether it has run any tests or listed files.

A small but important stage-transition rule: when the current visible work starts from an already-applied fix, a reproduction/validation rubric should score what the current segment itself does to verify behavior. Positive evidence includes running a focused test, small script, import-and-call check, materializing iterator or query outputs, checking object identity or mutation independence where relevant, rerunning a regression assertion, or otherwise executing the fixed behavior. Merely displaying the diff, reading the changed file, listing files, or referring in prose to earlier testing is useful context but is not functional validation. Do not credit validation that only occurred before the current segment, and do not penalize the current segment for not redoing implementation or documentation work that is already complete. When converting this experience into rubrics, keep the polarity positive and give current-stage validation meaningful weight when the fix is inherited; use implementation-presence rubrics only when branches visibly differ in implementation. Evidence mapping should look for commands, scripts, assertions, observed outputs, or test names executed in the current visible span, with diff inspection treated as lower-priority supporting evidence rather than validation.

When a fix changes what a method yields or returns, validation must also confirm that error/exception yielding behavior is preserved. A branch that fixes the primary symptom while silently dropping error yields should not receive the highest reproduction-fidelity score. The reproduction should include a scenario that triggers a processing error, such as faulty or malformed input, and verify the error is still yielded or raised after the fix. This distinction is critical because the primary symptom fix may appear correct in isolation while breaking an implicit error-handling contract that downstream consumers depend on. If the current stage inherits such a fix, the strongest evidence is a current-stage check of both the primary behavior and the error-preservation behavior; earlier checks may explain confidence but should not be scored as work performed by the current segment.

Avoid the tempting generic criterion 'must run the full test suite' or 'must reproduce before reading code'; the important evidence is a minimal, issue-specific before/after check or a regression test that would fail for the reported behavior and pass after the candidate fix. Equivalent validation forms should be accepted: a focused unit test, a command using the appropriate test runner, a concise script, or an interactive check can all be strong if they exercise the reported contract. Prioritize visible evidence such as exact commands, scripts, assertions, rendered output checks, query results, exception messages, or targeted test names that correspond to the original report. Do not confuse a test that only validates the primary symptom with one that also preserves error-handling contracts when the fix changes yield/return behavior. Do not confuse a test that checks a different error path with one that checks individual-item error yielding during processing. Preserve uncertainty where the visible evidence cannot separate branches rather than forcing overconfident distinctions.

A related rubric-generation failure is redundant validation weighting. Multiple rubrics that separately reward running existing suites, running extended suites, exercising command examples, and generally checking behavior can overlap in practice. If all of them are positive and moderately weighted, a continuation that performs broad but non-targeted proxy validation may outscore one that performs a focused check of the exact behavior or edge contract the fix is meant to correct. The generated rubric semantics must make the observable distinction explicit: targeted issue reproduction or contract verification is stronger evidence than merely running many commands. Broad suite passes are useful supporting evidence, but they are not equivalent to verifying the specific failure mode, specific behavioral distinction, or specific error path introduced by the fix.

When translating this into rubrics, consolidate overlapping testing criteria or lower their individual weights so their combined weight does not exceed the primary implementation-correctness rubric or the targeted behavior-verification rubric. Keep polarity positive for relevant validation, but reserve the highest scale levels for evidence tied to the reported contract: a focused regression assertion, a targeted command with observed expected output, a script exercising the exact edge case, or a test name/output clearly corresponding to the failure. A branch that runs broad suites without targeting the reported behavior should receive only partial validation credit, even if it ran more commands. A branch that both implements the correct fix and runs a focused targeted check should not be disadvantaged for running fewer total commands. Do not penalize thoroughness when a branch performs both targeted verification and broader regression checks; the correction is against duplicate credit for the same broad proxy activity, not against additional relevant evidence.

Judge evidence mapping should therefore separate: (1) primary implementation contract evidence, meaning the submitted code actually fixes the reported behavior without violating adjacent contracts; (2) targeted validation evidence, meaning current-stage execution exercises the exact failing scenario, edge path, or error-preservation behavior; and (3) broad regression evidence, meaning larger suites or unrelated checks that provide background confidence. The first two should usually dominate. The third should be lower-weight support unless it contains clearly identified tests for the reported behavior. If two proposed rubrics both reward essentially the same broad test run, merge them mentally or assign the duplicate one negligible weight. If one rubric rewards 'specific test commands' and another rewards 'extended tests,' check whether the specific commands actually exercise the decisive behavior; if not, do not let the pair drown out fix correctness or targeted verification.

A recurring rubric semantic and weighting error arises when generated rubrics for sibling continuations that share a parent trajectory credit evidence that is identical across all continuations. The most common form is inverting a caution about environment or workspace validation into a positive criterion: a negative sub-rubric warning against relying on installed-package or path validation gets rewritten as positive credit for targeting the correct workspace or install location. This inversion is harmful because environment-setup behavior—targeting a specific workspace path, using the correct working tree, or performing installed-package validation—is setup noise rather than implementation evidence, and is typically identical across sibling continuations. A criterion rewarding identical behavior is non-discriminative: it cannot separate correct from incorrect continuations and instead inflates scores uniformly, creating ties that include incorrect continuations. Visible evidence that should activate this correction: (1) a rubric criterion rewards targeting a specific workspace path, install location, or environment validation when all compared branches exhibit the same behavior; (2) a rubric criterion credits tests, diffs, or workspace behavior that appear in a shared parent segment rather than in the continuation's own visible span; or (3) a caution about environment validation has been semantically inverted into positive credit for environment targeting. When any of these are visible, remove or assign zero weight to the environment, workspace, or provenance criterion, and re-center the portfolio on continuation-specific evidence. The dominant weighted criterion should remain the primary implementation contract—the actual code change that fixes the reported bug—not environment mechanics. Add or retain a small final-submission integrity criterion: inspect the continuation's final submission step, not just earlier parent commands, and award full credit only when that final output includes a readable non-empty diff or patch for the intended change. Penalize a continuation whose final submission step produces a blank observation, a failed file read, or no visible patch content, even if an earlier parent step showed the correct diff; do not penalize intermediate failed attempts to read a patch file if a later final submission step visibly emits the patch. Keep any secondary regression criterion lower-weight, ensure it does not duplicate the primary fix or targeted validation, and do not allow shared parent evidence alone to decide among sibling continuations. Abstain from this shared-evidence gating sub-criterion when the review is not comparing sibling continuations, when continuations genuinely contain different implementation patches rather than inheriting the same parent patch, or when the portfolio already weights only continuation-specific final submitted patches and already includes a non-empty final-output check.

experiences.title: Require Bareiss NaN fix implementation beyond reproduction and diagnosis
experiences.description: Retrieve when a symbolic algebra determinant task involves an 'Invalid NaN comparison' TypeError from the Bareiss algorithm's cancel() pathway and trajectories show reproduction or diagnosis of the bug. The rubric portfolio must include a criterion for actual targeted implementation that prevents NaN generation or handles the comparison safely, validated by successful determinant computation. Do not let reproduction-only or diagnosis-only trajectories receive the highest scores when implementation evidence is absent.
experiences.context: Applies to tasks where computing a matrix determinant with symbolic entries raises TypeError: Invalid NaN comparison through the Bareiss algorithm → cancel() → factor_terms → expr.__lt__ pathway. The codebase typically has Python 3.10 compatibility issues (collections.Callable, collections.MutableSet, collections.Mapping) that block reproduction, so trajectories may spend visible effort on import fixes. The rubric portfolio must distinguish three stages: (1) environment compatibility setup—necessary but not the bug fix, (2) reproduction of the NaN comparison TypeError and diagnosis of the cancel(ret) call in the Bareiss function, and (3) targeted implementation that prevents NaN or handles the comparison, validated by a determinant computation returning a valid expression instead of nan or TypeError. A portfolio covering only stages 1–2 over-credits understanding without resolution and under-scores trajectories that proceed to actual fixes.
experiences.experience: Prior rubrics for this task type measured only whether the trajectory reproduced the NaN comparison TypeError and whether it diagnosed the cancel(ret) call in the Bareiss function. This narrowed the portfolio so that a trajectory completing reproduction and diagnosis received the unique maximum score, while trajectories that proceeded to implement actual fixes were under-scored or unscored. The missing criterion should credit visible evidence of a targeted code change to the Bareiss algorithm (e.g., modifying or guarding the cancel() call, adjusting the entry function, switching the determinant algorithm for symbolic matrices, or handling NaN in the comparison/factor_terms path) plus validation that the determinant computation succeeds without TypeError or nan. Environment compatibility edits (collections → collections.abc) are setup, not bug fixes, and must not be credited as implementation. Reproducing the TypeError cleanly is diagnosis progress, not resolution. Getting unevaluated Determinant objects instead of TypeError may indicate the computation path was not triggered, not that the bug is fixed. When the visible prefix shows only environment fixes, reproduction, or diagnosis without a targeted algorithmic change, the rubric should reflect incomplete progress and preserve uncertainty about whether a fix will follow, rather than awarding full credit for understanding alone.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Implements Targeted Fix for Bareiss NaN Comparison
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory makes a targeted code change to prevent NaN generation or handle the NaN comparison in the Bareiss determinant pathway, validated by a successful determinant computation that returns a valid symbolic expression instead of nan or TypeError. Equivalent implementations include modifying the cancel() call in the Bareiss function, adding NaN guards in the entry function, switching the determinant algorithm for symbolic matrices, or handling NaN in factor_terms or expr.__lt__. Environment compatibility fixes alone do not satisfy this criterion.

A trajectory that understands the root cause but has not implemented or validated a fix should not receive full credit when the task requires resolution.
