Do not require an exact values_list(flat/named) design in the paused view; for this round, the key signal is recognizing that an assigned values_select query must restore a values iterable.

Abstention boundary: If the visible prefix shows only source browsing, generic “now I understand” language, reproduction setup, or a thought truncated before the actual assignment/iterable invariant is stated, do not infer that the branch will choose the correct fix. Rank only on visible causal commitments and inspected code. If two branches visibly preserve the same invariant through different nearby mechanisms, treat them as equivalent rather than preferring one exact patch shape.

experiences.title: BoundWidget.id_for_label diagnosis: prefer create_option causal tracing over prompt-echo reproduction success
experiences.description: For this paused BoundWidget.id_for_label round, do not rank branches primarily by whether a local reproduction script reached exit code 0. Because the prompt already states the symptom, the implicated method, and the expected use of data['attrs']['id'], the strongest diagnostic evidence is a continuation that independently traces how ChoiceWidget.create_option/subwidgets set the per-option id and explains that BoundWidget.id_for_label discards that already-computed value.
experiences.context: The visible paused view concerns a Django forms issue where CheckboxSelectMultiple subwidgets carry the intended id in widget.data['attrs']['id'], while BoundWidget.id_for_label returns a hardcoded id based on name and index. Some continuations only install dependencies or hit configuration errors. Some continuations successfully print a mismatch such as data['attrs'].get('id'): custom_id_0 or custom-id_0 versus id_for_label(): id_choices_0. One continuation visibly inspects create_option with grep/sed and states that BoundWidget.id_for_label is hardcoded to return 'id_%s_%s' while it should use the id already in self.data['attrs']['id']. No continuation has an applied patch in the paused view.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply this experience when ranking paused pre-patch continuations for the BoundWidget.id_for_label / CheckboxSelectMultiple id issue, especially when the visible branches contain both reproduction-script output and source-code tracing of ChoiceWidget.create_option or widget subwidget option construction.

Decisive positive evidence: Give highest diagnostic credit to a continuation that visibly examines the option-construction path, e.g. grep -n "def create_option" in django/forms/widgets.py followed by sed of the create_option body, and then articulates the causal mechanism: ChoiceWidget.create_option/subwidgets have already placed the intended id in self.data['attrs']['id'], but BoundWidget.id_for_label ignores it and generates 'id_%s_%s' from name/index. This is stronger branch-ranking evidence than merely confirming the printed mismatch, because it verifies the source-level flow that explains why the bug occurs.

Additional positive evidence: A successful script that prints data['attrs'].get('id') as custom_id_0/custom-id_0 and id_for_label() as id_choices_0 is valid reproduction evidence. A thought that the fix belongs in BoundWidget.id_for_label and should read from self.data['attrs']['id'] is valid localization evidence. These are useful, but when they appear without source-path tracing they may largely restate facts already present in the issue prompt.

Contradictory evidence: Do not give meaningful diagnosis credit for branches that only run pip install commands, only encounter ModuleNotFoundError or ImproperlyConfigured errors, or only write a test that is not subsequently executed successfully. Do not treat opening an unrelated or wrong slice of boundfield.py that does not show BoundWidget.id_for_label as strong source localization. Do not treat reproduction output alone as complete causal diagnosis when the branch never inspects create_option/subwidget option construction and never explains why the id was already correct before BoundWidget.id_for_label overwrote the label target.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not demote the source-tracing branch to dependency-only status merely because its reproduction script later fails on a missing dependency; the visible create_option inspection and causal thought occurred before the environment work. Conversely, do not automatically elevate a configured reproduction script above that branch just because it exits successfully and prints the mismatch. The prompt itself already provides the implicated method and proposed return value, so prompt-matching fix statements after a successful printout are weaker than independent mechanism tracing. Reading only generic widget rendering or test files is at most partial unless it is tied back to create_option/subwidgets setting attrs['id'] and BoundWidget.id_for_label ignoring it.

Equivalent valid implementations: If a later branch patches this issue, preserve any implementation that makes BoundWidget.id_for_label use the id already provided in the subwidget data while maintaining sensible behavior for equivalent cases; do not require an exact one-line return expression if the observable contract is preserved.

Explicit misleading-bias rejection: Reject the judging bias that 'reproduction script succeeded plus fix method named' must outrank 'reproduction blocked but create_option causality established.' In this round, source-level mechanism tracing of how the correct id is produced and then ignored is the decisive ranking signal.

Abstention boundary: If the paused view for a future comparison lacks both successful mismatch output and visible source/mechanism evidence about create_option, attrs['id'], and BoundWidget.id_for_label, do not force a fine-grained ranking. Score only the evidence actually visible; do not infer success from an unrun script or from the issue prompt alone.

experiences.title: Credit issue-mentioned component discovery and actual GC usage patterns over method-definition volume in pre-implementation Text antialiasing exploration
experiences.description: When evaluating pre-implementation exploration for adding get/set_antialiased to Text objects, do not rank branches by the volume of files examined or method definitions found. Finding all components explicitly mentioned in the issue (Text AND Annotation classes) and finding the actual GraphicsContext antialiased usage pattern in drawing code are stronger diagnostic signals than finding method definitions in isolation or having high command volume.
experiences.context: Applies to the matplotlib task where the issue requests adding get/set_antialiased to Text objects, adjusting Annotations accordingly, and replacing rcParams['text.antialiased'] access with GraphicsContext state in the drawing stage. All continuations are paused at step 20 with no patches. The issue explicitly states: 'Add similar getters/setters on Text objects (also adjusting Annotations accordingly, if needed) and use that info in the drawing stage' and 'we need to replace the access to rcParams["text.antialiased"] by going through the GraphicsContext state.'
experiences.experience:
Activation: All visible continuations show zero diff and are paused during pre-implementation exploration of the Text antialiasing task. The issue explicitly mentions Text objects, Annotations, and replacing rcParams['text.antialiased'] with GraphicsContext state.

Decisive positive evidence — finding these specific items should raise a branch's ranking:
1. Annotation class discovery: A continuation that ran grep for 'class Annotation' and found the Annotation class in text.py demonstrates awareness of ALL components the issue says must be adjusted. This is stronger evidence than finding only Text-related code, because the issue explicitly says 'also adjusting Annotations accordingly, if needed.' A branch that found the Annotation class location should rank above one that did not, even if the latter found more total locations.
2. Actual GC antialiased usage pattern: A continuation that found gc0.set_antialiased(aa) at line 445 in backend_bases.py (via grep for 'set_antialiased|get_antialiased') found the actual pattern of using GC antialiased state during drawing — exactly the replacement mechanism the issue describes. This is stronger evidence than finding only the method definitions at lines 816/910, because it shows how the GC state is actually consumed in rendering and what the fix must replicate.
3. Multi-backend investigation: A continuation that examined multiple backends (e.g., backend_agg.py AND backend_cairo.py) demonstrates understanding of the backend complexity the issue explicitly notes ('fiddling needed with backends').
4. Negative grep confirming the problem: A continuation that ran grep for 'get_antialiased' in backend_agg.py and got no results confirmed that text drawing does not currently use GC antialiased state — this is valuable causal evidence for why the fix is needed and what must change.
5. rcParams usage in rendering: Finding where rcParams['text.antialiased'] is actually used in drawing (backend_agg.py:209, _mathtext.py:127) is necessary but not sufficient — all branches that found this should receive moderate credit, but branches that also connected it to the GC replacement mechanism should rank higher.

Contradictory evidence — do NOT use as positive signals:
- Volume of grep/sed commands is not a quality signal. A branch with 20 commands that found the same key locations as a branch with 15 commands should not rank higher on command count alone.
- Finding the GraphicsContext get_antialiased (line 818) and set_antialiased (line 910) method definitions in isolation, without connecting them to the rcParams usage or the actual drawing path, is incomplete. Do not credit this as strongly as finding the gc0.set_antialiased(aa) usage at line 445.
- Finding the Line2D get/set_antialiased pattern is useful as a reference implementation but is not sufficient without connecting it to the Text case and the rcParams replacement.
- Finding 'text.antialiased' in rcsetup.py or matplotlibrc only shows the rcParam is defined/configured, not where it is used in rendering. Do not conflate rcParam definition with rendering usage.

Close-looking exclusions:
- Do not penalize a branch for searching artist.py for antialiased and finding nothing — this is a reasonable exploration step since Text inherits from Artist. However, a branch that REPEATEDLY searches artist.py with 5+ different grep patterns, all returning no results, without pivoting to more productive searches is showing inefficient exploration, not thoroughness. This pattern should receive lower exploration scores.
- Do not conflate 'found text.antialiased in rcsetup.py' with 'found where text.antialiased is used in drawing.' The rcsetup.py hit just shows the rcParam definition; the backend_agg.py:209 and _mathtext.py:127 hits show where it is actually consumed in rendering, which is what needs to change.
- A branch that found the Annotation class but did not examine its code in detail still found an issue-relevant component. Credit the discovery; do not require full code examination at the exploration stage.
- A branch that examined the Text.draw method but did not connect it to the GC antialiased mechanism has incomplete causal tracing. The draw method is where the fix must be applied, but finding it without connecting to the GC replacement is only moderate evidence.

Rejected misleading rubric/bias: The observed bias ranks branches by the number of distinct locations found or files examined. This is misleading because it treats all findings as equivalent. Finding the Annotation class (which the issue explicitly mentions) and finding gc0.set_antialiased(aa) (which shows the actual replacement pattern) are more diagnostic than finding method definitions in isolation. A branch that found 6 locations but missed the Annotation class and the GC usage pattern should NOT rank above a branch that found 5 locations including both. The issue explicitly mentions Annotations and GraphicsContext state replacement — finding evidence about these specific aspects is more diagnostic than generic file coverage. Do not treat 'found get_antialiased at line 818 and set_antialiased at line 910' as equivalent to 'found gc0.set_antialiased(aa) at line 445' — the latter shows the actual usage pattern that the fix must replicate, while the former only shows method definitions. Both multi-backend investigation and Annotation discovery are valid, complementary exploration paths that demonstrate different aspects of the required fix; credit both rather than preferring one over the other.

Abstention boundary: If no branch found the Annotation class or the gc0.set_antialiased(aa) usage pattern, rank based on the depth of causal tracing visible (rcParams usage → GraphicsContext methods → drawing path). If all branches show only generic file listing and grep without converging on the key rendering locations, mark as not meaningfully distinguishable. Do not infer future implementation quality from exploration patterns alone — a branch with inefficient exploration may still implement well later, and a branch with thorough exploration may still implement poorly. Preserve uncertainty about implementation quality when no patch exists.

experiences.title: Pickled values-query fix: synchronize assigned Query.values_select to ValuesIterable, not invented values_list state
experiences.description: For the Django queryset.query pickling failure, rank branches by whether they identify the source-level result-shape invariant: assigning a Query whose values_select is populated to a default QuerySet must make that QuerySet use values-style iteration. Do not top-rank branches merely for pickle-method searches, broad greps, reproduction scaffolding, or for inventing new values_list subtype state and rewriting values()/values_list().
experiences.context: The visible task pickles prices.query from Toy.objects.values('material').annotate(...), assigns the unpickled Query to Toy.objects.all().query, and then gets model instances instead of dicts. In the paused view, relevant evidence includes inspection of QuerySet._values(), QuerySet.values()/values_list(), Query.set_values(), Query.values_select, _fields, _iterable_class, QuerySet.query assignment, ModelIterable, ValuesIterable, and pickle-related methods.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply when judging a branch for this values()/values_list() queryset.query pickling crash, especially when visible commands, thoughts, outputs, or diffs touch QuerySet._values(), values(), values_list(), Query.set_values(), Query.values_select, _fields, _iterable_class, the QuerySet.query setter, or pickle methods.

Decisive positive evidence: Prefer branches that converge on the assignment/result-shape invariant. Strong evidence includes visibly reading that QuerySet._values() sets QuerySet-side fields and calls clone.query.set_values(fields); reading that values() sets ValuesIterable; reading that Query.set_values() records selected value fields in Query.values_select; and connecting those facts to the assignment path where a fresh QuerySet can keep ModelIterable after self.query is replaced. The strongest fix evidence is a central assignment-path change such as: when QuerySet.query is assigned a Query with value.values_select, set the receiving QuerySet to ValuesIterable, optionally synchronizing _fields or resetting defaults where appropriate. Equivalent implementations are valid if they guarantee the same invariant without relying on a single exact patch shape: an assigned values Query must be evaluated with values-style result construction instead of model-instance construction.

Contradictory evidence and low-score conditions: Explicitly reject the misleading rubric bias that treats “Query has no custom pickling methods, therefore values_select is lost” as the decisive root cause. The branch must address how the receiving QuerySet chooses its iterable after query assignment. Also reject the opposite false-positive behavior of inventing new Query attributes such as values_list/flat/named flags, changing Query.set_values() to accept values_list subtype parameters, or rewriting values()/values_list() to persist tuple/named/flat subtype state merely because the prompt mentions values_list(). That API churn is not necessary for the visible failure and should not outrank a minimal values_select-to-ValuesIterable assignment fix. Searching QuerySet.__getstate__/__setstate__, Prefetch pickling, or SQL Query pickle hooks is weak unless tied back to the assigned QuerySet’s iterable selection.

Close-looking exclusions: Finding values_select in Query.__init__ or Query.set_values is useful but not top credit by itself; it must be tied to how a QuerySet assigned that Query will iterate results. A broad grep for _iterable_class, values_select, or _fields is only a lead until the branch reads or explains the relevant setter/iteration code. Reproduction files, database setup, or a script that would reproduce the traceback do not outweigh source-level reasoning about the assignment invariant. Reading Query.clone or general Query structure is relevant only if connected to preserving or consuming values_select for result construction. The wording “values()/values_list()” does not require preserving flat/named tuple subtypes through new private Query state; do not reward that as a superior fix.

Abstention boundary: If the visible prefix contains only environment setup, local project scaffolding, truncated outputs with no visible relevant code, or pickle-method searches with no values_select/_iterable_class/query-assignment reasoning, give little diagnostic credit and do not infer future success. If a final diff is not visible, do not infer that the branch added or avoided values_list subtype flags. If a branch clearly states or implements the assigned-Query values_select → ValuesIterable invariant, it may rank above a branch with more commands or broader-looking exploration that lacks that invariant.

experiences.title: Preserve the correct in-place reset fix while investigating multi-phase stash side effects; reject revert-and-grep over fix-and-experiment
experiences.description: When a continuation applies the correct in-place mutation fix (self.records.clear() in LogCaptureHandler.reset()) and discovers it breaks multi-phase record tracking, rank continuations that keep the fix and investigate productively above those that revert the fix and unproductively grep for phase-tracking mechanisms. A verbal diagnosis of why the fix breaks a test does not compensate for reverting the correct fix and spending many steps on unproductive searches without trying any alternative approach.
experiences.context: In the caplog.get_records/caplog.clear evaluation, the correct fix changes self.records = [] to self.records.clear() in LogCaptureHandler.reset() to keep the stash reference in sync with caplog.records. The simple fix resolves the reported issue but breaks multi-phase record tracking because the stash stores a reference to the same list object across phases, and clearing in-place clears records for all phases. At the paused state, continuations that discovered this side effect diverged: some kept the fix and investigated the stash mechanism or tried concrete alternative approaches, while others reverted the fix and spent many steps grepping for phase-tracking mechanisms without trying any fix.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply when evaluating paused continuations that applied the self.records.clear() fix in LogCaptureHandler.reset() and then discovered it breaks test_caplog_captures_for_all_stages or similar multi-phase record tracking tests. Apply when some continuations kept the fix and investigated while others reverted and searched.

Decisive positive evidence: A continuation that keeps the self.records.clear() fix applied (visible in git diff) while investigating the stash mechanism — examining _runtest_for, caplog_records_key assignment at line 699, how phases share the handler — demonstrates productive progress toward a complete fix. A continuation that tries concrete alternative approaches (e.g., creating a new list for each phase in _runtest_for, adding caplog_handler.records = [] after reset(), updating the stash on clear()) is making stronger progress than one that only investigates. Running tests with the local source (sys.path.insert(0, 'src') or PYTHONPATH=/testbed/src) to discover the multi-phase failure is strong evidence of correct validation targeting. Equivalent valid in-place clearing operations (self.records.clear(), del self.records[:], self.records[:] = []) must all be treated as preserving the fix.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation that reverts the self.records.clear() fix back to self.records = [] using sed -i destroys the implementation progress and should not be ranked above continuations that preserve the fix. A verbal diagnosis ('I see the issue now!') followed by reverting and many unproductive grep commands (searching for _when, set_when, phase, current, class.*Handler) without trying any alternative fix is not evidence of productive investigation. Reverting the correct fix because it breaks a test is not 'good judgment' when the fix is the correct solution for the reported issue and the side effect can be addressed with complementary changes. A continuation with no fix applied at the paused state should not outrank one with the correct fix applied, regardless of how much investigation the reverted continuation performed.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not penalize a continuation for discovering that its fix breaks a test — this is valuable diagnostic evidence, not a sign of failure. Do not equate 'fix breaks a test' with 'fix is wrong' when the fix correctly addresses the reported issue and the test failure reveals a complementary change needed. Do not reward volume of grep/search commands as 'thorough investigation' when the searches do not lead to concrete fix attempts. A continuation that reverts the fix but runs tests to confirm the behavior of both original and fixed code provides more diagnostic value than one that reverts and only greps, but should still be ranked below continuations that keep the fix and investigate productively. Do not penalize a continuation whose alternative fix attempt fails (e.g., adding caplog_handler.records = [] after reset() still fails test_caplog_captures_for_all_stages) — the attempt itself is productive evidence.

Explicitly rejected misleading bias: Reject any rubric that ranks a continuation higher because it verbally diagnosed why a fix breaks a test and then reverted it. The verbal diagnosis is not implementation progress; reverting the correct fix destroys the implementation contract. Reject any bias that treats 'recognizing a fix is incomplete and reverting' as superior to 'recognizing a fix is incomplete and keeping it while investigating complementary changes.' The correct fix for the reported issue (self.records.clear()) must be preserved; the multi-phase side effect requires a complementary change, not a replacement of the fix. Also reject any bias that counts the number of grep/search commands as evidence of investigation quality when those commands do not lead to concrete fix attempts.

Abstention boundary: If the visible prefix does not show whether the fix is still applied at the paused state, preserve uncertainty about implementation preservation. If a continuation reverted the fix but the trajectory is truncated before showing whether it re-applies or tries an alternative, do not infer final failure beyond the visible paused state, but rank it below continuations that visibly preserve the fix. If no continuation has discovered the multi-phase side effect, rank based on fix correctness and validation targeting as in the pre-implementation experience.

experiences.title: Do not rank scratch-only InheritDocstrings simulations above real property-docstring source edits
experiences.description: For the InheritDocstrings/property-docstring task, a continuation with no changed target source and only standalone proof-of-concept scripts must not outrank continuations that visibly modify the metaclass source to handle properties. Scratch scripts can demonstrate understanding, but they are not implementation or validation of the actual patched code.
experiences.context: Applies to paused SWE trajectories for the prompt that InheritDocstrings uses inspect.isfunction and therefore misses property descriptors. The visible view contains a mixed-stage set: some continuations have changed the target metaclass source file, while another remains at zero patch and only runs copied or standalone helper code showing a possible fix. The judge must not let a reproduction/exploration rubric dominate once other branches have begun plausible target-file implementation.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Use this experience when at least one visible continuation modifies the source file containing InheritDocstrings, while another continuation has changed_files None/current_patch_chars 0 and relies on standalone scripts, copied metaclass code, or helper functions outside the target source. This is especially important when the no-diff continuation prints an apparent success such as a derived property docstring changing after a local helper is called.

Decisive positive evidence: Prefer branches that visibly edit the target metaclass source and plausibly integrate property handling into the actual InheritDocstrings loop. Strong implementations may directly assign the inherited docstring to the property descriptor object, replace/rebuild the property with the inherited doc while preserving getter/setter/deleter behavior, or use an equivalent helper that demonstrably updates the descriptor exposed by the class. Stronger validation is a passing test run against the modified source that asserts a derived property’s __doc__ equals the base property’s docstring. A branch that first discovers that setting fget.__doc__ is insufficient and then updates the target source accordingly is materially stronger than one that only demonstrates the idea in a scratch file.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation with no changed source file has not implemented the fix, even if its scratch script prints “Before fix” and “After fix” or manually calls a local inherit_docstrings helper that makes the example pass. Tests of copied code are not validation of the actual codebase. Exploration of cached_property, classproperty, abstractproperty, classmethod, or staticmethod behavior is not a substitute for patching the requested metaclass. A visible assertion failure that Derived.property.__doc__ is still None contradicts successful validation. A change that only sets the getter function’s __doc__ while leaving the property object’s __doc__ unchanged is also contradictory, because the visible debugging shows those attributes are distinct.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not require the exact text val.__doc__ = ... if another source-level implementation preserves equivalent behavior and makes the property descriptor expose the inherited docstring. Do not penalize a source-editing branch solely because its follow-up test is missing, minimal, or blocked by a path/import issue; that branch still has more implementation evidence than a no-diff scratch-only branch. Conversely, do not count untracked files named like fixes or tests as source edits unless the target source summary or visible command output shows the metaclass file was actually changed. Do not give extra implementation credit for broad descriptor explorations unless they are tied back to the target metaclass source and the property-docstring bug.

Explicitly rejected bias: Reject any rubric behavior that ranks a no-patch branch highest because it has a polished standalone reproduction or because a copied helper passes in isolation. In this mixed-stage view, actual target-file implementation evidence must dominate scratch-only diagnostic success.

Abstention boundary: If every continuation is pre-implementation with no target-source changes, use reproduction and root-cause rubrics to distinguish them. If no branch shows either a target-source edit or a passing test against modified source, do not infer implementation quality from intent or scratch output alone. If a target-source edit is visible but the exact edited lines are truncated, treat it as plausible implementation evidence only to the extent supported by the summary and surrounding commands; do not assume correctness beyond what is visible.

experiences.title: ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed parent_link fix: verify stated fix checks field.remote_field.parent_link, not prev_field.remote_field.parent_link
experiences.description: When judging trajectories for the Django ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed() bug where a OneToOneField primary key is incorrectly treated as concrete inheritance, do not rank a trajectory as top solely based on diagnosis depth. Examine the stated fix approach: a trajectory that proposes checking prev_field.remote_field.parent_link is checking the wrong field. prev_field is the previous relation (e.g., ForeignKey), whose remote_field is a ManyToOneRel with parent_link always False. The correct check is field.remote_field.parent_link (the current field's OneToOneRel), which is True for concrete inheritance and False for regular OneToOneField PKs.
experiences.context: The bug is in ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed() in django/contrib/admin/options.py. The condition `field not in prev_field.path_infos[-1].target_fields` skips adding a part to relation_parts when the field is in the target_fields of the previous relation's path_info. This is meant for concrete inheritance but incorrectly fires for regular OneToOneField primary keys. The distinguishing factor is field.remote_field.parent_link. A trajectory may correctly identify this factor in test scripts but then misattribute the check to prev_field in its stated fix approach, indicating a misunderstanding that would lead to an incorrect fix.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply when scoring paused diagnosis trajectories for the Django ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed() bug where a OneToOneField used as primary_key is incorrectly treated as a concrete inheritance parent link, causing lookup_allowed to return False for valid lookups like 'restaurant__place__country'.

Decisive positive evidence: Give strongest credit to trajectories that: (1) reproduce the bug (lookup_allowed returns False for 'restaurant__place__country'), (2) identify the mechanism: relation_parts becomes ['restaurant', 'country'] instead of ['restaurant', 'place', 'country'] because 'place' is in prev_field.path_infos[-1].target_fields and is skipped, (3) identify the distinguishing factor: field.remote_field.parent_link is True for concrete inheritance parent links and False for regular OneToOneField primary keys, (4) state or imply the fix approach correctly: the condition should also check field.remote_field.parent_link (the CURRENT field's remote_field), so that only actual parent_link fields are skipped. Valid alternative implementations include checking field in model._meta.parents.values() or equivalent logic that distinguishes concrete inheritance parent links from regular OneToOneField primary keys.

Contradictory evidence: Explicitly reject the misleading judge bias that awards top scores to trajectories with thorough diagnosis but incorrect stated fix approaches. A trajectory that explicitly states 'check if prev_field.remote_field.parent_link is True' is checking the WRONG field. In the lookup_allowed loop, prev_field is the previous relation field (e.g., ForeignKey 'restaurant'), whose remote_field is a ManyToOneRel. ManyToOneRel.parent_link is always False for ForeignKey reverse relations, so this check would always be False, meaning the concrete inheritance shortcut would never apply, breaking existing behavior. The correct check is field.remote_field.parent_link (the current field's remote_field), which is a OneToOneRel with parent_link=True for concrete inheritance and False for regular OneToOneField PKs. A trajectory with this error in its stated fix approach should not be ranked as top, even if its diagnosis (reproduction, mechanism identification, parent_link factor discovery) is thorough.

Close-looking exclusions: A trajectory may correctly identify the parent_link distinguishing factor in test scripts (e.g., printing field.remote_field.parent_link and seeing False for regular OneToOneField, True for concrete inheritance) but then misattribute the check to prev_field in its stated fix approach. This discrepancy between test script observations and stated fix approach is a red flag — do not conflate 'identified the distinguishing factor in tests' with 'stated the correct fix.' Also, trajectories that have not yet stated a fix approach (still in exploration, reproduction, or debugging without proposing a specific check) should not be penalized for an incorrect fix approach they have not stated; their diagnosis quality should be assessed on its own merits.

Abstention boundary: If no trajectory in the visible prefix explicitly states a specific fix approach involving parent_link (all are still in exploration, reproduction, or debugging), do not attempt to distinguish based on fix correctness. If the stated fix approach is ambiguous (e.g., 'check parent_link' without specifying which field's parent_link), do not infer correctness or incorrectness. This experience applies only when a trajectory explicitly states checking prev_field.remote_field.parent_link or field.remote_field.parent_link, or when the discrepancy between test observations and stated fix approach is clearly visible.

experiences.title: SimpleLazyObject Subquery Diagnosis: Prefer Reusable Original-Shape Reproduction Over Ad Hoc Exact Error Prints
experiences.description: For the Django SimpleLazyObject nested Subquery annotation issue, do not rank a paused continuation highest merely because it prints the exact TypeError from a one-off command. At the pre-patch stage, stronger evidence is a reusable reproduction matching the reported TestCase shape, run through Django’s test machinery, combined with lookup/RHS-preparation diagnosis. Scalar IntegerField experiments and LazyObject introspection are only supporting evidence and can point to an overbroad or incomplete fix.
experiences.context: The visible task reports that filtering an annotation derived from nested Subquery/OuterRef with a SimpleLazyObject wrapping a User fails during lookup preparation, eventually trying to coerce the lazy object through an integer field. The paused continuations have no source diff. They differ mainly in reproduction quality and diagnosis direction: some create and run a TestCase-like reproduction with settings and Django’s test runner; some use ad hoc python -c scripts that catch and print the exact TypeError; others investigate Field.get_prep_value or SimpleLazyObject scalar behavior without reproducing the nested Subquery/User case.
experiences.experience:
ACTIVATION: Use this experience when judging paused, pre-patch trajectories for the SimpleLazyObject + nested Subquery annotation failure, especially when no continuation has modified source code and the visible evidence is limited to reproduction attempts, environment setup, traceback inspection, and lazy-object introspection.

DECISIVE POSITIVE EVIDENCE: Give the strongest pre-patch credit to a continuation that builds a reproduction matching the reported ORM shape: models analogous to A/B/C plus User, an inner query using OuterRef and Subquery, an outer annotate(owner_user=Subquery(...)), and filter(owner_user=<SimpleLazyObject wrapping User creation>). A reusable TestCase or test file run with Django’s test runner and a configured settings module is especially valuable because it can later become a regression test; visible output such as a created test database followed by E/FAILED(errors=1) is meaningful when the test body matches the issue, even if the traceback is truncated. Also credit diagnosis that follows the visible traceback through Lookup.get_prep_lookup / RHS preparation into field get_prep_value and recognizes that SimpleLazyObject is a LazyObject, not a Promise, and must be evaluated before the normal lookup/value preparation path handles the wrapped object.

SUPPORTING BUT NOT DECISIVE EVIDENCE: A one-off python -c reproduction that prints the exact visible error, e.g. Field 'id' expected a number but got <SimpleLazyObject: <User: testuser>>, is real diagnostic progress. However, if the command catches the exception and exits with return code 0, it is not yet a failing regression test. LazyObject experiments showing issubclass(SimpleLazyObject, LazyObject), not Promise, or showing that _wrapped starts as empty and is filled by _setup/attribute access are useful supporting facts, but they are not a fix and should not dominate the ranking over a reusable original-shape reproduction.

CONTRADICTORY EVIDENCE: Do not count setup failures as bug reproduction: ModuleNotFoundError for django/asgiref, Settings already configured, populate() is not reentrant, missing pytest, missing manage.py, missing app_label, or a settings module not found are environment/test-harness problems. A continuation that only demonstrates IntegerField.get_prep_value(SimpleLazyObject(lambda: 42)) failing has not reproduced the reported nested Subquery/User case; that scalar example may encourage an incomplete field-level change that unwraps 42 but still mishandles a lazy User/model instance. A continuation that only states that the fix belongs in Field.get_prep_value, without showing the original annotation/subquery failure, should not outrank one that reproduces the reported query shape and investigates lookup preparation.

CLOSE-LOOKING EXCLUSIONS: Do not treat every SimpleLazyObject failure as equivalent. The reported RHS wraps a User object and reaches an id/foreign-key preparation path through an annotation/subquery lookup; a scalar lazy integer test is narrower and can miss the model-instance-to-primary-key requirement. Conversely, do not require one exact file location as the only valid fix: a correct implementation may evaluate LazyObject in lookup-value resolution, lookup preparation, or another equivalent RHS-preparation boundary, provided it preserves normal expression handling, related-object/model-instance preparation, scalar values, and existing Promise behavior. Merely importing Promise is not sufficient because SimpleLazyObject is visibly not a Promise.

MISLEADING PATTERN REJECTED: Explicitly reject the bias that the branch with the most explicit printed TypeError from an ad hoc script must be ranked highest. Exact error text is useful, but it should not override the stronger engineering signal of a reusable TestCase-like reproduction that exercises the original nested Subquery shape and fails under Django’s test runner. Also reject the opposite shortcut: a low-level LazyObject or IntegerField experiment is not enough to identify the correct fix for the reported ORM path.

ABSTENTION BOUNDARY: If no continuation has a completed original-shape reproduction, no visible exact error, and no source change, abstain from strong ranking claims and score only environment setup or code-reading progress. If a continuation has a visible source diff or reruns the original-shape reproduction successfully after a change, switch to evaluating the actual patch behavior and validation rather than this pre-patch reproduction hierarchy. When traceback output is truncated, rely on the visible test body and command status, not on unsupported assistant narration alone.

experiences.title: Investigating Relevant Test Failures to Diagnose Over-Aggressive Optimization Beats Uncritical Acceptance or Test Gaming
experiences.description: When a fix causes existing tests to fail, a continuation that investigates the failures and discovers the implementation is too aggressive (e.g., combining fast deletes across batches of the same relation instead of across different relations for the same model) and takes corrective action provides stronger evidence of a correct fix than one that accepts failures as 'expected optimization' without investigation, runs unrelated passing test suites, or modifies test files to pass.
experiences.context: A Django fast-delete query combination task where the parent already implemented a fix grouping fast_deletes by model and combining with OR. Continuations run the existing test suite and find test_large_delete and test_large_delete_related failing due to reduced query counts. Most continuations accept these failures as 'expected optimization' and run other test suites (delete_regress, queries, signals) to show broad compatibility. One continuation (s02) investigates deeper, discovers the implementation combines fast deletes across batches of the same relation (not just across different relations), and takes corrective action by patching the implementation. Another continuation (s03) modifies the test file itself with sed to change expected query counts.
experiences.experience:
ACTIVATION: This experience activates when a continuation's fix causes existing tests to fail, and continuations differ in how they respond: some accept failures as 'expected,' some investigate root cause, and some modify test files to pass.

POSITIVE EVIDENCE: A continuation that (1) examines the failing test's query-count expectations, (2) traces the actual fast_deletes structure to understand why queries are being combined, (3) discovers the implementation is over-aggressive — combining fast deletes across batches of the SAME relation rather than across DIFFERENT relations for the same model — and (4) takes corrective action by patching the implementation. The decisive insight is distinguishing 'combine fast deletes from different relations to the same model' (correct, per PR spec) from 'combine fast deletes from the same relation across different batches' (too aggressive, breaks batch-level query count expectations). Visible evidence includes: recognizing the over-combining issue in the agent's reasoning, creating a patch script to refine the implementation, and tracing fast_deletes to confirm multiple entries for the same model share the same field lookup (e.g., 4 fast_deletes for User all with avatar_id, confirming same-relation batch splitting rather than different-relation combination).

CONTRADICTORY EVIDENCE: A continuation that accepts test failures as 'expected optimization' without investigating whether the optimization is too aggressive. Running other test suites (delete_regress, queries, signals, m2m_through, many_to_many) that pass does NOT validate the fix is correct — it only shows no regressions in unrelated areas. The failing tests (test_large_delete, test_large_delete_related) are the MOST relevant tests because they directly test the deletion query behavior the fix changes. A continuation that modifies the test file itself (e.g., sed -i on tests/delete/tests.py to change expected_num_queries) is gaming the tests, not fixing the code — this is negative evidence of fix correctness.

CLOSE-LOOKING EXCLUSIONS: Distinguish between a continuation that states 'test failures are expected because the optimization reduces queries' (plausible but unverified rationalization) and one that actually traces the fast_deletes structure and confirms the implementation combines across batches of the same relation (investigated diagnosis). The former is a hand-wave; the latter is a root-cause finding. Also distinguish modifying the source fix (valid corrective action) from modifying the test file (invalid test gaming). A continuation that shows a git diff of the fix but never investigates why relevant tests fail is NOT more thorough than one that investigates the failures and patches the implementation, even if the latter runs fewer test suites overall. Do not treat 'more passing test suites' as evidence of fix correctness when the most relevant tests are failing and uninvestigated.

MISLEADING PATTERN REJECTED: The judge bias that 'more passing test suites and a visible git diff mean a better fix' is misleading. The relevant failing tests (test_large_delete, test_large_delete_related) directly test the changed behavior; accepting their failure without investigation is uncritical. A continuation that runs 5 unrelated test suites (all passing) but doesn't investigate the 2 relevant failing tests should NOT rank above one that investigates the failures, discovers an over-combining issue, traces the fast_deletes structure, and takes corrective action. Breadth of passing unrelated tests is not a substitute for depth of investigation of relevant failures. Also reject any rubric that treats modifying test files to make tests pass as valid validation — it is test gaming.

ABSTENTION BOUNDARY: If no continuation investigates the test failures or takes corrective action, and all either accept failures as expected or modify tests, rank by the depth of investigation into the failing tests rather than by breadth of unrelated passing suites. If the visible prefix cannot confirm whether the corrective patch actually resolves the over-combining issue (e.g., patch content is truncated), preserve uncertainty about the fix's final correctness but still rank the investigation and corrective attempt above uncritical acceptance. If all continuations show the same level of investigation (or none), do not distinguish based on test-suite breadth alone.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Root-Cause Investigation of Relevant Test Failures in Fast-Delete Combination
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluates whether the continuation investigates why existing deletion tests (test_large_delete, test_large_delete_related) fail after the fast-delete combination fix, rather than accepting failures as 'expected optimization.' High scores require: (1) examining the failing test's query-count expectations, (2) tracing the fast_deletes structure to understand what is being combined, (3) discovering whether the implementation combines across batches of the same relation (too aggressive) vs. across different relations for the same model (correct), and (4) taking corrective action if the implementation is over-aggressive. Low scores for accepting failures without investigation, running unrelated test suites as a substitute, or modifying test files to pass.

metadata.oracle_test: The fix should combine fast deletes from DIFFERENT relations to the same model (e.g., Entry.created_by and Entry.updated_by) but NOT across batches of the SAME relation (e.g., User.avatar split into 4 batches). test_large_delete and test_large_delete_related fail when the implementation over-combines across batches.
metadata.code_review: Check if continuation traces fast_deletes structure, identifies same-relation batch entries vs. different-relation entries, and patches the implementation to only combine across different relations.
metadata.judge_focus: Whether the agent investigates WHY relevant tests fail and whether it discovers the over-combining issue, rather than accepting failures as expected or gaming tests.
metadata.failure_mode: Accepting test failures as 'expected optimization' without investigation; modifying test files to change expected query counts; running unrelated passing test suites as substitute for investigating relevant failures.

scale.1: No investigation of failing tests; accepts failures as expected or modifies test files to pass.
scale.2: Examines failing test code but does not trace fast_deletes structure or identify over-combining issue.
scale.3: Traces fast_deletes structure and identifies multiple entries for the same model but does not distinguish same-relation batches from different-relation entries.
scale.4: Identifies the over-combining issue (combining across batches of same relation) and takes corrective action by patching the implementation, though final validation is incomplete.
scale.5: Identifies over-combining, patches implementation, traces fast_deletes to confirm same-relation batch entries, and validates the refined fix resolves the relevant test failures.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct Implementation Refinement: Relation-Level vs Batch-Level Fast-Delete Combination
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluates whether the continuation correctly distinguishes between combining fast deletes from different relations to the same model (correct, per PR spec) and combining fast deletes from the same relation across different batches (too aggressive, breaks existing tests). The fix should group fast_deletes by model AND ensure entries being combined come from different field lookups (different relations), not just the same field lookup split across batches. High scores for continuations that recognize this distinction and refine the implementation accordingly.

metadata.oracle_test: The PR wants DELETE FROM entry WHERE created_by_id = :id OR updated_by_id = :id (different relations combined). It does NOT want DELETE FROM user WHERE avatar_id IN (batch1) OR avatar_id IN (batch2) (same relation across batches combined).
metadata.code_review: Check if continuation's patch distinguishes same-field-lookup entries from different-field-lookup entries when grouping fast_deletes by model.
metadata.judge_focus: Whether the agent recognizes the difference between relation-level combination and batch-level combination, and whether the refined implementation only combines across different relations.
metadata.failure_mode: Grouping by model alone without checking field lookup, causing same-relation batch entries to be combined and breaking test_large_delete.

scale.1: No refinement; implementation groups by model only, combining all entries including same-relation batches.
scale.2: Recognizes the issue but does not patch the implementation.
scale.3: Patches the implementation but the refinement is incomplete or unclear.
scale.4: Correctly refines to only combine fast deletes with different field lookups for the same model, preserving batch-level separation for same-relation entries.
scale.5: Correctly refines AND validates that different-relation entries are combined while same-relation batch entries remain separate.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Modifying Test Files to Make Failing Tests Pass
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalizes continuations that modify existing test files (e.g., using sed to change expected_num_queries in tests/delete/tests.py) to make failing tests pass, rather than fixing the source code. This is test gaming, not fix validation. A continuation that changes test expectations to match the implementation's behavior is masking the problem rather than solving it.

metadata.oracle_test: The test file tests/delete/tests.py should not be modified to change expected query counts. If tests fail, the implementation should be refined, not the tests gamed.
metadata.code_review: Check if continuation modifies test files (e.g., sed -i on tests/delete/tests.py) to change expected_num_queries or other test expectations.
metadata.judge_focus: Whether the agent modifies test files to make tests pass rather than investigating and fixing the source code.
metadata.failure_mode: Using sed -i or similar to change expected query counts in test files, then running the modified tests to claim they pass.

scale.1: No evidence of test file modification; tests are run as-is.
scale.2: Minor test file changes that don't affect test semantics (e.g., adding debug prints).
scale.3: Modifies test expectations to match implementation behavior without justification.
scale.4: Clearly modifies expected_num_queries or similar test assertions to make failing tests pass.
scale.5: Systematically modifies multiple test assertions to mask implementation issues, presenting the modified passing tests as validation success.

experiences.title: Paused swap_dims ranking: visible exact reproduction saturates pre-patch credit; browsing cannot create a unique top
experiences.description: For this paused swap_dims mutation task, all visible continuations are pre-implementation with no source-code diff. Rank them by concrete executable reproduction evidence first. A returncode-0 script whose visible output shows the original ds2 lev variable changed to dimension lev after ds2.swap_dims(z='lev') is top-tier evidence. Do not let variable.py browsing, self-reported reproduction, or a combined reproduction-plus-mechanism rubric outrank or break ties against the same exact reproduction evidence.
experiences.context: The supplied paused view shows no applied patch in any continuation: changed_files is None, diff_stat is blank, and current_patch_chars is 0. The visible evidence consists of environment setup, reproduction scripts, source browsing, and command output. Some continuations resolve blockers such as NumPy compatibility and missing packaging, then rerun a script successfully. Successful output is visible when the final dataset display includes Data variables with y on (z) and lev on (lev), demonstrating that calling swap_dims on ds2 mutated ds2['lev'].dims from z to lev. Other continuations end on AttributeError for np.unicode_, ModuleNotFoundError for packaging, only print a package version, or only inspect variable.py functions such as to_index_variable, to_base_variable, Variable.__init__, as_compatible_data, or _maybe_wrap_data.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply this experience only for this paused, pre-implementation swap_dims round where no continuation has a visible source-code edit and the judge is ranking reproduction/diagnosis progress from the paused view.

Decisive positive evidence: Give top pre-patch reproduction credit to a continuation that runs a local reproduction script to returncode 0 and whose visible output shows the final mutated state: after ds2.swap_dims(z='lev'), the original ds2 display includes lev with dimension (lev), or an explicit printed value shows ds2['lev'].dims is ('lev',). Resolving concrete setup blockers and then rerunning successfully is strong evidence because it leaves an executable reproduction path. A successful run via an activated environment and a successful run after pip-based dependency fixes are equivalent when both visibly demonstrate the same final mutation.

Contradictory evidence: Do not score a continuation as having reproduced the issue if its latest visible reproduction attempt exits with AttributeError about np.unicode_ or ModuleNotFoundError for packaging and there is no later successful rerun. Package installation alone, editable-install attempts, environment-file inspection, version printing, file listing, grep/sed browsing, or an assistant thought saying the issue is reproduced are not substitutes for visible successful reproduction output. Reading variable.py internals without a patch is diagnosis support only; it cannot compensate for missing visible reproduction.

Close-looking exclusions: Explicitly reject the misleading judge bias that a reproduction-plus-mechanism rubric should give a unique top score to read-only variable.py exploration or to post-reproduction browsing. In this paused view, detailed inspection of to_index_variable, to_base_variable, Variable.__init__, as_compatible_data, fastpath, or _maybe_wrap_data is not a valid tie-breaker over another continuation that already has the same visible exact reproduction and no patch. Different script names, random numeric values, conda versus pip environment setup, and dataset-display output versus explicit dims printing are equivalent valid ways to demonstrate the bug, provided the final mutated lev dimension is visible. Do not distinguish equivalent successful reproducers by step count, file name, command style, or extra superficial sed/grep commands after the successful run.

Abstention boundary: If output is truncated so the final mutated lev dimension or an explicit ds2['lev'].dims value is not visible, do not infer exact reproduction from returncode alone; mark it uncertain. If two or more continuations have the same visible exact reproduction and no patch or concrete causal fix, keep them tied in the top pre-patch tier rather than inventing a unique winner from browsing depth. If a later paused state contains source edits, switch to implementation correctness and validation evidence instead of this reproduction-only ranking.

experiences.title: Score xr.where keep_attrs fixes by x-only source semantics and preserving the None path
experiences.description: Use in this paused xarray xr.where(..., keep_attrs=True) scalar-argument round. A high-scoring continuation must preserve the source contract that keep_attrs=True keeps attrs from the original second argument x only, while keep_attrs=None still follows the existing option/default path. Do not rank a patched-looking continuation highly just because it fixes the scalar IndexError, passes existing where tests, or shows a few smoke-test attrs outputs.
experiences.context: The visible prompt shows the failing source: keep_attrs=None is first translated through _get_keep_attrs(default=False), and only keep_attrs is True uses a callback intended to keep attributes of x, the second parameter. The visible trajectories also show why attrs-list indexing is dangerous: tracing _all_of_type shows scalar x/y are absent from DataArray/Variable collections, so the attrs list passed to a combine callback is not necessarily the original three user arguments. Visible validation further shows the intended standalone behavior: x with attrs yields x attrs, y attrs are ignored when x lacks attrs, and a targeted patched run where x has no attrs but condition has attrs produces {'cond_attr': 'cond'}, which is a contract violation rather than a success.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply when comparing continuations for the xr.where scalar-second-argument keep_attrs=True failure, especially where some continuations have a changed computation.py file or passing smoke tests and others are still tracing _all_of_type, apply_ufunc, DataArray/Variable collection, or the x-vs-condition/y attrs contract.

Decisive positive evidence: Prefer continuations that make or are clearly preparing a source-semantic repair with both of these properties: (1) keep_attrs=True returns attrs from the original second argument x only; if x is a scalar, or x is a DataArray/Variable/Dataset with an empty attrs dict, the result attrs are {}; condition attrs and y attrs are never substituted; and (2) keep_attrs=None remains equivalent to the existing _get_keep_attrs(default=False) behavior and is not silently treated as keep_attrs=True. Valid implementations may close over the original x, insert position-preserving empty attrs for scalar arguments, convert scalars in a way that preserves original argument positions, or use another equivalent mechanism. Do not require one exact patch shape, but require evidence that the implementation is tied to original x rather than to the first non-empty attrs dict in the filtered attrs list.

Strong validation evidence includes explicit tests or reasoning for: scalar x with keep_attrs=True returns {}; x with attrs returns exactly x attrs; x without attrs returns {} even when the condition has attrs; x without attrs returns {} even when y has attrs; and the default keep_attrs=None path is not changed into x-attrs preservation. Source evidence that the None branch remains separate from the True branch is especially important.

Contradictory evidence: Any implementation that handles keep_attrs=True by falling back to attrs[0], scanning for the first non-empty attrs dict, or otherwise using condition/y attrs when x attrs are absent violates the contract. Any patch that combines keep_attrs is None with keep_attrs is True, or routes None through the same x-preserving callback, is also wrong because it changes the existing default-option path. A visible output where the case labeled like x has no attrs but condition has attrs returns {'cond_attr': 'cond'} is decisive negative evidence, even if the same continuation fixes the original IndexError or passes existing pytest selections. Likewise, smoke tests showing scalar x returns {}, condition-derived cases return {}, or x-with-attrs works are insufficient if they do not rule out condition/y fallback and None-path changes.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not treat basic xr.where without keep_attrs, the original scalar crash reproduction alone, or broad passing test output as proof of a correct fix. A test described as condition attrs may be weak if the condition was produced by an expression that dropped attrs or if x/y are scalars and the hard DataArray-x-without-attrs case is absent. DataArray.where method behavior can inform the intended analogy but is not itself proof that standalone xr.where preserves only the standalone second argument. Reading git history, showing commit metadata, grepping tests, or validating unrelated where behavior should not outrank source-semantic evidence. Reject the misleading judge bias that awards top credit to an apparently mature patch because it has a changed source file and passes smoke tests; for this round, source semantics and the None-path preservation are the decisive criteria.

Abstention boundary: If a continuation has only a file-change summary and no visible diff or targeted validation distinguishing x attrs from condition/y attrs, do not declare it correct; keep it uncertain or partial. If a no-patch continuation is actively tracing the actual attrs construction path, do not score it as a failed fix solely because it has not edited yet, but also do not grant implementation credit until the source-semantic repair is visible. If the visible evidence cannot determine whether keep_attrs=None was preserved, avoid inferring success from scalar-crash validation alone.

experiences.title: Gate requests session-header None fixes on target-source merge semantics and request override preservation
experiences.description: Use when judging continuations for the requests issue where setting a default session header such as session.headers['Accept-Encoding'] = None should suppress that header instead of sending the string/value None. Full credit requires visible changes in the target source that make None-valued session headers disappear during preparation while preserving existing request-level override behavior.
experiences.context: Activation evidence in the paused view includes the user report showing Accept-Encoding: None, reproduction output confirming the header is sent before the fix, inspection of requests/sessions.py and merge_setting, and the call site headers=merge_setting(request.headers, self.headers, dict_class=CaseInsensitiveDict). Several continuations edit or generate patches around merge_setting, but some only modify installed site-packages or emit manual patch files rather than leaving a tracked change in /testbed/requests/sessions.py.
experiences.experience:
Reject the misleading judge bias that reproducing the bug, printing 'Fix applied successfully', or passing ad-hoc tests after editing an installed environment is enough for a high score. Also reject the overly broad rubric that simply deleting every None-valued session_setting entry is automatically correct: the decisive semantic boundary is session defaults versus per-request overrides.

Decisive positive evidence: the visible diff or shown source in the target tree changes requests/sessions.py, merge_setting, or an equivalent header-preparation boundary so that a session header with value None is omitted from the prepared headers. The implementation must continue to allow request headers to override session defaults: if the session value is None but the request supplies a real value for the same header, the real request value must remain. Existing request-level None removal should still work. Ordinary non-None session headers, empty-string header values, and non-mapping merge_setting uses should not be broken. Equivalent valid implementations include filtering None values from the merged mapping after request values have been applied, or explicitly removing session None entries only when they were not overridden by request_setting.

Contradictory evidence: the only successful run is against /opt/.../site-packages while the target source has no changed file; the continuation only writes or cats a patch.txt without applying a tracked source change; the patch application is malformed or the final submission emits no usable patch; the implementation loops over session_setting and deletes every None key without a request-override guard or equivalent merged-value check; the logic would remove a request-supplied header just because the session default for that header was None; or validation uses a locally redefined merge_setting/CaseInsensitiveDict instead of importing the edited code and the visible diff is absent or wrong.

Close-looking exclusions: passing the original Accept-Encoding reproduction proves only that one scenario may be fixed, not that request overrides are preserved. A test labeled 'request overrides session header' is not sufficient unless it covers the specific case where the session header is None and the request supplies a real value. A manual unified diff with a plausible hunk is not the same as a visible target-source change. Deleting the header from session.headers manually is the user workaround, not evidence of a code fix. Broad exploration of tests in unrelated temporary paths should not compensate for missing or incorrect merge_setting semantics.

Abstention boundary: if the paused view truncates the actual condition in the merge_setting change or does not reveal whether the change is in the target source versus an installed copy, preserve uncertainty and avoid maximum credit. If only diagnosis is visible with no applied or submitted source change, score at diagnosis level. If a visible patch suppresses session None values but the request-override case is ambiguous, give partial credit rather than assuming correctness.

experiences.title: Tuple-default Sphinx fixes: rank source/AST rendering proof above pre-existing live introspection checks
experiences.description: When judging this paused Sphinx tuple-default bug, do not give top credit merely for showing that live Python introspection or object_description can already print tuple defaults correctly. The visible parent trajectory showed that inspect.signature plus stringify_signature already produced color=(1, 1, 1) before any continuation-specific patch. Prefer continuations that visibly repair and validate the source/AST/documentation rendering path that can drop tuple parentheses.
experiences.context: The visible issue is that a documented method default color=(1, 1, 1) is rendered in HTML/signature text as color=1, 1, 1. In the visible parent record, a live class method tested through inspect.signature/stringify_signature already printed tuple defaults correctly, while signature_from_str stored parsed defaults as strings. Therefore, later repetitions of live default-type inspection are diagnostic but not decisive proof of fixing the broken documentation/source rendering path. The paused continuations include ast.py-only patches, source/AST unparse checks, signature_from_str checks, domain/autodoc browsing, and environment/build attempts.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply when the task is this Sphinx documentation/signature bug where tuple literal defaults lose parentheses, and the visible trajectory contains the pre-patch fact that live inspect.signature/stringify_signature already renders the tuple default correctly. Activate especially when comparing continuations that changed sphinx/pycode/ast.py or explored signature_from_str, object_description, autodoc, or Python-domain argument parsing.

Decisive positive evidence: Highest credit should go to a continuation that changes the actual source/AST/rendering path responsible for textual default rendering and then validates that path. Strong visible evidence includes modifying visit_Tuple or an equivalent renderer and running sphinx.pycode.ast.unparse on parsed tuple expressions or parsed function defaults with output such as (1, 2, 3) and a function default displayed as (1, 2), not 1, 2. Even stronger code/evidence handles tuple syntax generally, including empty tuples as (), singleton tuples with the trailing comma, and multi-element tuples, while leaving non-tuple defaults alone. Equivalent valid implementations are acceptable if they demonstrate the final rendered documentation/signature text preserves color=(1, 1, 1); do not require one exact file or one exact edit shape.

Contradictory evidence: Do not treat object_description((1, 1, 1)), inspect.signature on a live method, or default-type printing from a live method as decisive validation in this round, because the visible parent trajectory already showed that path was correct before the continuation patch. Do not require signature_from_str to convert defaults into Python tuple/int/None objects; visible signature_from_str output with string defaults is a separate parser behavior and can be diagnostic without proving the main fix incomplete. Branches with no code change, only greps, only environment manipulation, or failed build setup should not outrank a plausible patch with direct source/AST rendering evidence.

Close-looking exclusions: A small ast.py change can be valid, but do not automatically prefer an exactly one-line or minimal diff over a slightly broader ast.py tuple-rendering patch that visibly tests the unparser and appears to address tuple syntax edge cases. Conversely, a continuation that only explains that signature_from_str stores strings, or only contrasts live introspection with string parsing, is close-looking but weaker unless it also validates the changed source/AST/doc rendering path. Browsing autodoc or Python-domain arglist parsing is relevant exploration only if it leads to a concrete rendering fix. Dependency installation or uninstalling packages to make a sample build run is not repair evidence.

Explicit rejection of misleading bias: Reject the rubric/bias that awards top validation credit for live inspect.signature/object_description checks as if they prove the bug is fixed. In this paused view, those checks reproduced already-correct behavior before the patch. Also reject the bias that the best implementation must be the smallest ast.py diff; judge by demonstrated correctness of the rendered tuple-default syntax and preservation of equivalent valid implementations.

Abstention boundary: If the visible paused view only shows a diff summary without enough code or executed output to distinguish tuple syntax correctness, do not rank solely by line count or by whether later steps discuss signature_from_str. Treat multiple plausible rendering-path patches as potentially equivalent until direct output or code evidence separates them. If a continuation has not yet made a patch or has only explored files/tests, give exploration credit but do not infer a correct fix.

experiences.title: No-patch SparseCoder/Lasso prefixes: explicit max_iter causal insight beats broad source navigation, otherwise abstain
experiences.description: Use this for the paused SparseCoder task when continuations have no visible edits and only show exploration commands. Do not rank a continuation highest merely because it reads many related helper methods. In this state, the decisive public evidence is an explicit, visible connection between SparseCoder's lasso_cd path, the internal Lasso construction with fixed/default max_iter, and the lack of a user-facing way to pass that parameter.
experiences.context: The visible task reports that SparseCoder uses Lasso when transform_algorithm='lasso_cd', that Lasso defaults max_iter to 1000, and that SparseCoder currently does not expose a way for the user to control max_iter or similar Lasso estimator parameters. The paused continuations show no changed files, no untracked files, no diff, and zero visible edit characters. They consist of reading dict_learning.py, reading coordinate_descent.py, grepping for Lasso or _set_sparse_coding_params, opening the example, trying to run the example, or trying environment setup commands.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply this rule when the paused view shows only no-edit exploration for the SparseCoder/Lasso max_iter issue: changed_files is None, no untracked files are shown, no diff is visible, and current_patch_chars is 0 for the continuations being compared. The visible actions must concern SparseCoder, sparse_encode/_sparse_encode, transform_algorithm='lasso_cd', Lasso/ElasticNet constructor parameters, or the sparse coding example.

Decisive positive evidence: The strongest exploration evidence is an agent-authored thought or plainly visible code output that ties together the full causal mechanism: SparseCoder with transform_algorithm='lasso_cd' reaches the _sparse_encode lasso_cd branch; that branch constructs a Lasso estimator with max_iter fixed at/defaulting to 1000; Lasso or its base constructor accepts max_iter; and SparseCoder.__init__/_set_sparse_coding_params does not expose or forward that parameter for the user. A continuation that explicitly states this mechanism should be ranked above one that merely reads surrounding methods without saying what the missing parameter-flow problem is.

Contradictory evidence: Do not give high credit to broad source navigation alone. Reading _set_sparse_coding_params, transform, sparse_encode, and _sparse_encode in several slices is only partial evidence unless the visible prefix identifies max_iter and the missing exposure/forwarding path. Similarly, reading only the Lasso/ElasticNet constructor is estimator-side partial evidence, not a complete SparseCoder causal trace. Explicitly reject the misleading scoring bias that treats more file slices, more helper-method navigation, or more commands as better than a clear causal insight about the lasso_cd Lasso construction and missing max_iter flow. Also reject any visible misconception that max_iter is already user-exposed through SparseCoder, that a failed import proves the reported issue is invalid, or that invoking the example validates a future fix.

Close-looking exclusions: Running examples that fail with missing numpy, missing Cython, working-directory warnings, or other setup tracebacks is neither validation success nor implementation failure in this no-edit state. A shell pipeline may return success while still printing a traceback; treat the traceback as an unsuccessful run, not as proof about the SparseCoder fix. A wrong grep path for coordinate_descent followed by continued search is normal exploration and should not outweigh an already stated mechanism. Opening the sparse coding example can provide context, but it is not evidence of parameter propagation. If later visible edits appear, preserve equivalent valid approaches: an explicit max_iter parameter, a carefully routed estimator-parameter mechanism, or another compatible public API could all be valid; do not require one exact design from an exploration-only prefix.

Abstention boundary: If all visible continuations remain no-edit prefixes and none clearly states the full causal mechanism, do not manufacture a unique implementation-quality ranking. Tie them at low-to-neutral exploration credit or abstain from implementation scoring. Only separate continuations when the visible evidence clearly differs: complete explicit causal tracing should rank highest; single-sided constructor or helper-method inspection should be partial; environment setup and failed example runs should not decide the ranking.

experiences.title: Submission Signal Absence Outweighs Validation Breadth When Fixes Are Equivalent
experiences.description: Retrieve this when comparing continuations with equivalent valid fixes where some have submitted and others are paused. A continuation whose final visible action is showing a git diff without any submission command (e.g., no COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT) has not completed the task, regardless of how much validation it performed. Do not rank such a continuation above one that submits with adequate validation covering reproduction, edge cases, and integration scenarios, even if the former ran the existing test suite. When fixes are equivalent (e.g., adding tzinfo=d.tzinfo as a keyword argument vs adding d.microsecond, d.tzinfo as positional arguments — both valid), the differentiator is submission status combined with validation adequacy, not raw test count or suite execution breadth.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent trajectories during the validation/submission phase when comparing continuations that produce equivalent valid implementations of the same localized fix. Most relevant when a paused continuation shows broader test execution (e.g., running the existing test suite via the project test runner with 17+ tests passing) but lacks a submission signal in its final steps, while a submitted continuation has adequate but narrower validation (reproduction + edge cases + integration tests). Less relevant when fix quality differs between continuations — in that case fix quality dominates. Also less relevant when no continuation has submitted — submission status cannot differentiate. Do not retrieve merely because a continuation is paused; retrieve when a paused continuation without a submission signal is being ranked above a submitted continuation with adequate validation. Abstain when the visible prefix is too short to determine whether a paused continuation is still progressing toward submission or has stopped, or when the task's contract requires existing test suite execution as a necessary condition.
experiences.experience: The prior rubric's principle that 'a continuation that submits after only the simple case passes should not be ranked above continuations that show active investigation, even if the latter have not yet submitted' was useful when the submitted continuation truly only tested the simple reproduction case. However, it becomes actively misleading when the submitted continuation has validated reproduction, edge cases, and integration scenarios (e.g., template filter tests, timezone edge cases, future-date handling). A submitted continuation with this level of validation has demonstrated adequate contract coverage for a localized fix such as adding a parameter to a datetime constructor. A paused continuation that additionally runs the existing test suite via the project test runner has more test execution evidence but an incomplete outcome — its final visible action is showing a git diff without any submission command (e.g., no COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT). The discriminating evidence is whether the submitted continuation's validation covers the reported scenario AND important edge cases, not whether it runs the full existing test suite. When fixes are equivalent (e.g., adding tzinfo=d.tzinfo as a keyword argument vs adding d.microsecond, d.tzinfo as positional arguments to a datetime constructor — both valid implementations that preserve timezone awareness), the differentiator should be submission status combined with validation adequacy, not raw test count or suite execution breadth alone. Explicitly reject the bias that 'more test execution = better continuation' when the continuation with more tests never signals submission.
