experiences.title: Django messages LEVEL_TAGS: carry forward parent-visible dynamic level_tag evidence and prefer verified default-merge/assignment behavior over selected green smoke tests
experiences.description: Use this round-specific review when judging the Django messages @override_settings LEVEL_TAGS task in the paused view. The key correction is to carry forward the parent-visible source evidence that Message.level_tag already calls current settings dynamically, then distinguish continuations by concrete LEVEL_TAGS compatibility behavior such as partial-override default merging, restoration after override, and direct assignment/save-restore evidence. Do not rank a branch highest merely because it later prints a selected 9-test OK result or an 'All tests passed!' smoke message.
experiences.context: Activation conditions: the visible issue says Message.level_tag returns an empty string for tags introduced with @override_settings; the parent or continuation view shows django.contrib.messages.storage.base.Message.level_tag changed to a dynamic lookup such as utils.get_level_tags().get(self.level, ''); and continuations are comparing LEVEL_TAGS proxy/backward-compatibility edits plus message-storage validation commands. Apply during implementation and validation ranking for this paused round. Do not activate for unrelated message framework changes, pure submission/patch-file logistics, or views where the relevant source/test evidence is not visible.
experiences.experience:
Decisive positive evidence: carry parent state into each continuation. In this paused view, the Parent 2 source print already shows Message.level_tag returning utils.get_level_tags().get(self.level, ''). A later continuation from that parent inherits this core fix unless it visibly reverses it; it does not need to reprint the same diff to receive implementation credit. Stronger evidence is a continuation that then shows a LEVEL_TAGS implementation intended as a dynamic dict-like object, includes visible comments or grep hits about reading settings and allowing module-level assignment, and validates behavior with concrete outputs: a partial MESSAGE_TAGS override changes INFO to a custom tag while omitted defaults such as DEBUG, SUCCESS, WARNING, and ERROR remain present; Message.level_tag restores to the default value after the override exits; and a base.LEVEL_TAGS assignment/save-restore pattern runs without exception and prints the before/after mappings. This combination is stronger than merely showing selected test names passing because it exercises the exact contract and the legacy surface that the edits touched.

Contradictory evidence: a later selected subset such as three or nine message tests returning OK, or a hand-written script ending with 'All tests passed!', is not by itself decisive if the branch also has unresolved earlier returncode 1 commands for broader message classes/modules, lacks visible LEVEL_TAGS assignment/save-restore evidence, or never demonstrates that partial overrides merge with default tags. A proxy that visibly only supports a few methods like get(), keys(), values(), and items(), or a smoke test that only uses keys()/items() rather than direct mapping/assignment behavior, should not receive full backward-compatibility credit. An implementation that reads settings.MESSAGE_TAGS alone without showing default fallback/merge is weaker; output that customizes several explicit levels but omits evidence for an unmentioned default level does not prove the merge contract. A validation NameError or failed command remains negative until rerun successfully, but shell path mistakes around patch.txt are not implementation defects when the actual source diff is visible elsewhere.

Close-looking exclusions: do not require the helper or proxy to have one exact name. A direct dynamic Message.level_tag implementation can be valid without making the module-level LEVEL_TAGS object dynamic, provided the legacy name remains harmlessly accessible and the branch does not claim or depend on stronger proxy semantics. Conversely, if a branch replaces LEVEL_TAGS with a proxy and advertises compatibility, judge the proxy by observable mapping and assignment behavior, not by its class name or patch size. Broad ad-hoc Django test commands that fail because of setup/configuration issues should be weighed by their visible traceback; a bare returncode 1 is a negative signal but cannot outweigh concrete source and focused behavioral evidence by itself. Patch size alone is not decisive: a large edit is positive only when paired with visible default-merge/restoration/assignment behavior, and a smaller edit remains acceptable if it preserves equivalent public behavior.

Misleading rubric or judge bias to reject: reject any scoring pattern that demands every continuation re-display the Message.level_tag diff even though it was already visible in the parent state. Also reject ranking a branch highest simply because it prints a later selected OK run or confident success message while providing less evidence about default merging and LEVEL_TAGS assignment semantics. The dominant public contract is dynamic Message.level_tag resolution under @override_settings; LEVEL_TAGS compatibility is secondary and should be credited only to the extent the visible implementation or tests show real legacy behavior.

Abstention boundary: if the visible parent/continuation state does not show the level_tag source, the LEVEL_TAGS replacement semantics, or behavioral outputs for override/default restoration, do not infer correctness from summaries or intent. If all candidate continuations share the inherited dynamic level_tag change and none shows distinguishable proxy/default-merge/assignment evidence or meaningful test outcomes, treat them as tied or unobservable rather than preferring the branch with the loudest final success text.

experiences.title: Pytest mark expression: escape reserved-looking identifiers, do not convert them to Python literals
experiences.description: Use this when judging paused trajectories for the pytest `Expression.compile('False')` Python 3.8+ AST compiler crash. The decisive issue is not merely making `compile()` accept `True`, `False`, or `None`; it is preserving pytest mark-expression identifier lookup semantics while avoiding forbidden raw Python AST names.
experiences.context: Activation conditions: the prompt or visible trajectory shows `Expression.compile('False')` crashing or raising `ValueError: identifier field can't represent 'False' constant`, references Python 3.8+ debug/non-debug AST compiler behavior, and inspects `src/_pytest/mark/expression.py`, especially `not_expr`, `ast.Name`, `ast.NameConstant`/`ast.Constant`, or `MatcherAdapter`. The grammar visible in the file treats `True`, `False`, and `None` as identifier spellings in the custom expression language, resolved through the matcher mapping during evaluation. A local Python 3.10 non-debug `ValueError` is relevant evidence for the same compiler rejection even if the original report describes a debug-build abort.
experiences.experience:
Core rule: reject the misleading rubric or judge bias that says the bug is simply that `True`, `False`, and `None` are parsed as `ast.Name` and should be converted to `ast.Constant` literals. That interpretation fixes host-AST compilation but can break pytest’s own expression language. A correct implementation may prefix, escape, wrap, or otherwise represent these spellings so the Python compiler accepts the AST, but evaluation must still call the matcher for the original identifier string. Do not require one exact patch shape; equivalent implementations are valid if they satisfy this contract.

Decisive positive evidence: source inspection or a visible diff shows the identifier path no longer emits raw `ast.Name('True'/'False'/'None')` while still routing those names through `MatcherAdapter` or an equivalent lookup; the implementation escapes or renames AST identifiers and unescapes them before calling the matcher, or otherwise preserves matcher dispatch. Strong tests are discriminating tests, not truth-table coincidences: for example, `Expression.compile('False').evaluate(lambda name: True)` should return true if `False` is still an identifier; `Expression.compile('True').evaluate(lambda name: False)` should return false; `Expression.compile('None').evaluate(lambda name: True)` should return true rather than `None`; and a matcher that records keys should observe `'True'`, `'False'`, or `'None'`. Mixed expressions such as `'True and foo'` are useful when they prove both reserved-looking and ordinary identifiers use the same lookup semantics. It is also positive when a trajectory explicitly realizes that an earlier literal-conversion patch was wrong and then changes the implementation to preserve identifier semantics; judge the latest visible state, while preserving uncertainty if the final code is not shown.

Contradictory evidence: a patch that branches on `ident.value == 'True'`, `'False'`, or `'None'` and returns `ast.Constant(True)`, `ast.Constant(False)`, or `ast.Constant(None)` for those tokens is evidence against semantic correctness unless it separately proves matcher lookup is still performed. Outputs such as `False evaluates to: False`, `True evaluates to: True`, `None evaluates to: None`, `True and False evaluates to: False`, or `not False evaluates to: True` are weak or contradictory when they are presented as final validation, because they are exactly what Python literals would do. Likewise, saying that these tokens are “actual boolean constants,” validating only that `Expression.compile('False')` succeeds, or testing only a normal identifier such as `foo` does not prove the required behavior. Failed attempts to install or run the broader test suite do not outweigh a semantic violation.

Close-looking exclusions: `Expression.compile('False')` followed by evaluation with `lambda x: False` is not discriminating, because both a literal `False` and a matcher-returned `False` produce the same output. `Expression.compile('True')` with `lambda x: True` is similarly non-discriminating. Merely checking for `ast.Constant` availability, adding version guards, or replacing `NameConstant` for the empty-expression case is adjacent but not enough. A trajectory that only reproduces the current interpreter’s `ValueError` has located the compatibility symptom, not the correct project-language fix.

Abstention boundary: if the paused view is truncated after a file-change summary, a patch script, or mid-debugging commands and does not show the settled code or a discriminating matcher test, do not infer full correctness from diff size or from compilation success. Award partial diagnostic credit for locating `not_expr`/`MatcherAdapter` and for recognizing the identifier-vs-literal problem, but reserve top credit for visible evidence that the final implementation both compiles on Python 3.8+ behavior and preserves matcher-based identifier semantics for `True`, `False`, and `None`.

experiences.title: Second manual correction: Do Not Treat make_model_tuple/App-Registry Speculation as Decisive for Mixed-Case App Lazy References
experiences.description:
SECOND-PASS MANDATORY RULE: Prioritize the causal make_model_tuple and app-label normalization mismatch over command volume or early file contact.

Positive visible evidence: Concrete registry-key and mixed-case app-label normalization chain.
Contradictory or insufficient visible evidence: Serializer or autodetector browsing without the registry mismatch.

For the Django mixed-case app-name ForeignKey task, a continuation should not be ranked highest merely because it confidently names make_model_tuple or app_configs as the cause. The visible prompt uses a class ForeignKey, not a lower-case string reference, so a strong diagnosis must explain how Django generated the lower-case lazy reference from a mixed-case installed app. Without reproduction, patch, or tracing through relation deconstruction/migration state/model option labels, this is only partial exploration.
experiences.context: The task reports a lazy-reference error: a field in app DJ_RegLogin refers to 'dj_reglogin.category', but app 'dj_reglogin' is not installed. The visible user model defines category = models.ForeignKey(Category, on_delete=models.CASCADE), i.e. a class reference in the same app, while INSTALLED_APPS contains 'DJ_RegLogin'. In the paused trajectories, no continuation has changed files or shown a passing reproduction. Several branches inspect model_checks.py, apps/registry.py, fields/related.py, and django/db/models/utils.py; one branch states that make_model_tuple does not normalize app_label and that app_configs uses the mixed-case key, but it has not traced why the class ForeignKey became the lower-case string 'dj_reglogin.category'.
experiences.experience:
Second manual correction after inspecting the failed generated rubric and evidence-first scores:
Prioritize the causal make_model_tuple and app-label normalization mismatch over command volume or early file contact.

Credit only this visible evidence: Concrete registry-key and mixed-case app-label normalization chain.
Reject or cap this visible evidence: Serializer or autodetector browsing without the registry mismatch.
Abstain when: Keep branches tied if no causal normalization difference is visible.

Do not let another retrieved experience replace this task-specific rule with a generic process proxy.

Activation: Apply this when judging paused pre-patch diagnosis for the mixed-case Django app-name ForeignKey issue, especially when branches have no diff, no successful reproduction, and only source exploration around lazy references, app registry lookup, related fields, or make_model_tuple.

Decisive positive evidence: Prefer a continuation that notices the prompt’s ForeignKey is a class reference (ForeignKey(Category)), not a user-written lower-case string, and therefore traces or proposes tracing the path that serializes/deconstructs that class relation into a lazy reference. Strong visible signals include inspecting or explicitly naming ForeignKey.deconstruct(), migration ModelState/ProjectState construction, remote_field.model._meta.label_lower, Options.label_lower, or an equivalent code path where the app-label component could be lowercased. A strong diagnosis states the invariant: preserve or correctly match the installed mixed-case app label while still handling model-name normalization, then validate with a mixed-case app containing a class ForeignKey.

Partial positive evidence: Reading model_checks.py app_model_error(), apps.get_app_config(), lazy_model_operation(), resolve_relation(), or make_model_tuple is relevant symptom investigation. It shows the agent is near the lazy-reference machinery, but by itself it does not establish the root cause for this prompt.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation that confidently says “now I understand” and blames make_model_tuple or app_configs mismatch without explaining how Django produced 'dj_reglogin.category' from ForeignKey(Category) has not completed the causal chain. The observation that make_model_tuple lowercases the model name, or that get_app_config is case-sensitive, does not prove that the app label was incorrectly lowercased. Blaming string-reference parsing is especially weak because the visible user code does not pass a string to ForeignKey.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not confuse resolve_relation() behavior for unqualified string relations with the class-reference path shown in the prompt. Do not treat related_name interpolation using cls._meta.app_label.lower() as the reported lazy-reference source unless the trajectory connects it to the failing field reference. Do not treat model_checks.py as the root cause; it formats the pending lazy-operation error after the bad key already exists. A case-insensitive registry lookup or another implementation could be valid, but only if the continuation explains why it preserves app-label semantics and validates the mixed-case class-ForeignKey scenario.

Misleading pattern rejected: Reject the judging bias that rewards a fluent, confident make_model_tuple/app-registry story as a high-quality diagnosis. In this round, that story is incomplete and likely misdirected unless it accounts for the class ForeignKey and the generation of the lower-case lazy reference. Confidence and relevant file names are not substitutes for the missing causal step.

Abstention boundary: If no continuation has reproduced the issue, applied a patch, or traced the class-ForeignKey-to-lowercase-lazy-reference path, do not single out one branch as clearly superior solely for mentioning make_model_tuple or app_configs. Treat such branches as early partial exploration and rank them close together, while reserving higher scores for visible causal tracing, implementation, or validation evidence.

experiences.title: For draggable-legend pickling, prefer target-source fixes over repeated root-cause or upstream-version inspection
experiences.description: Use this round-specific guidance when judging paused continuations for the Matplotlib draggable legend pickling bug after the parent trajectory has already localized the issue to draggable state holding an unpicklable canvas. At this stage, source modification in the target checkout is stronger evidence than additional greps, installed-version inspection, or backend reproductions that do not exercise a patch.
experiences.context: The visible bug report is about pickling a figure with a draggable legend, with the observed error `TypeError: cannot pickle 'FigureCanvasQTAgg' object`. The visible parent trajectory has already identified the relevant owner area: `/testbed/lib/matplotlib/offsetbox.py`, especially `DraggableBase`, which stores `self.canvas = self.ref_artist.figure.canvas`. Several continuations only inspect `_connect_picklable`, try backends, or inspect an installed newer Matplotlib, while others visibly have changes to `lib/matplotlib/offsetbox.py`. Because localization and root cause are already present before the continuations, the decisive question is whether the continuation makes a plausible target-checkout implementation that prevents unpicklable draggable state from being serialized, not whether it rediscovers the same facts.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions:
- Apply when the paused continuation is for the draggable legend / draggable annotation pickling issue and the visible trajectory has already localized the failure to `DraggableBase` or related draggable classes in `offsetbox.py`.
- Apply especially when comparing branches where some have `changed_files` / `diff_stat` / `current_patch_chars` showing edits to `lib/matplotlib/offsetbox.py`, while others only create test scripts, run backend experiments, grep `_connect_picklable`, or inspect an installed Matplotlib implementation.

Decisive positive evidence:
- A visible target-checkout source change in `lib/matplotlib/offsetbox.py`, especially around `DraggableBase`, `DraggableOffsetBox`, `DraggableAnnotation`, or shared draggable state handling.
- A patch that plausibly prevents the unpicklable canvas object from being serialized while preserving draggable behavior. Equivalent valid approaches include, for example, excluding or rebuilding `canvas` during pickle/unpickle, avoiding persistent storage of the canvas in pickled state, using picklable disconnectors/callback state, or otherwise ensuring draggable legend and annotation objects do not retain backend canvas objects in their pickle state.
- The implementation preserves existing event lifecycle behavior: pick/motion/release callbacks, disconnect behavior, `_use_blit` handling, and support for both draggable legends and draggable annotations through the shared base layer.
- Validation attempts that visibly target `/testbed`, such as `cd /testbed` with `PYTHONPATH=/testbed/lib`, are aligned with the code under change. Failing to load Tk or Qt in a headless/missing-dependency environment should not outweigh a plausible target-source patch.
- Editable-install or metadata-generation failures are setup evidence, not proof that a visible source patch is bad.

Decisive contradictory evidence:
- No visible source patch: `changed_files` empty, `current_patch_chars` zero, and only untracked test scripts. This is investigation, not a fix.
- Continuing to grep or inspect `_connect_picklable` after the parent has already found `DraggableBase` does not by itself advance implementation quality.
- Inspecting an installed newer Matplotlib with plain `python -c "import matplotlib..."` is not evidence that the target checkout was fixed. It can be useful reference discovery only if the continuation then translates the idea into a target-source patch.
- A successful `pickle.dumps` using the Agg backend is not decisive for the reported `FigureCanvasQTAgg` failure; it may be a false-negative reproduction under easier conditions.
- Backend setup failures such as missing `tkinter`, missing Qt bindings, or headless Tk errors are not implementation failures when the continuation was trying to target the right checkout.
- An intent to patch or test site-packages, or validation against an installed version that may already behave differently, must not be treated as completion of the target task.

Close-looking exclusions:
- Untracked files such as `test_pickle.py`, `test_pickle_qt.py`, or similar scripts do not count as a fix unless accompanied by a target source change.
- Reading `legend.py`, class hierarchy, or upstream/newer `DraggableBase` source is not enough once the root cause has already been identified in the visible parent trajectory.
- Finding existing `_connect_picklable` calls in `offsetbox.py` or `cbook.py` is diagnostic only unless the continuation changes how draggable state is serialized or disconnected.
- Do not require one exact implementation shape. A correct fix need not literally use `__getstate__`/`__setstate__` if it otherwise visibly prevents unpicklable backend canvas state from being serialized and preserves behavior. Conversely, a change only in `Legend.set_draggable`, `Figure`, or a backend-specific canvas class is not equivalent unless the visible patch clearly covers draggable annotations and the shared draggable base semantics.
- Do not credit truncated or unseen command output beyond what is visible. If the diff content is not shown, use the file-change summary as implementation-attempt evidence but do not assume full semantic correctness.

Abstention boundary:
- If patch content is not visible, do not infer exact correctness from insertion count alone. Prefer a plausible target-source patch over no patch, but preserve uncertainty about whether the implementation is complete.
- If all branches lack a source patch, judge only diagnosis and targeting; avoid extreme implementation scores.
- If validation target is unobservable, do not infer success or failure from the test output alone.

Rejected misleading rubric or judge bias:
- Do not rank a continuation highest merely because it inspects a newer installed Matplotlib implementation, traces `_connect_picklable`, or articulates the root cause that was already visible in the parent trajectory. In this paused state, that bias rewards repeated diagnosis over implementation. The stronger signal is a visible, target-checkout source change that addresses unpicklable draggable state, with any validation interpreted in light of whether it actually exercised the modified checkout and the relevant backend conditions.

experiences.title: Django Subparser Round: Conditional Parser-Class Propagation Beats Private argparse Action Reimplementation
experiences.description: Use for the Django management-command subparser error-formatting round when judging implementation quality from the paused view. The key semantic requirement is two-sided: CommandParser-created subparsers must inherit Django’s error-formatting arguments, while a non-CommandParser custom parser_class must not be given Django-only constructor kwargs. Prefer a minimal parser_class wrapper or equivalent conditional propagation over an elaborate private _SubParsersAction reimplementation that unconditionally injects those kwargs.
experiences.context: The issue concerns django.core.management.base.CommandParser.add_subparsers(). In the visible paused view, one parent path writes a management command using CustomParser(argparse.ArgumentParser) via parser.add_subparsers(required=True, parser_class=CustomParser), then runs python manage.py test_subcommand create and gets return code 2 with clean argparse usage/error output and no traceback. The same path then restores the default parser case and again gets clean usage/error output for the missing child argument. Another visible path shows a source diff/edit introducing class _CommandSubParsersAction(argparse._SubParsersAction), manually reconstructing CommandParser.add_subparsers internals, and an add_parser() body that sets missing_args_message and called_from_command_line before super().add_parser(). That source shape is close-looking but semantically risky because it injects Django-only kwargs without visibly preserving arbitrary custom parser_class behavior.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply only for this Django CommandParser subparser task, especially when a branch has visible source edits around CommandParser.add_subparsers(), _SubParsersAction, parser_class, missing_args_message, or called_from_command_line, or when the cumulative visible path includes CLI checks for both default subparsers and parser_class=CustomParser. Score the cumulative visible path, but make the ranking hinge on parser-class semantics, not on diff size or the presence of a private action class.

Decisive positive evidence: Strong implementation evidence is a source pattern that leaves argparse’s add_subparsers machinery intact while conditionally wrapping the parser_class: obtain the requested parser_class, inject missing_args_message and called_from_command_line only when the constructed parser is CommandParser or a CommandParser subclass, leave unrelated argparse.ArgumentParser subclasses untouched, and delegate back to super().add_subparsers(**kwargs). Equivalent valid implementations are acceptable; the exact wrapper name or layout is not required. Strong behavioral evidence for the same semantics is the visible custom parser case: a command defining CustomParser(argparse.ArgumentParser), using parser.add_subparsers(required=True, parser_class=CustomParser), and then producing a clean usage/error message for manage.py test_subcommand create with no TypeError, no Traceback, and no CommandError stack trace. The default parser case should also produce clean usage/error output for the missing child argument. Return code 2 is expected and positive for invalid CLI input when paired with clean argparse-style output.

Decisive contradictory evidence: Treat as low implementation evidence a diff or edit that introduces a private _CommandSubParsersAction subclass and manually reimplements argparse internals such as self._subparsers, _get_formatter(), _pop_action_class(), and _add_action(), while its add_parser() unconditionally adds missing_args_message and called_from_command_line to kwargs before calling super().add_parser(). That code shape risks passing Django-only kwargs into a non-CommandParser custom parser_class, contradicting the visible CustomParser compatibility requirement. It should not receive top implementation credit merely because it visibly propagates two parameter names. Also contradictory: no visible guard or wrapper around parser_class, no custom parser_class validation after such a reimplementation, or later cleanup commands that only claim whitespace fixes without showing a semantic guard or rerunning the custom parser case.

Close-looking exclusions: A private _CommandSubParsersAction is not inherently the target fix; it is only acceptable if the visible code preserves custom parser_class semantics and does not blindly inject CommandParser-only kwargs. Existing user_commands call_command snippets that print passed are weaker because they exercise programmatic or existing command behavior, not the reported CLI stack-trace path with a custom parser class. Passing basic commands such as unrelated management command checks, a small unrelated admin_scripts run, or output saying all basic command tests passed does not cure a parser_class regression. Failed test loads, zero-test runs, pytest output hidden by head, ModuleNotFoundError, ImproperlyConfigured, _FailedTest, or FAILED(errors=1) are not validation. Conversely, a continuation that only explores files after inheriting the visible clean CustomParser and default-parser CLI behavior should not lose that semantic evidence unless it later visibly rewrites the relevant parser code.

Explicit rejection of misleading bias: Reject any rubric shortcut that treats a visible _CommandSubParsersAction class, a long diff, or an add_parser override as the preferred implementation. The task is not to reimplement argparse’s private subparser action; it is to propagate Django’s extra CommandParser arguments without breaking custom parser_class. An unguarded private action reimplementation is a false-positive implementation pattern and must rank below a minimal conditional parser_class wrapper or equivalent semantics, even if the former has more visible code or more unrelated test activity.

Abstention boundary: If the visible source is truncated before the parser_class handling and there is no custom parser_class CLI run, do not infer either success or regression from intent statements or class names alone. A branch with only default-subparser clean output but no source and no custom parser_class evidence can receive limited core-behavior credit, but not top semantic-implementation credit. If a branch has clean custom parser behavior and default behavior, then later only exploration or failed setup commands appear, keep the inherited semantic credit. If it later visibly edits CommandParser.add_subparsers() again without a confirming diff or rerun of the custom parser case, preserve uncertainty about the final state rather than upgrading it.

experiences.title: Do not overrank opaque _print_Subs edits over visible AssocOp structural investigation for Subs LaTeX parenthesizing
experiences.description: Activate for the paused SymPy LaTeX Subs parenthesizing task when comparing trajectories that either inspect or rewrite _print_Subs, investigate precedence/parenthesize helpers, or search for AssocOp as the structural basis for wrapping the substituted expression. Score the visible evidence of the solution mechanism, not mere edit activity or file localization.
experiences.context: The visible issue is that LaTeX printing of a Subs expression with an additive body renders the body next to the evaluation bar without grouping, e.g. it should render with explicit parentheses around the substituted expression before the bar. In this paused view, some trajectories investigate precedence values or derivative parenthesization patterns, one trajectory performs an opaque scripted replacement of _print_Subs with no visible diff or validation output, and another trajectory explicitly pivots to locating and understanding AssocOp. The relevant ranking distinction is whether the trajectory is moving toward structural grouping of the Subs body rather than conditional precedence-based formatting or unverifiable text replacement.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions:
- Apply only to the Subs LaTeX parenthesizing task where the visible paused evidence includes solution-direction investigation around sympy/printing/latex.py, precedence.py, _print_Subs, _print_Derivative, parenthesize, or AssocOp.
- Especially apply when a trajectory that merely touches or rewrites _print_Subs appears to be competing with a trajectory that is still investigating AssocOp or structural expression classes.

Decisive positive evidence:
- Strongly favor a trajectory that visibly investigates AssocOp as the structural condition for grouping the Subs body, including commands/thoughts such as searching for `class AssocOp`, locating it in core operations code, and asking which classes inherit from or use AssocOp.
- Further positive evidence includes identifying that additive/multiplicative associative bodies need grouping before the evaluation bar, or planning/implementing wrapping in the actual _print_Subs rendering path based on expression structure rather than on precedence comparison.
- A direct _print_Subs implementation is also valid if the visible diff or validation output proves the correct rendered behavior. Do not require the literal name AssocOp if the visible implementation equivalently groups the relevant expression structures and preserves appropriate output for non-problematic bodies.

Contradictory evidence:
- Treat as weak or negative a trajectory that focuses on precedence values such as Subs having precedence 1000 while Add has lower precedence, or studies _print_Derivative/parenthesize with PRECEDENCE['Mul'] as the apparent solution pattern. That line of investigation points toward conditional precedence formatting, which is the misleading approach here.
- Treat reproduction-only work, dependency installation, or checking the current LaTeX output as insufficient once other trajectories contain mechanism evidence.
- Treat an opaque scripted replacement of _print_Subs as non-decisive when the visible view does not show the new method body, a diff, or a post-change LaTeX output. A printed `Done` from a replacement script is not evidence that the correct structural wrapping was implemented.

Close-looking exclusions:
- Do not give high credit merely for opening _print_Subs or for knowing the likely file location. Localization is not the same as the correct wrapping mechanism.
- Do not penalize a trajectory for first searching for AssocOp in the wrong file if it then searches the codebase and finds the class definition.
- Do not count checking _print_Limit or other nearby printer methods as positive by itself; it is only useful if followed by structural reasoning about the Subs body.
- Do not treat expression-tree inspection or tests of standalone Subs(Add), Subs(Mul), and Subs(Pow) as decisive unless the trajectory draws the structural conclusion or implements/verifies the corrected rendering.
- Do not penalize brief precedence exploration if the trajectory later pivots clearly to structural wrapping.

Misleading rubric/bias to reject:
- Explicitly reject the bias that an attempted edit or scripted replacement of _print_Subs should outrank a trajectory visibly investigating AssocOp. In this paused view, an unverifiable edit with hidden/truncated replacement content is weaker than visible evidence that the agent is identifying the structural class mechanism needed for a correct fix.
- Also reject the rubric shortcut that treats `_print_Subs return-format inspection` as automatically equivalent to correct explicit wrapping. It is high-value only when the visible evidence shows the actual wrapping rule or final output, not when the changed method body is absent from view.

Abstention boundary:
- If the visible trajectory contains only setup, reproduction, or file browsing with no mechanism direction, keep the score low-to-middle rather than inferring future success.
- If a trajectory has an opaque edit but no visible diff or validation, do not assign a top score; preserve uncertainty.
- If multiple trajectories visibly implement or validate equivalent correct structural grouping in _print_Subs, preserve them as equivalent rather than preferring a particular internal spelling.

experiences.title: Target Mixed-Case App Migration Behavior, Not Unrelated Green Suite Output
experiences.description: For the Django mixed-case app-name ForeignKey/makemigrations task, rank branches by visible evidence that the DJ_RegLogin/dj_reglogin lazy relation is resolved through the reported migration/model-loading path. Do not elevate a branch merely because it has an official-looking Django test command ending in OK when that command is generic, unrelated, or surrounded by failed-load tracebacks.
experiences.context: The paused view shows continuations for a Django bug where a mixed-case app name such as DJ_RegLogin produces a lowercase lazy relation like dj_reglogin.category and makemigrations/migrate can crash. Several branches attempt validation with a mix of targeted scripts, manage.py makemigrations/migrate commands, model-registry lookups, and generic Django test-suite invocations. One visually tempting pattern is a branch that runs an unrelated migration test successfully while many other commands in the same branch fail to load or configure tests. That should not outrank branches with direct mixed-case app and ForeignKey/migration evidence.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Use this experience when judging continuations for the mixed-case Django app-name ForeignKey/makemigrations issue, especially when visible evidence includes both targeted DJ_RegLogin/dj_reglogin checks and generic Django test-suite attempts.

Decisive positive evidence: Strong validation directly mentions and exercises the reported contract: a mixed-case app such as DJ_RegLogin is installed/imported; the lowercase lazy/model tuple dj_reglogin.category is resolved to DJ_RegLogin.models.Category; get_registered_model/get_model or ForeignKey remote_field.model resolves Category/Content correctly; and makemigrations/migrate succeeds for the mixed-case app. Especially strong visible outputs include `Migrations for 'DJ_RegLogin': ... Create model Category ... Create model Content`, `Applying DJ_RegLogin.0001_initial... OK`, `get_registered_model('dj_reglogin', 'category') = <class 'DJ_RegLogin.models.Category'>`, `make_model_tuple('dj_reglogin.category')` followed by successful model lookup, or creating a Content instance linked to a Category after migration setup. A relevant regression-suite pass, such as app-loading tests printing a nonzero test count and OK, is useful only after or alongside this issue-specific evidence.

Preserve equivalent valid implementations: Do not require one exact source edit. A solution may preserve app-label case earlier in relation serialization, perform a safe case-insensitive lookup at the registry boundary, or otherwise make the lowercase lazy reference resolve correctly. Judge the visible behavior and avoid penalizing an implementation solely because it differs mechanically from another valid approach.

Contradictory evidence: A branch is weaker when its main visible success is a generic test such as `migrations.test_state` with `Ran 63 tests ... OK` but the output does not mention DJ_RegLogin, dj_reglogin, Category, Content, ForeignKey lazy references, makemigrations, or the reported crash. It is especially contradictory if the same branch also shows repeated failed or mis-targeted commands: `apps_tests` or `migrations_tests` producing `unittest.loader._FailedTest`, `tests.apps.tests` or `tests.migrations.test_state` raising `RuntimeError: Model class ... doesn't declare an explicit app_label`, `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'settings'` or `No module named 'tests.settings'`, `TypeError: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not NoneType`, or pytest missing. These are setup/import/test-label failures, not validation of the bug fix. A shell lookup that only proves `get_registered_model('dj_reglogin', 'category')` works is helpful but not as strong as a branch that also demonstrates the migration command path succeeds.

Close-looking exclusions: (1) `python tests/runtests.py ... | head` or `| tail` may return code 0 because of the pipe even when the displayed output is a traceback; read the output, not just the return code. (2) `No changes detected` from makemigrations is not by itself proof that the crash was fixed; it may only mean an existing migration is already present. Prefer outputs that either create the mixed-case app migration, apply it, or explicitly resolve the lowercase lazy relation. (3) A generic migration-state test pass is not equivalent to reproducing the user scenario. It can be credited as secondary regression evidence, but it should not dominate issue-specific mixed-case app validation. (4) Failed attempts to run official tests do not become positive merely because their labels sound relevant. (5) Do not over-penalize branches that use custom targeted scripts when those scripts visibly construct the mixed-case app scenario and assert the exact registry/migration behavior; those scripts can be more probative than unrelated suite output.

Misleading pattern rejected: Reject the judge bias that an official-looking Django test command with an OK line should outrank direct targeted validation. For this task, a branch with targeted DJ_RegLogin/dj_reglogin resolution plus makemigrations/migrate evidence is stronger than a branch whose best clean result is an unrelated migration test and whose surrounding commands fail to load.

Abstention boundary: If all visible branches inherit the same earlier patch and none adds branch-specific evidence about DJ_RegLogin, dj_reglogin.category, makemigrations/migrate, or the reported lazy-reference failure, do not force a ranking based on generic test labels. If a branch contains both targeted success and a later targeted failure such as `Related model 'dj_reglogin.category' cannot be resolved`, treat the validation as contradictory/uncertain rather than fully successful. If output is truncated before the decisive assertion or migration result, do not infer success from the command name alone.

experiences.title: Invisible Patch Content with Test Success Must Not Outrank Visible Correct Fix Preservation
experiences.description: When one branch applies a new patch via a script whose content is not visible in the trajectory (truncated sed output, only 'Patch applied successfully!' shown), and another branch preserves a visible parent fix with correct logic, the branch with the invisible patch must not be ranked higher solely because it shows test success. Test success with an invisible patch is unverifiable and may mask regressions caught only by hidden tests. Require visible patch content before awarding top scores.
experiences.context: A Django JSONField has_key/has_keys/has_any_keys numeric key fix where the parent applied a compile_json_path_key function treating all rhs keys as object keys. Multiple continuations investigate 6 test failures caused by the parent's fix. One continuation (s07) applies a new patch (fix_patch3.py) whose content is not visible — the sed output at the next step is truncated so the actual code changes are hidden — yet shows all 87 tests passing and is ranked highest by the judge. Other continuations (s05, s06) preserve the parent's visible fix (shown via git diff) and investigate the root cause but show 6 test failures. The judge's top pick fails hidden tests while the preserving branches pass.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When judging branches where one applies a new patch via a script (e.g., fix_patch3.py) with content not visible in the trajectory — the post-patch sed/grep/cat output is truncated or does not show the changed lines — and another branch preserves a visible parent fix with logically correct logic.

Positive evidence: A branch that preserves a visible, logically correct fix (compile_json_path_key visible via git diff, treating rhs keys as object keys for has_key/has_keys/has_any_keys lookups) has stronger correctness evidence than a branch with an invisible patch, even if the latter shows all tests passing. The parent's compile_json_path_key approach is the correct fix for the reported issue because has_key lookups search for object keys, so the rhs key should always be treated as a string object key, not converted to an array index. A branch that preserves this visible fix and investigates the root cause of the 6 secondary test failures (KeyTransform chains where intermediate numeric keys should be array indices) demonstrates understanding without introducing unverified changes.

Contradictory evidence: Test success (87 tests passing, 'OK (skipped=8), Failures: 0') with an invisible patch is NOT sufficient to rank highest. When the post-patch sed output is truncated so the actual code changes are not visible, the judge cannot verify what the patch does. 'Patch applied successfully!' followed by truncated sed output is not visible patch content. A branch that changes the approach from the parent's visible RHS-based fix to a new LHS-based approach (per the assistant's thought: 'the real distinction should be based on the LHS') without showing the resulting code is making an unverifiable change that may fail hidden tests. The visible test suite passing does not guarantee hidden tests pass, especially when the patch content is invisible.

Close-looking exclusions: Distinguish (a) a branch that shows the modified code via sed/grep/cat with the actual changed lines visible from (b) a branch where the sed output is truncated and the key changes are hidden. Only (a) provides verifiable patch evidence. A branch that runs `sed -n '198,230p'` after applying a patch but whose output is truncated at the critical lines (showing only 'sql = template % lhs' and 'return sql, tuple(lhs_params) + tuple(rhs_params)' without the changed logic in between) has NOT shown its patch content. Do not treat 'Patch applied successfully!' or test_edge_cases.py passing as substitutes for visible patch content. Also distinguish a branch that preserves the parent's fix (git diff shows compile_json_path_key, no new changes) from a branch that reverts or replaces it — the former maintains a visible correct approach, the latter introduces an invisible change.

Misleading pattern rejected: Reject the bias that 'all visible tests pass, therefore rank highest' when the patch content is invisible. The judge ranked s07 highest because 87 tests passed, but s07's fix_patch3.py content was not visible (truncated sed output) and s07 changed the approach from the parent's visible correct fix. This is the same error as conflating 'made a change' with 'fixed the bug' — test success with an invisible patch that changes a visible correct approach is not validation. A branch that preserves a visible, logically correct fix (compile_json_path_key for rhs keys) should rank above a branch with an invisible patch, even if the latter shows more tests passing, because the visible fix's correctness can be verified from the code while the invisible patch's cannot.

Abstention boundary: If no branch shows both visible patch content AND test success, rank by the strength of visible fix logic rather than test success alone. A visible fix with correct logic (compile_json_path_key treating rhs keys as object keys) is stronger evidence than an invisible patch with test success. If all branches have invisible patches or no patches, the event is unobservable and branches should be scored by diagnostic quality and visible fix logic, not by test counts.

experiences.title: Second manual correction: Priority visible-state rule: Test suite regression discovery must outweigh manual HTML verification breadth when ranking autodoc_typehints description-mode fix continuations
experiences.description:
SECOND-PASS MANDATORY RULE: Exact regression execution plus fixture localization is one evidence class; wording detail alone cannot produce a unique winner.

Positive visible evidence: Exact failing test and documented-init fixture inspection.
Contradictory or insufficient visible evidence: Broad HTML checks without the exact configuration test.

MANDATORY RULE: A legacy overfit card changed tie-aware selection using evidence already present in this exact visible trajectory. Its text is retained only as a starting point and must pass the standard recall@6 gate again.

Background: Retrieve when evaluating continuations that verify a fix for autodoc_typehints = "description" causing autoclass to show a spurious return type for classes. Judge whether the continuation ran the actual test suite (test_ext_autodoc_configs.py) and discovered the failing regression test (test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init), not merely whether it performed multiple manual build-and-check cycles with different autodoc_typehints modes. A continuation that builds and checks HTML output with description, both, and signature modes but never runs test_ext_autodoc_configs.py or only runs it at the very last step with truncated output has not discovered the critical regression: the fix is too broad and removes return type for classes with explicitly documented __init__ methods where it should be preserved.
experiences.context: Applies when the visible task concerns autodoc_typehints = "description" causing autoclass to include a spurious return type from __init__. The parent trajectories already applied a fix to merge_typehints in sphinx/ext/autodoc/typehints.py that skips return type for classes. Continuations are in the verification phase (steps 40-60). The key differentiator is whether the continuation runs test_ext_autodoc_configs.py and discovers the failing test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init, which tests _ClassWithDocumentedInit — a class with an explicitly documented __init__ where the return type should still appear when :special-members: __init__ is used. A common misleading rubric rewards the continuation for the breadth of manual verification (number of builds, modes tested, HTML grep commands) rather than for discovering the specific regression test failure.
experiences.experience:
Second manual correction after inspecting the failed generated rubric and evidence-first scores:
Exact regression execution plus fixture localization is one evidence class; wording detail alone cannot produce a unique winner.

Credit only this visible evidence: Exact failing test and documented-init fixture inspection.
Reject or cap this visible evidence: Broad HTML checks without the exact configuration test.
Abstain when: Equivalent reproduction without a fix remains tied.

Do not let another retrieved experience replace this task-specific rule with a generic process proxy.

Priority override for rubric generation and weighting:
A legacy overfit card changed tie-aware selection using evidence already present in this exact visible trajectory. Its text is retained only as a starting point and must pass the standard recall@6 gate again.

Reject any generated rubric whose direction, anchors, or weighting contradicts that rule. Apply it only to the matching visible task and stage; otherwise abstain.

Activation: When ranking continuations that verify a fix for the autodoc_typehints = "description" class return type bug, where all continuations show zero changed files (fix already applied by parent) and are in the verification/testing phase. The fix modifies merge_typehints to skip return type for classes, but this is too broad and breaks test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init.

Decisive positive evidence: A continuation that runs python -m pytest tests/test_ext_autodoc_configs.py and observes FAILED tests/test_ext_autodoc_configs.py::test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init has discovered the critical regression. This is stronger evidence of fix quality assessment than any amount of manual HTML verification. A continuation that then examines the _ClassWithDocumentedInit test fixture and recognizes that the fix is too broad — it removes return type for all classes, including those with documented __init__ methods where the return type should be preserved — demonstrates the deepest understanding of the issue. A continuation that articulates that the test expects the return type of __init__ to be shown when using :special-members: __init__ and that the fix was too broad has identified the root cause of the regression.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation that performs extensive manual verification — building with description, both, and signature modes, checking HTML output for return types, testing with methods and exception classes — but does not run test_ext_autodoc_configs.py until the very last visible step, or runs it with truncated output, has NOT discovered the regression in the visible prefix. Manual HTML verification cannot catch the _ClassWithDocumentedInit edge case because it requires :special-members: __init__ or equivalent explicit documentation of __init__, which the manual test setup does not include. Do not rank such a continuation above one that found and began investigating the failing test.

Close-looking exclusions: Running test_ext_autodoc.py (which passes with 69 passed, 1 skipped) is NOT equivalent to running test_ext_autodoc_configs.py (which contains the failing test). A continuation that runs test_ext_autodoc.py -k typehint and sees it pass has not validated the fix against the regression test. Similarly, running test_ext_autodoc_autoclass.py (18 passed) or test_ext_autodoc_autofunction.py (13 passed) does not substitute for test_ext_autodoc_configs.py. Do not credit partial test suite execution as if it were full validation. Also, running test_ext_autodoc_configs.py -k typehints at the very last step with truncated output does not demonstrate discovery of the failure unless the FAILED text is explicitly visible in the output.

Misleading rubric rejection: Do not reward a continuation for the QUANTITY of manual verifications (number of builds, number of modes tested, number of HTML grep commands, number of passing test files) when it has not run the specific test suite that contains the regression test. The misleading pattern is: more builds plus more HTML checks plus more passing test files equals more thorough verification. This is false when the test suite contains a specific regression test (test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init) that manual verification cannot replicate. A continuation with extensive manual build-and-check cycles that never runs test_ext_autodoc_configs.py is LESS thorough than one that runs it once and finds the failure. The judge bias that over-credits visible manual verification breadth while under-crediting test suite regression discovery leads to incorrect branch rankings.

Abstention boundary: If no continuation in the visible state has run test_ext_autodoc_configs.py, do not differentiate based on which tests they DID run or how many manual verifications they performed. If all continuations are still in manual verification mode without any test suite execution, preserve uncertainty. If a continuation has run test_ext_autodoc_configs.py but the output is truncated and the failure is not visible, do not assume it found the failure unless the FAILED text is explicitly visible in the output. Equivalent implementations are acceptable: a continuation that discovers the regression through a different test or through direct examination of the _ClassWithDocumentedInit case without running the exact test name is also credited, as long as it identifies the too-broad-fix problem.

experiences.title: Final-submission visibility dominates for the Q & Exists commutativity fix
experiences.description: When the paused view is at the final handoff for the Django Q(...) & Exists(...) TypeError task, rank continuations primarily by whether they visibly deliver the corrected patch, not by extra validation breadth or confident parent-state summaries. A blank final submission observation is decisive negative evidence compared with an otherwise identical continuation whose final observation contains the patch diff.
experiences.context: The task is to make Q(...) & Exists(...) and Q(...) | Exists(...) work like the existing Exists(...) & Q(...) and Exists(...) | Q(...) cases. The visible parent state already shows the intended mechanism: Q._combine must stop raising TypeError for every non-Q operand and instead cooperate with Python's binary-operator fallback, while reverse operator handling must allow conditional expressions such as Exists to combine with Q. The visible patch summary for the completed fix modifies django/db/models/expressions.py and django/db/models/query_utils.py with 17 insertions. Several continuations have the same changed files and patch size, but differ in whether the final submission command actually emits the patch text in the observation.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Use this experience only for final-round continuations on the Q(...) & Exists(...) commutativity issue where the parent state already contains the fix and validation, the continuation is mainly creating or submitting /tmp/patch.txt, and the visible summaries show the same two changed files and the same 17-insertion diff shape. In this setting, the decisive distinction is final delivery evidence, not additional exploration.

Decisive positive evidence: Prefer continuations whose final submit step visibly outputs a patch diff after the COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT command, or otherwise has an immediately visible submitted artifact. The visible diff should show the known correct shape: changes in django/db/models/expressions.py and django/db/models/query_utils.py, including reverse handling for conditional expressions and Q-side cooperation through NotImplemented/fallback behavior. Additional visible positive evidence includes command output showing Q() & Exists(...), Q() | Exists(...), Exists(...) & Q(), and Exists(...) | Q() all construct successfully, while Q() & object(), Q() | object(), or Q() & F(...) still raise TypeError. Existing Q tests passing is useful but secondary when the final patch is visibly delivered.

Decisive contradictory evidence: If the final step is `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat /tmp/patch.txt` but the observation is blank, treat that as a finalization/delivery failure in this paused view. Do not rank such a continuation above an otherwise identical continuation whose final observation contains the patch diff. A non-empty changed_files summary, identical diff_stat, prior parent validation, or confident narration cannot overcome the absence of visible submitted patch text at the final handoff. Also penalize any visible patch that only adds reverse methods while leaving Q._combine to raise TypeError before Python can try the reverse operation, or any patch that makes Q combine with arbitrary non-conditional objects instead of preserving TypeError.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not over-reward extra ad-hoc SQL/query execution, exhaustive type-discrimination scripts, or rerunning a small test class when the submitted patch is the same and already validated in the parent. Conversely, do not penalize a correct visible submission just because it does not add more tests during the final one-step continuation. A raw SQL string comparison reporting `Equal: False` is not by itself contradictory when the displayed SQL only differs by predicate order and both operand orders construct successfully; result-set semantics or absence of TypeError are the relevant signals. Diff output may be truncated, but if the visible portions and summary match the correct two-file 17-insertion patch and the final submission contains actual patch text, treat it as delivered.

Abstention boundary: If every continuation has blank final submission output but all share the same changed files, diff_stat, and parent validation, do not fabricate a ranking from validation-rubric minutiae; mark the final delivery evidence as uncertain and fall back to visible patch/test evidence. If the final diff is entirely hidden by truncation and no patch content is visible anywhere in the continuation or parent, abstain from asserting correctness of the implementation. Preserve equivalent valid implementations that satisfy the behavioral contract by any sound operator-protocol approach; do not require exact line placement or exact helper-method names.

Reject the misleading rubric bias: In this final-submission view, it is wrong to let broad validation rubrics such as database query execution, existing-suite breadth, or many conditional-expression cases dominate the ranking while ignoring whether the patch was visibly submitted. That bias can incorrectly prefer blank final submissions and underrate continuations that actually deliver the same correct patch. Final artifact visibility is the highest-weight signal for this round.

experiences.title: Unnecessary Secondary-Backend Modifications Introduce Regression Risk When Core Fix Already Applied by Parent
experiences.description: When a parent trajectory has already implemented the core fix (adding methods, modifying the primary backend), continuations that make additional backend modifications via blanket sed replacements can introduce regressions. Do not rank a continuation higher for modifying more backend files. A continuation that only investigates without modifying preserves the working state and may be superior.
experiences.context: A matplotlib task to add get_antialiased/set_antialiased to Text objects. Parent 1 already added the methods to text.py, added gc.set_antialiased in Text.draw, and modified backend_agg.py to use gc.get_antialiased(). Continuations from Parent 1 differ in whether they additionally modify backend_cairo.py. The cairo modification uses a blanket sed replacement (s/mpl.rcParams["text.antialiased"]/gc.get_antialiased()/) that may not be correct for cairo's FontOptions.set_antialias context. The judge ranked a continuation that made this additional cairo modification as the best, but the modification likely introduced a regression. The continuation that only investigated without modifying passed.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When scoring continuations from a parent that has already made core implementation changes (visible in the parent trajectory), and some continuations make additional backend modifications while others only investigate.

Positive evidence: A continuation that only investigates (grep, sed -n for reading) without making additional file modifications preserves the working state from the parent. When the parent's core changes are correct, this is safer than introducing additional modifications that may cause regressions. Investigation of remaining rcParams references (e.g., in _mathtext.py) without modifying them is valid scope analysis that preserves the working state.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation that makes additional backend modifications (visible sed -i commands to backend files beyond the primary backend) is not necessarily making progress. The additional modification may introduce a regression, especially when the backend has different antialiasing semantics (e.g., cairo uses FontOptions.set_antialias with cairo.ANTIALIAS_DEFAULT/cairo.ANTIALIAS_NONE, which is a different pattern than the Agg backend's antialiased= parameter) or when the modification is a blanket sed replacement that doesn't account for the backend's specific context. Do not treat the presence of additional sed -i modifications as evidence of superior progress.

Close-looking exclusions: Distinguish between (a) a sed -i command that MODIFIES a file and (b) a sed -n command that only READS a file. Only (a) introduces change risk. A continuation that reads additional backend files to understand the scope is performing valid investigation. Do not penalize investigation; penalize unnecessary modifications that may cause regressions. Also distinguish between the primary backend (already modified by the parent) and secondary backends (newly modified by the continuation) — modifications to secondary backends are scope extensions with regression risk, not core fix completion. A blanket sed replacement that works for one backend's API pattern may not work for another backend's different API pattern.

Explicitly rejected misleading bias: Reject any rubric or scoring tendency that treats the number of file modifications as a proxy for implementation completeness, or that assumes modifying more backends = more thorough fix. Specifically reject the assumption that a blanket sed replacement extending a fix to a secondary backend is necessary or correct just because the task mentions backends in general. The task's mention of backends does not mean every backend needs the same modification pattern. Reject the bias that a visible sed -i command is stronger evidence of progress than investigation-only commands when the parent has already applied the core fix.

Abstention boundary: If no continuation has made additional backend modifications (all are investigation-only or all make the same modifications), this experience does not apply. If the visible state doesn't show whether a modification is correct or harmful (e.g., no test output is visible), preserve uncertainty about the modification's correctness but do not assume more modifications = more progress. If the parent has not yet made core changes, this experience does not apply — in that case, continuations that make core changes should be ranked above investigation-only ones.

experiences.title: Django MTI child PK reset: exact-scenario bug-contract validation outranks edge-case test quantity; visible AssertionErrors are decisive contradictory evidence
experiences.description: For the Django multi-table inheritance bug where setting the parent PK (uid) to None on a child model overwrites the existing object instead of creating a new one, a continuation showing 'TEST PASSED: obj.f is True - the original object was NOT overwritten' from a test of the exact PR scenario provides stronger validation than one showing 'OK: New object was created as expected' from an unverifiable run_test.py plus multiple passing edge case tests. Visible AssertionErrors in final tests must be treated as decisive contradictory evidence. Failed patch attempts don't negate a working final fix applied via an alternative method.
experiences.context: The bug requires fixing _save_parents in django/db/models/base.py to not sync the parent PK from the child link field when the parent PK was explicitly set to None. Multiple continuations apply fixes and show tests passing, but differ in validation specificity. The judge ranked continuations with more edge case tests higher, but the continuations with explicit bug-contract validation and no visible errors should rank higher.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When evaluating continuations for the Django multi-table inheritance bug where setting a parent PK field (e.g., uid) to None on a child model should create a new object but instead overwrites the existing one, and multiple continuations show tests passing but differ in validation specificity and edge case test quantity.

Decisive positive evidence: A continuation that creates a test (test_pr.py) reproducing the EXACT PR scenario — setting self.uid = None on a child model, saving, and verifying the original object's f field remains True — and shows 'TEST PASSED: obj.f is True - the original object was NOT overwritten' provides decisive validation. This explicitly validates the bug contract: the original object was NOT overwritten and a new object was created (Total Derived objects: 2, Total Item objects: 2, original pk=1 f=True, new pk=2 f=False). A continuation that first shows this test FAILING with the parent's fix alone (correctly identifying insufficiency) and then PASSES after applying the complete fix demonstrates correct diagnostic workflow. Additional validation with test_issue.py confirming 2 objects created with correct f values strengthens the evidence.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation whose final test step shows an AssertionError (e.g., in a multi-level inheritance test where pk doesn't change after reset, indicating the fix breaks multi-level inheritance) has visible contradictory evidence that must lower its ranking regardless of how many other tests pass. A continuation showing 'OK: New object was created as expected' from run_test.py is weaker evidence than 'TEST PASSED: obj.f is True - the original object was NOT overwritten' because the former doesn't explicitly assert the original object was not overwritten, and run_test.py's content is not visible so it may test pk=None instead of uid=None (a different scenario). Explicitly reject the misleading judge bias that ranks a continuation higher solely because it has more passing edge case tests (e.g., 5 edge case tests) — edge case test quantity does not compensate for lack of explicit bug-contract validation. Also reject the bias that treats 'OK: New object was created as expected' as equivalent to 'TEST PASSED: obj.f is True - the original object was NOT overwritten' — the latter validates both halves of the bug contract (new object created AND original not overwritten).

Close-looking exclusions: Do not penalize a continuation for multiple failed patch attempts (malformed patches, sed errors, hunk failures) if the final fix is applied via an alternative method (e.g., a Python script that modifies the source) and validated with passing tests — the final state matters more than intermediate failures. Do not infer that run_test.py tests the exact PR scenario (uid=None) if its content is not visible — it may test pk=None instead. A continuation that correctly identifies the parent's fix is insufficient (test_pr.py FAILS) and is actively investigating _save_parents logic is on the right track even if it hasn't applied the complete fix in the visible prefix — its investigation depth (examining __dict__, field structure, related_descriptors) is relevant diagnostic work. Equivalent valid implementations include: modifying _save_parents to clear the child link field when parent PK is None, or modifying both _set_pk_val and _save_parents — both are valid if they pass the exact bug scenario test. Do not treat all continuations that fail to run the Django test suite (no pytest, settings not configured, ModuleNotFoundError) as equally validated — environment setup failure is not validation, but a continuation with explicit bug-contract test passing has stronger evidence than one with only generic 'OK' messages.

Abstention boundary: If no continuation shows explicit bug-contract validation ('original NOT overwritten') and all show only generic 'OK' or 'new object created' messages, validation specificity cannot distinguish them — rely on other evidence (visible errors, investigation depth, fix completeness). If all fix code is truncated and no test output is visible, fix correctness cannot be determined from visible evidence alone. If a continuation's final test shows an AssertionError, that is decisive contradictory evidence regardless of fix code visibility or how many other tests pass.

experiences.title: SimpleLazyObject Diagnosis: ForeignKey.get_prep_value Code Path and LazyObject Mechanics Trump Promise Handling Discovery, Encoding Distractions, and Unexecuted Test Scripts
experiences.description: When diagnosing a SimpleLazyObject regression where int(value) fails on a lazy-wrapped model instance in a queryset filter, finding the Promise handling in Field.get_prep_value is relevant context but not sufficient for high diagnostic credit. The critical evidence is finding ForeignKey.get_prep_value in related.py (the actual code path for the reported ForeignKey-based issue) and understanding that SimpleLazyObject is a LazyObject, not a Promise. Exploring encoding.py (force_str/force_text) is a distraction — those functions handle lazy strings (Promise), not LazyObject-wrapped model instances. An unexecuted test script is not reproduction evidence. An agent that finds the actual field code path and LazyObject mechanics should rank above one that finds Promise handling but explores irrelevant encoding paths and creates an unexecuted test script.
experiences.context: Pre-patch diagnosis of a Django ORM issue where SimpleLazyObject wrapping a User object fails with TypeError: int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a number, not 'SimpleLazyObject' when used in a queryset filter with a subquery annotation. The error occurs through IntegerField.get_prep_value calling int(value) because the base Field.get_prep_value only handles Promise objects (via _proxy____cast) but not LazyObject/SimpleLazyObject. The User is accessed via a ForeignKey (C.owner pointing to User), so ForeignKey.get_prep_value in related.py delegates to target_field.get_prep_value. All agents were paused at step 20 with no patch applied.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When evaluating pre-patch diagnosis trajectories for a SimpleLazyObject or LazyObject handling regression in Django ORM, where the reported error is a TypeError from int(value) or similar type conversion on a lazy-wrapped model instance used in a queryset filter.

Positive evidence: An agent that finds ForeignKey.get_prep_value in related.py (line 972-973: `return self.target_field.get_prep_value(value)`) has identified the actual code path for the reported issue — the User object is accessed via a ForeignKey (C.owner), so ForeignKey.get_prep_value delegates to target_field.get_prep_value, which calls int(value) on the unresolved SimpleLazyObject. An agent that examines the LazyObject class and understands _wrapped/_setup mechanics (how _wrapped starts as empty and _setup populates it) has begun tracing how SimpleLazyObject should be resolved. An agent that finds the Promise handling in Field.get_prep_value (line 805: `if isinstance(value, Promise): value = value._proxy____cast()`) has found relevant context but must recognize that SimpleLazyObject is NOT a Promise — it inherits from LazyObject — so this existing handling does not cover the reported case.

Contradictory evidence: An agent that finds the Promise handling but then explores encoding.py (force_str, force_text) has gone down a distraction path — the fix is not about string encoding; force_str handles lazy strings (Promise), not LazyObject-wrapped model instances. An agent that creates a test script file but does not execute it has not reproduced the error — the script was written but never run, so no reproduction evidence exists and no error was triggered. An agent that explores more files is not necessarily making better progress if the additional files (encoding.py) are not on the fix path.

Close-looking exclusions: Finding `if isinstance(value, Promise): value = value._proxy____cast()` in Field.get_prep_value is NOT sufficient for high diagnostic credit because SimpleLazyObject does not inherit from Promise — it inherits from LazyObject. The existing Promise handling is the mechanism that works for lazy strings but NOT for SimpleLazyObject, which is the core of the regression. Exploring force_str/force_text in encoding.py is NOT relevant to this fix — those functions handle lazy strings (Promise), not LazyObject-wrapped model instances. Creating a test script file without executing it is NOT reproduction evidence — the script was written but never run, so no error was triggered and no validation occurred.

Misleading evidence pattern rejection: Do not rank an agent higher solely because it found the Promise handling in get_prep_value AND explored more files (encoding.py, resolve_lookup_value) AND created an unexecuted test script. The Promise handling discovery is relevant context, but the encoding.py exploration is a distraction from the actual fix path, and the unexecuted test script provides no reproduction evidence. An agent that finds ForeignKey.get_prep_value in related.py — the actual code path for the reported ForeignKey-based issue — and examines LazyObject mechanics (_wrapped, _setup, empty sentinel) has stronger diagnostic evidence, even with fewer files explored and no test script, because it has identified where the fix needs to happen and how SimpleLazyObject differs from Promise. The judge bias toward broader file exploration and test script creation must not override the quality and relevance of the diagnostic findings.

Abstention boundary: If the visible prefix shows only directory listing and broad grep without finding any of the key code paths (ForeignKey.get_prep_value in related.py, Field.get_prep_value Promise handling, LazyObject class definition), score at the lowest level. If an agent found the Promise handling but the visible prefix ends before determining whether it recognized SimpleLazyObject is not a Promise, do not infer the recognition; score based only on what is visible. If an agent created a test script but the visible prefix ends before execution, do not infer whether the script would reproduce the error; the absence of execution output means no reproduction evidence.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Diagnostic Code Path Identification: ForeignKey.get_prep_value and LazyObject vs Promise Distinction
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the agent has identified the actual code path causing the SimpleLazyObject regression: ForeignKey.get_prep_value in related.py delegates to target_field.get_prep_value, which calls int(value) on the unresolved SimpleLazyObject. High scores require finding this code path AND understanding that SimpleLazyObject is a LazyObject (not a Promise), so the existing Promise handling in Field.get_prep_value does not cover it. Agents that examine LazyObject._wrapped/_setup mechanics demonstrate deeper understanding of how the lazy object should be resolved.
