reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory is flawed if it treats the issue as only a `modelform_factory()` default-argument inheritance problem or addresses the symptom at a wrong layer, and does not show that a callback declared solely on a ModelForm's own `Meta` is consumed by the normal form field construction path. This includes patches or plans that only omit/conditionally set a generated class attribute, manually copy a parent `Meta` callback in the factory, validate only factory-created forms, suppress output in a late rendering or choice-yielding layer, or mention the attractive idea without showing how the Meta option reaches final form-field construction. Without evidence that direct Meta-only forms and factory-created forms both invoke the callback when fields are built and that existing behavior for other configurations is preserved, the trajectory should not rate highly.

metadata.environment: Django ModelForm and model form factory code
metadata.risk_signal: trajectory focuses on generated factory class attributes, inherited parent Meta values, attractive terminology, or isolated code inspection without end-to-end path tracing
required_visible_evidence: the normal ModelForm options/metaclass path reads the current class's Meta callback
field construction receives that callback through the standard option path
tests or reasoning include a callback defined only in Meta, not also as a class attribute
factory explicit callback behavior remains covered through the same option path
existing behavior for other form/widget/blank configurations is preserved
misleading_evidence_to_discount: a base form that also defines a class-level callback
mentioning or restating the attractive idea without code-path evidence
isolated grepping or opening of related methods without showing the full construction path
suppressing the symptom in a late rendering or choice-yielding layer

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly integrates the Meta callback into the standard ModelForm option/field-building path, covers direct Meta-only and factory-created forms, and preserves existing behavior for other configurations.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mostly uses the standard option path but has limited test evidence for direct Meta-only forms, explicit factory callback behavior, or preservation of existing behavior.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory recognizes both factory inheritance and direct Meta semantics but implementation or tests still rely partly on special-case factory handling or wrong-layer suppression.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory changes only factory class-attribute handling, parent-Meta copying, or late-layer symptom suppression and validates factory behavior, with no convincing direct Meta-only coverage or end-to-end path tracing.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory explicitly assumes preserving `FactoryForm.Meta.formfield_callback`, avoiding `None` in factory attrs, or restating the attractive idea is sufficient, while leaving the general ModelForm Meta option ignored during field generation.

experiences.title: Do not equate exact parameter-wiring shape with effective user opt-out
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for an Ansible/Python fix that adds a boolean authentication option through shared URL helpers, especially when the module builds its options from a shared argument spec and delegates to helper functions.
experiences.context: This applies in Ansible-style module code where a user-facing module such as `uri` delegates request handling to shared utilities like `url_argument_spec()`, `fetch_url()`, `open_url()`, and a `Request.open()` method. Concrete activation evidence includes a `use_netrc` or equivalent boolean, a shared argument spec imported by the module, reads from `module.params` or explicit helper arguments, and request-opening code where a `.netrc` lookup can assign or overwrite a Basic `Authorization` header. A tempting rubric is to require a specific checklist such as declaring the option directly in the module's local `argument_spec`, adding it to every wrapper signature, and updating every consumer of the shared utility. That checklist can be misleading when the module already imports a shared argument spec, when `fetch_url()` reads values from `module.params`, or when the visible trajectory is still early exploration. The useful boundary is behavioral: the user-facing false value must actually prevent the `.netrc` fallback from setting Basic auth, while the unspecified/default value must preserve existing behavior. Do not demand identical new-parameter handling across distinguishable helper paths when one path already preserves a pre-existing public/default contract and another path is where the new option must take effect. A close-looking contraindication is a change about unrelated auth mechanisms, proxy/SSL flags, or generic helper signature cleanup that never exposes or guards a `.netrc`-based credential fallback. Abstain when the visible material has not reached the effective argument source or the request-opening/netrc guard, or when the task text explicitly requires an exact integration point rather than an effective opt-out.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded or penalized trajectories based on whether `use_netrc` appeared at named call-chain locations or was declared directly in the `uri` module. That can understate good trajectories because adding the option to the shared URL argument spec may already expose it to the module, and passing `module.params['use_netrc']` directly to `fetch_url()` can be sufficient without changing an intermediate helper signature. It can also overstate bad trajectories because superficial appearances of threading do not guarantee that `use_netrc: false` actually reaches the `.netrc` lookup; for example, a gate that checks an object default instead of the resolved per-call value leaves the opt-out ineffective. A better rubric should focus on semantic evidence: the user can set the option through the module's effective argument spec, the value read from `module.params` or an explicit argument reaches the request-opening logic, the `.netrc` lookup and Basic `Authorization` overwrite are skipped only when the resolved option is false, and the default continues to preserve existing behavior. When there are multiple helper branches, evaluate each branch by its observable contract rather than requiring the new boolean to be applied uniformly everywhere: preserve existing default behavior where the option is unset, and require the resolved user value only at the branch that controls the `.netrc` fallback. Avoid making “declared directly in the module-local `argument_spec`” or “all shared utility consumers were updated” mandatory unless visible code structure or task text makes those exact integration points necessary.

experiences.title: Do not reward collapsing complementary records as deduplication
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug report complains about duplicate aggregated records, but the visible code/model shows multiple heterogeneous records under the same key because different input maps or phases populate different fields. The rubric must make the field-level distinction between true duplicates (identical content) and complementary records (different fields) affect the score, so that patches preserving complementary records do not tie with patches that over-collapse them.
experiences.context: Applies in Go conversion/parser tasks like a Trivy-to-Vuls converter where output is an aggregation such as a map from source to a slice of content records, and the trajectory has identified separate append paths for severity data and CVSS score/vector data. The misleading case is generating a rubric that demands exactly one object per source and merging all fields into that object, even though visible tests/model structure may treat severity-only and CVSS-only content as distinct record shapes and only repeated severities or repeated identical CVSS records are true duplicates. The original one-object-per-source idea may still be appropriate when the visible data contract, tests, or schema explicitly requires a single homogeneous record per key and there is no evidence that different records under the key encode different semantic categories. Just as a target contract may accept multiple valid representations for the same entity, a target contract may accept multiple valid record shapes per source key; the rubric must not hardcode one canonical arrangement and treat all multi-record deviations as equivalent defects.
experiences.experience:
Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the agent consolidated all same-source CveContent records into a single object, merging VendorSeverity severities with CVSS scores/vectors. That is tempting because the issue text says duplicate objects and one entry per source, and agents often validate by counting source keys. However, this criterion can over-reward over-consolidation: a patch may replace a source slice with a singleton, overwrite existing records across repeated vulnerabilities, or merge severity-only and CVSS-only records that the converter/model keeps as different content forms. A better rubric should distinguish true duplicates from complementary records. It should prioritize visible evidence that the agent preserves all non-duplicate CVSS score/vector records, consolidates multiple severity strings for the same source without losing or repeating severities, skips exact duplicate CVSS entries caused by repeated package detections, and keeps unrelated package/library conversion behavior intact. Avoid generating a broad criterion that treats every same-source record as a duplicate or judges success by array length alone; require field-level preservation and narrow converter changes instead.

The decisive observable distinction is field-level: whether records under the same key carry identical content (true duplicate) or different fields (complementary). This distinction must affect the score so that a patch preserving complementary records does not receive the same score as a patch collapsing them, even if both deviate from a hardcoded one-object-per-source ideal. A rubric that hardcodes one canonical record form and labels all multi-record arrangements as equivalent defects will tie scores between valid complementary-preserving patches and invalid over-collapsing patches, masking the real defect. If the visible diff does not reveal whether same-source records are identical or complementary (e.g., truncated diff, only counts shown, or records added indirectly), do not infer the distinction; preserve uncertainty rather than scoring as if all multi-record arrangements are equivalent.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-collapsing heterogeneous CVE content
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement or strongly commit to over-consolidating heterogeneous CVE content records: treating any repeated source key as a duplicate, replacing the source's content slice with a single record after processing both severity and CVSS inputs, or updating expectations merely to remove separate CVSS/severity records. This flaw is present when the visible code/model shows different input maps or conversion paths populate different fields, but the proposed fix collapses them without proving that complementary CVSS scores/vectors, references, dates, and existing package/library conversion behavior are preserved. The correct direction is narrower: consolidate repeated severity values deterministically and avoid exact duplicate CVSS records while preserving distinct non-duplicate content data. The rubric must not tie the score of a patch that preserves complementary records with the score of a patch that over-collapses them; the field-level distinction (identical vs. complementary content) must separate the two so that valid multi-record arrangements are not penalized the same as invalid over-consolidation.

evidence_to_check: Whether the aggregation value type is a slice or otherwise permits multiple records per source
Whether separate conversion paths populate severity fields versus CVSS score/vector fields
Whether the agent's patch uses source-only maps or singleton assignment that overwrites existing content
Whether validation only counts source occurrences instead of inspecting preserved fields
Whether unrelated package/library conversion logic is changed while fixing CVE content duplication
Whether the visible diff reveals whether same-source records are identical or complementary, or is truncated/indirect so the distinction cannot be observed
preferred_positive_evidence: Deduplicates identical repeated records caused by repeated vulnerability/package occurrences
Combines multiple severity values without duplicates and with deterministic ordering
Preserves CVSS2/CVSS3 scores and vectors as distinct content when they are not exact duplicates
Keeps the change scoped to CVE content aggregation

scale.1: No evidence of over-consolidation; the trajectory distinguishes duplicate repeated data from complementary severity/CVSS records and preserves unrelated conversion behavior.
scale.2: Minor risk only; the agent discusses one-per-source language but also inspects field preservation and has not implemented source-only overwrites.
scale.3: Moderate concern; the plan or partial patch deduplicates by source but contains some safeguards for preserving severity and CVSS fields.
scale.4: Clear flaw; the patch or plan replaces each source with a singleton merged record or removes separate records without adequate field-level preservation.
scale.5: Severe flaw; the patch collapses all same-source records, overwrites prior content across repeated CVE occurrences, validates only by counts, or also disrupts unrelated package/library conversion logic.
scale.uncertain: The visible diff does not reveal whether same-source records are identical or complementary (truncated, indirect, or count-only evidence); do not infer the distinction or score all multi-record arrangements as equivalent.

experiences.title: Disambiguate Non-Unique Composite Index Deletion
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django schema/migration task involves deleting a legacy composite index that shares columns with a unique constraint, especially when introspection can report unique constraints as indexes; if a backend is named, validation evidence should exercise that backend's constraint lookup behavior rather than relying on unrelated test-suite volume.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django schema editor or migration operations when the reported failure is that removing an index_together entry on fields also present in unique_together causes constraint lookup to find more than one database object. Concrete activation evidence includes inspection of the composed-index deletion path, introspection output showing multiple objects for the same columns, a named backend whose constraint metadata can classify unique constraints as indexes, or a reproduction where ordinary index deletion collides with an existing unique constraint. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or modified the schema deletion path, backend constraint introspection, or has reproduced the duplicate match. It is less useful for unrelated index creation, migration autodetector-only changes, generic test-runner setup work, or tasks whose main requirement is avoiding index recreation when moving declarations to Meta.indexes rather than fixing the crash during deletion.
experiences.experience:
For this cluster, the useful semantic boundary is between deleting an ordinary composite index and deleting a unique constraint. The important observable evidence is that the agent recognizes a unique constraint may also satisfy index=True in database introspection, so an index_together deletion lookup using only index=True can match both the non-unique index and the unique constraint on the same columns.

A good rubric should treat as strongest evidence a fix or plan that narrows the ordinary index deletion predicate to target non-unique indexes, preserves the existing unique-constraint deletion path, and validates that removing index_together leaves unique_together intact. When a backend is named or backend-specific introspection is part of the failure, validation should target the reported constraint behavior on that backend: reproducing the multi-constraint lookup, checking the relevant introspection output, or otherwise showing that the deletion predicate selects the correct database object there. Large numbers of existing tests on a different backend are only supporting evidence if they do not exercise the actual duplicate-constraint lookup.

Do not overfit to generated suffix names such as _idx or _uniq, require an exact call-site-only patch shape, or broaden the task into solving all declaration-refactor/recreation behavior unless the trajectory explicitly addresses that separate requirement. Also avoid judging mainly by test-command volume: setup and broad-suite activity may be noisy, while direct introspection evidence and focused schema-editor reproduction are often more decisive.

Close-looking contraindication: do not apply this card to a trajectory that is only about changing model declaration style, avoiding index recreation during a declaration move, creating indexes, or adjusting the migration autodetector without addressing the ordinary-index deletion lookup. Conversely, if a trajectory both runs broad suites and directly reproduces the backend-specific duplicate-constraint scenario, distinguish the direct reproduction from the suite volume rather than treating them as the same kind of evidence.

Abstain from the backend-specific validation rule when the task does not name a backend, the available evidence does not reveal which backend is being exercised, or the duplicate-constraint behavior is clearly backend-agnostic. If the visible work lacks test execution but contains precise introspection analysis or a focused schema-editor reproduction, preserve that as potentially decisive evidence; if it contains only broad testing with no constraint-specific reproduction or introspection, remain conservative.

experiences.title: Scoped Edit Coherence After Implementation Starts
experiences.description: Retrieve when the task appears localized or mechanically scoped and the visible trajectory already includes source edits, especially if there are signs of brittle sed/script edits, repeated same-file surgery, unrelated file churn, shared-helper rewrites for a class-specific issue, unrelated file deletions, or a need to distinguish a clean targeted patch from edit thrash or collateral damage.
experiences.context: Apply in SWE-agent trajectories for coding tasks after the agent has begun modifying files or is near final review. This is most useful when the requested change should be narrow or systematic: a one-line propagation bug, a small template/filter fix, a local UI markup adjustment, a class-specific display or repr adjustment, or a command rename where all touched files should follow an obvious mapping. It is also useful when the recent steps show high-risk editing behavior such as repeated line-number sed operations, deletion/reinsertion of method blocks, accidental duplicate replacements, broad generated rewrites, shared/global helper changes for a localized request, unrelated file deletions, or untracked environment workaround edits mixed with the task patch. Do not retrieve as a primary criterion during pure discovery before edits exist. Do not treat it as sufficient for semantic correctness when the hard part is an algorithmic boundary, compatibility contract, output ordering, or domain-specific behavior; in those cases pair it with a rubric about the actual semantic invariant. For explicitly broad refactors, use this only to flag incoherent wholesale deletion or circular-import risk, not to penalize legitimate multi-file consolidation.
experiences.experience:
The useful judgment is not simply whether the diff is small; it is whether the visible editing process and resulting direction remain coherent, scoped, and reviewable for the stated task while avoiding collateral damage. This rubric correctly helps when the agent repeatedly edits the same block with brittle commands, leaves evidence of syntax damage, changes unrelated runtime-compatibility files, updates tests/config to match an incomplete implementation, deletes unrelated files, or performs automated broad replacements or shared-helper rewrites without checking all affected registrations/references/callers. It should reward trajectories where the agent identifies the narrow source of the bug, makes a targeted change in the relevant class/module or a systematically bounded set of files, inspects the diff, preserves existing behavior for unrelated callers, and runs focused validation without hiding failures through unrelated test/config churn.

For localized class-specific fixes, explicitly distinguish a direct class/module change from a global helper rewrite or unrelated deletion. Positive evidence includes a small insertion or replacement in the target file, delegation to existing infrastructure, no unrelated file deletions, no backup/directories or generated artifacts folded into the patch, and no broad behavioral change to shared helpers unless the shared change is minimal and demonstrably preserves other callers. Negative evidence includes deleting unrelated package files, large deletion counts with no task mapping, creating backup copies of removed files, rewriting a shared helper so all callers change when a class-specific method would suffice, or using broad replacements without inspecting the affected surface. Untracked exploratory test files or scratch files, by themselves, are not collateral damage unless they are incorporated into the patch or used to mask the implementation state.

Avoid the tempting wrong criterion of equating 'minimal' with 'correct': a one-line change can still miss a required edge case, parameter ordering, compatibility behavior, or acceptance scenario. Conversely, an empty or not-yet-applied patch after a trajectory has identified the correct localized approach should usually be treated as uncertain/intermediate rather than as incoherent or fully correct. Preserve equivalent implementations: a shared-helper edit can be acceptable when the issue is genuinely shared or the change is narrow, behavior-preserving for other callers, and validated accordingly; a multi-file patch can be coherent when each touched file follows an obvious required mapping. Prioritize visible evidence such as diff scope, deletion counts, whether modified files map directly to the requested behavior, whether repeated sed/script edits caused malformed code or duplicate decorators, whether old aliases/tests/docs are changed consistently rather than opportunistically, whether temporary environment fixes are kept out of the task patch, whether shared helpers are protected from unintended global behavior changes, and whether the agent verifies the exact edited behavior after the final edit.

Suggested rubric shape: use a positive scoped-coherence rubric with high weight when the task is localized. Award high scores for targeted, reviewed, behavior-preserving edits with focused validation; award low scores for destructive global rewrites, unrelated deletions, malformed code, or masking churn; assign middle scores when the approach is plausibly localized but unvalidated, when no patch exists yet but the trajectory has identified the correct narrow fix, or when a shared-helper change may be legitimate but evidence about collateral behavior is incomplete.

experiences.title: IDN Punycode Must Be Wired Into the User-Facing Link Flow
experiences.description: Use this when a web/TypeScript monorepo task asks for IDN/Punycode URL safety and the trajectory has found generic URL helpers plus an existing component-level link click/display path. The useful rubric should judge whether the agent connects hostname punycode conversion to the actual link confirmation/rendering flow through a visible source diff, not merely whether it adds a standalone URL helper or investigates the root cause.
experiences.context: Applies in frontend web applications, especially TypeScript monorepos with shared utility packages and component packages, where the bug is observed when users click or view links containing Unicode hostnames. Retrieve this experience once the trajectory has visible evidence of both generic URL utilities and the UI path that extracts, sanitizes, confirms, or displays external links. It is most useful after the agent has inspected relevant link handlers, confirmation UI, URL helper tests, or existing punycode-related code. It is less applicable for purely backend URL storage tasks, tasks that only require a library utility with no user-facing integration, or very early exploration before the relevant link entry point has been located.
experiences.experience:
The earlier rubrics correctly emphasized the core invariant: convert only the hostname of an IDN URL to ASCII/Punycode while preserving protocol, path, query, fragment, auth, and port. However, in this setting that criterion is too generic by itself. A trajectory can satisfy it superficially by adding a helper in a shared URL file, while leaving the actual clicked/displayed link path unchanged, or by modifying unrelated helpers such as validation, prefixing, or search-param serialization. The better rubric should focus on whether the agent has identified the user-facing link extraction/confirmation/rendering flow and wired the punycode-normalized URL into that flow through a visible source diff. Prioritize visible evidence such as: inspection of existing link-click code that already distinguishes raw href from browser-encoded href; recognition of browser compatibility comments around Punycode/IDN handling; a helper placed where the link UI can import it without unnecessary dependency churn; replacement of the displayed/confirmed link value with a hostname-only Punycode version; and focused tests or examples showing a Unicode hostname becomes an xn-- hostname while path/query/hash remain unchanged.

Do not conflate investigative signals with implementation evidence. Locating the link handler, explaining why hostname punycode conversion is needed, reproducing the IDN bug, grepping for existing tests, or planning to wire the helper into the flow are useful process signals but are not evidence of a correct fix. A rubric that heavily rewards diagnosis, root-cause explanation, or test discovery will over-score trajectories that explore thoroughly without producing a visible source diff that actually connects punycode conversion to the link flow. Prefer rubrics that primarily evaluate visible implementation quality. If no repository diff is visible or the diff is too incomplete to determine whether the punycode-normalized URL is actually used by the link display/click/confirmation path, preserve uncertainty about implementation quality and give at most limited process credit for faithful investigation rather than inferring success from the agent's plan or diagnosis.

Avoid tempting but weak criteria like 'adds a toPunycode function somewhere,' 'uses the native URL API,' or 'covers all URL entry points' unless the trajectory also shows the function is used by the specific user-facing path described in the task. Also avoid rewarding broad edits to unrelated URL utilities, validators, or dependency manifests when the visible issue is in the link display/click confirmation path. Equivalent implementations may place the conversion at different layers as long as the visible diff guarantees the displayed/confirmed link uses a hostname-only punycode URL; do not require one exact file, line, or syntactic expression.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: User-Facing IDN Link Flow Integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate through a visible source diff that the IDN/Punycode fix is integrated into the actual user-facing link handling flow where external links are extracted, displayed, sanitized, confirmed, or opened. A strong solution does not stop at a standalone URL helper or at investigating the root cause: it identifies the relevant component-level link path, normalizes only the hostname to ASCII/Punycode, preserves the rest of the URL, handles raw versus browser-encoded href values safely, and avoids unrelated changes to validators, search-param helpers, or generic URL prefix logic unless directly required by the link flow. Investigative signals—locating code, explaining the bug, reproducing the failure, or planning a fix—are not substitutes for a visible implementation that wires the conversion into the link path.

expected_visible_evidence: A source diff that wires hostname-only punycode conversion into the link display/click/confirmation path, not merely investigation or planning.
The agent inspects the UI link click/render/confirmation path, not only generic shared URL utilities.
The agent notices existing IDN or Punycode-related handling, browser compatibility comments, or raw-versus-encoded href extraction in that path.
The proposed or implemented conversion is actually used before displaying or confirming the external link shown to the user.
The conversion targets only the hostname/domain labels and preserves protocol, pathname, query string, fragment, port, and credentials when present.
Tests, examples, or reasoning cover a Unicode hostname becoming an xn-- hostname without punycoding path/query/fragment content.
anti_evidence: Only investigates, reproduces, or plans without producing a visible source diff that wires punycode into the link flow.
Only adds an unused helper in a generic shared URL file.
Changes unrelated URL utilities, validators, or query-string behavior without tying them to the displayed link path.
Relies on broad claims about all URL entry points without showing the concrete user-facing path from the task.
Punycode-converts entire URL strings, paths, query parameters, or fragments rather than just the hostname.
Ignores existing browser compatibility or raw href extraction behavior already present in the link handling code.
Rewards diagnosis, root-cause explanation, or test discovery as if they were implementation evidence.
metadata.applicability_stage: Most judgeable after repository search has located both URL helpers and the component/link handling path; premature during the first few exploratory commands. If no source diff is visible, preserve uncertainty about implementation quality rather than inferring success from investigation.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has connected IDN/Punycode handling to the user-facing link flow; it only explores unrelated files, discusses generic URL conversion, or investigates without any implementation plan.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent identifies generic URL helpers or Punycode libraries, reproduces the bug, or explains the root cause, but has not inspected or planned integration with the actual link display/click/confirmation path. Investigation is present but implementation is absent.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent understands hostname-only Punycode conversion and has found the relevant link or URL files, but the visible diff still centers on an isolated helper or broad entry-point changes rather than clear wiring into the user-facing link flow. Planning is present but actual integration is incomplete or unclear.
scale.4: Strong evidence: a visible source diff identifies the concrete link handling path and feeds a hostname-only Punycode URL into the displayed/confirmed link while preserving other URL parts and respecting existing raw/encoded href behavior.
scale.5: Very strong evidence: the trajectory clearly implements a minimal integrated fix in the link display/click confirmation flow through a visible source diff, reuses or places the helper at an appropriate component-accessible layer, preserves all non-host URL components, avoids unrelated utility regressions, and includes focused tests or explicit examples for Unicode-hostname IDN links.

experiences.title: Append-slash redirects must preserve query placement
experiences.description: Use when a Django/admin redirect bug concerns APPEND_SLASH dropping query strings and the trajectory is inspecting or changing redirect URL construction. Also use when evaluating validation for that fix: query-placement-specific evidence should remain distinct from generic regression testing.
experiences.context: Applies in Django-style codebases when the task explicitly involves a slash-appending redirect that currently uses a path-only value and loses QUERY_STRING, especially in AdminSite.catch_all_view() or analogous final catch-all routing. This is most useful once the trajectory has located the redirect line, proposed an edit, or shown validation evidence, because the visible evidence can show whether the constructed Location is /path/?a=b rather than /path/ or /path?a=b/. It may be premature during pure code exploration. It should not be generalized to unrelated redirect tasks where query preservation is not part of the contract, and it should not require one exact helper implementation if the visible code constructs the same URL semantics correctly. Generic successful test-suite output is useful only as regression evidence unless it clearly includes a query-bearing append-slash redirect case.
experiences.experience:
The useful criterion in these cases is not merely “uses get_full_path()” or “preserves the query string.” The discriminative boundary is that the redirect must append the slash to the path component before the ? and keep the original query component intact. A patch that changes request.path to request.get_full_path() but then formats "%s/" around it can appear to preserve parameters while producing /foo?id=123/, which is wrong; the rubric should explicitly catch this ordering bug. Conversely, a manual construction from the existing path plus ? plus QUERY_STRING can satisfy the task even if it does not use Django’s idiomatic helper, so avoid making the helper name the sole pass condition.

Keep targeted query-placement validation separate from generic regression testing. A broad test run with passing output supports regression safety, but it does not by itself prove that a slashless URL with a query redirects to /path/?query. Award targeted validation only when the visible evidence creates or runs a focused case, assertion, or equivalent manual check for a query-bearing append-slash redirect and maps the observed Location to the required slash-before-query semantics. If the evidence only shows unrelated or broad tests, do not infer targeted validation from that output. If the evidence shows the edit but no validation steps, preserve uncertainty about validation rather than assuming it occurred.

Also avoid adding speculative requirements such as deployment-prefix handling unless the task or trajectory specifically investigates them; those can make the rubric too strict for the visible issue. Prioritize visible evidence from the edit and focused checks: the redirect target for a slashless URL with id=123 becomes /.../?id=123, no-query redirects still become /.../, and unresolved or no-append cases retain existing 404/routing behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct query-preserving append-slash redirect
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the slash-appending redirect constructs a Location whose path has the missing trailing slash inserted before any query string, while preserving the original query string and leaving the surrounding redirect/404 conditions unchanged. Strong evidence includes replacing a path-only redirect with an API or construction that explicitly supports appending the slash before ?, or focused verification demonstrating a URL like /admin/auth/foo?id=123 redirects to /admin/auth/foo/?id=123 rather than dropping the query or appending the slash after the query.

observable_evidence: The edited redirect no longer uses only a path value that omits QUERY_STRING.
The slash is inserted into the path component before the query separator.
The original query string is retained without moving the slash after query parameters.
Existing conditions for whether to redirect versus raise 404 are not broadened or removed.
avoid_overfitting_to: Requiring a specific helper name when equivalent URL construction is visible.
Accepting any query-preserving change that produces /path?query/.
Adding unrelated deployment-prefix or routing requirements not raised by the task or trajectory.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the redirect preserves query strings or fixes the slash placement.
scale.2: Recognizes that query strings are involved but proposes or leaves code that likely drops them, appends the slash after the query, or changes unrelated redirect conditions.
scale.3: Shows partial progress toward preserving the query string, but the slash/query ordering or preservation of existing no-query/404 behavior remains ambiguous.
scale.4: Clearly updates the redirect so query strings are preserved and the slash is placed before the query, with little or no evidence of unrelated routing changes.
scale.5: Provides decisive code and/or focused verification showing /path?query redirects to /path/?query, no-query redirects remain correct, and existing redirect eligibility/404 behavior is preserved.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrong slash/query ordering or query loss
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize evidence that the proposed redirect still drops the query string or appends the slash after the query component. This includes constructions that call a full-path helper and then blindly append / to the whole result, producing /path?query/, or edits that preserve the original path-only behavior while claiming query preservation.

observable_evidence: The redirect Location is constructed from a full path and then suffixed with / without separating the query component.
A shown or inferable result is /path?x=1/ instead of /path/?x=1.
The query string is omitted from the redirect target despite being present on the incoming request.
The fix changes redirect eligibility or error behavior in a way that masks the query-placement issue.
avoid_overfitting_to: Penalizing equivalent correct constructions that do not use a preferred helper.
Treating ambiguous code as definitely wrong when slash/query ordering cannot be determined from the visible evidence.
Counting generic passing tests as disproving a visible wrong Location construction.

scale.1: No evidence of query loss or slash-after-query construction.
scale.2: Minor ambiguity or concern about query handling, but no clear wrong Location semantics.
scale.3: Likely query preservation problem or slash placement ambiguity remains unresolved.
scale.4: Clear evidence the query is dropped or the slash may be appended to the full URL including the query.
scale.5: Decisive evidence of the wrong redirect target, such as /path?query/ or /path/ with the original query lost.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Targeted validation of query-placement behavior
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory specifically validates the append-slash redirect for a URL that contains a query string, checking that the resulting Location preserves the query and places the slash before ?. This targeted validation is distinct from broad regression testing; generic test-suite success should not receive credit here unless the visible evidence identifies a focused query-bearing redirect case.

observable_evidence: A test, assertion, or manual check uses a slashless URL with a query string.
The expected or observed Location is /path/?query rather than /path?query/ or /path/.
The validation also considers the no-query case or unchanged 404/routing behavior when visible and relevant.
The evidence ties the check to the modified append-slash redirect path rather than to unrelated URL handling.
avoid_overfitting_to: Requiring one exact test framework, helper, or assertion style.
Treating broad passing test output as targeted query-placement validation.
Penalizing a focused manual check solely because it is not part of a formal test suite, while still weighing it less than an integrated regression test.

scale.1: No query-placement-specific validation; only code changes, discussion, or generic tests.
scale.2: Mentions the need to test query preservation but does not show a concrete query-bearing redirect check.
scale.3: Shows a simplified or manual query-bearing redirect check, but the asserted slash/query ordering or redirect path is incomplete.
scale.4: Creates or runs a focused validation that checks /path?query redirects to /path/?query.
scale.5: Provides focused validation for the query case plus relevant no-query or unchanged error behavior, with clear evidence tied to the edited redirect.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Regression safety remains separate from targeted query validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that the change does not break existing behavior by running relevant tests or equivalent checks. This should be scored separately and with lower weight than the semantic fix and targeted query-placement validation, because passing broad tests alone does not establish that query strings are preserved with the slash in the correct position.

observable_evidence: Explicit test runner invocation with clear passing output.
Relevant existing tests are run after the redirect change.
The output or discussion distinguishes broad regression safety from the focused query-placement behavior.
avoid_overfitting_to: Conflating broad regression testing with targeted query-bearing append-slash validation.
Awarding full semantic-fix credit based only on passing existing tests.

scale.1: No regression testing or equivalent safety check is shown.
scale.2: Attempts regression testing but results are failed, incomplete, or blocked by setup issues.
scale.3: Runs some checks, but relevance or results are unclear.
scale.4: Runs at least one relevant test group or equivalent check with clear passing results.
scale.5: Runs multiple relevant checks with clear passing results while keeping them distinct from targeted query-placement validation.

experiences.title: Do not use methodical debugging, patch presence, or fix abstraction level as proxies for root-cause-to-fix alignment
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when an agent is tracing a complex framework bug step-by-step, but the key evaluation question is whether the agent's stated root cause matches the visible failure mode and whether any implemented patch directly addresses that root cause — not whether the debugging process is orderly, whether a patch exists, or whether the fix is at a presumed-correct 'general' abstraction level rather than a 'specific' call site. Also retrieve it when a rubric set for a mixed bug-fix trajectory narrows to diagnosis or investigation alone: reproduction, root-cause identification, and fix implementation/validation are separate evidence dimensions, and source inspection alone must not substitute for executing the failing path or validating a fix.
experiences.context: Applies in Python framework/library bug fixes such as Django ORM, Matplotlib axes/autoscale, or SymPy polynomial internals where the trajectory shows reproduction attempts, environment setup, code inspection, tracing, and one-at-a-time hypotheses, but the candidate direction may still target an intermediate symptom instead of the contract-breaking boundary. Concrete activation evidence includes visible creation or execution of a reproduction script, observed traceback or failing behavior, dependency setup needed to run the scenario, source reading or grepping, a stated root cause, a proposed patch, or a regression check. The source rubric may still be appropriate early in an investigation when the main visible risk is shotgun-editing many unrelated areas without isolating failures. It is misleading as a final-review or late-debugging criterion when the agent has already narrowed to a plausible subsystem and correctness depends on preserving a specific behavior: per-parent slicing semantics, shared-axis unit propagation, queryset immutability/select-list invariants, lazy related-object normalization, or algebraic factor preservation. Evidence boundary: reading source files, tracing class hierarchies, or forming a plausible explanation is investigation, not reproduction, unless the agent executes a scenario that triggers the reported failing path; a patch is not fix progress unless it is tied to the identified root cause and checked, or at least clearly planned to be checked, against the reported behavior. Close-looking contraindication: do not apply this warning to collapse every early debugging rubric into an implementation demand when the visible work is only setup or when the task being assessed is explicitly limited to diagnostic explanation; in that case, preserve the narrower diagnostic boundary while not treating it as evidence of reproduction or validation. Abstain when the prefix does not contain enough evidence to determine whether the agent's root-cause analysis is correct, when no branch has both a stated root cause and a patch to compare alignment, or when all visible continuations are at the same stage so investigation depth alone cannot distinguish likely correctness.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent tested hypotheses one at a time and avoided shotgun debugging. That is useful process guidance, but in these cases it often over-valued trajectories that were orderly yet still wrong: the agent traced a real symptom, then patched a nearby mechanism without proving that the patch satisfied the user-visible invariant. A better rubric should focus on validated root-cause-to-fix alignment while keeping reproduction, diagnosis, and implementation/validation distinct when all three are visible parts of the work. Avoid the tempting criteria 'the agent is being systematic, so the patch is likely correct,' 'a patch exists, so the trajectory is further along,' and 'the agent read the relevant code, so the bug has effectively been reproduced.' Instead, prioritize visible evidence that the agent executed or prepared a scenario capable of triggering the failing path, identified the exact semantic boundary from the task, explained why the proposed code change enforces that boundary, and either ran or planned a regression check matching the original scenario. Do not let a single root-cause rubric stand in for separate evidence about reproduction and fix validation when the trajectory contains enough information to assess those dimensions separately. Do not assume a 'general mechanism' fix is inherently superior to a 'specific call site' fix, or vice versa — the correct abstraction level is determined by whether the fix directly addresses the identified root cause, not by the level's generality. A trajectory with correct root cause identification but no patch yet should not be ranked below a trajectory with an incorrect patch at an assumed 'general' abstraction level that does not address the identified root cause. Likewise, a trajectory that reproduces the failure but has not yet implemented a fix should be distinguished from one that only inspects code without executing the failing path, while still being distinguished from one that implements and validates an aligned fix. Penalize trajectories where tests still fail after a patch is applied, broad edits are made after a failed hypothesis, reproduction is claimed from a script that does not exercise the failing path, or the agent repeatedly inspects or traces the same area while missing visible evidence that the issue lies in a different layer. Do not penalize solely for absence of a patch when root cause identification is correct and visible in the prefix, but also do not treat investigation-only work as equivalent to reproduction or implementation progress.

experiences.title: Restore ModelForm M2M Semantics in Custom Save Overrides
experiences.description: Use this when a Django task concerns a ModelForm subclass whose custom save() bypasses normal many-to-many persistence, especially when the trajectory has inspected both the subclass save() and BaseModelForm.save(). As a narrow sibling within the same ModelForm save lifecycle, also apply the default-transfer lesson only when the visible issue is a declared ModelForm/model field with a model default that is omitted from submitted data but receives a meaningful value in cleaned_data and should be carried into the saved model object.
experiences.context: Applies in Django code when the reported bug is that a form subclass manually calls super().save(commit=False), mutates the model object, then saves it directly, causing ManyToManyField-backed form data to be dropped. It is most useful once the trajectory has localized the relevant save() override or has begun editing or testing it. It is less useful as a sole criterion during very early code exploration before the agent has inspected the save path, and it should not be narrowed to an exact spelling of the fix if the visible code preserves the same ModelForm contract. The sibling construct_instance clause is explicitly separate: it activates only for the omitted-submitted-value plus model-default pattern where the field participates in normal ModelForm construction and cleaned_data contains a derived meaningful value. It does not apply to arbitrary extra cleaned_data keys, fields excluded from the form field set, or generic validation rewrites.
experiences.experience:
The useful rubrics in the many-to-many custom-save cases focused on the real semantic contract: after a valid form has populated cleaned_data and the model object is saved, many-to-many form data must be persisted using Django’s save_m2m/_save_m2m mechanism, while password hashing, return behavior, and commit=False deferred-save behavior remain intact. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was not generic test activity, dependency installation, or ad hoc script output; it was whether the trajectory identified that the custom save() bypassed BaseModelForm.save(commit=True) and restored the missing relation-saving step after the object has been saved. A better rubric should accept equivalent implementations that call the public save_m2m hook or the underlying _save_m2m at the correct time, and should optionally reward preserving or exposing deferred save_m2m for commit=False. Avoid brittle criteria requiring an exact call shape, exact test command, or official regression test before judging implementation quality. Also avoid giving high credit merely because the agent reproduced that relation data is missing; reproduction is useful but incomplete unless the trajectory has applied or is clearly about to apply the localized save semantics fix.

Small reusable sibling lesson for ModelForm default-transfer tasks: if the visible failure is not many-to-many but instead a declared form/model field with a model default that was omitted from submitted data while cleaned_data contains a meaningful derived value, the decisive rubric should judge value-aware save-time transfer in construct_instance. Reward localization to the default-skipping condition combining f.has_default() with widget.value_omitted_from_data(), and reward fixes that preserve the model default when the omitted field’s cleaned value is empty for that form field, but save the cleaned value when cleaning produced a meaningful non-empty value. Do not require changes to _post_clean, full_clean, validation exclusion logic, raw submitted data mutation, global widget behavior, or model default definitions. Do not treat a field excluded from normal ModelForm construction, or an arbitrary key inserted into cleaned_data, as the target behavior. Penalize close-looking fixes that only check whether the key exists in cleaned_data, because omitted optional fields commonly have empty cleaned values and those empties should not blindly overwrite model defaults. If the visible diff or explanation does not show whether empty cleaned values are distinguished from meaningful cleaned values, preserve uncertainty and give only partial implementation credit.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: ModelForm-Compatible M2M Persistence
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should restore Django ModelForm many-to-many save semantics in the custom form save path: keep using commit=False where needed for local mutations such as password hashing before saving; when commit=True, save the model object first and then persist cleaned many-to-many/private relation data through the form’s save_m2m/_save_m2m mechanism; when commit=False, preserve the standard deferred workflow so callers can save the object and then call save_m2m. Judge from visible code inspection, edits, and validation output, while accepting semantically equivalent implementations rather than requiring one exact method spelling.

primary_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies that the custom save() override calls the parent with commit=False and therefore bypasses BaseModelForm.save(commit=True).
The implementation saves many-to-many data only after the model object has been saved and has a primary key.
Password hashing via set_password and returned-object behavior are preserved.
The commit=False path is not broken and preferably exposes or preserves deferred save_m2m behavior.
acceptable_fix_variants: Call the public save_m2m hook after saving the object when it is available.
Call the underlying _save_m2m after saving the object, with deferred save_m2m assignment for commit=False.
Use another local implementation only if it clearly delegates to the same cleaned_data relation-saving behavior.
non_decisive_evidence: Installing dependencies or repeatedly adjusting standalone Django settings.
Running unrelated tests without inspecting the actual save semantics.
Reproducing that many-to-many data is missing but not applying the save-path fix.

scale.1: The trajectory has not identified the overridden save() as the cause and shows no concrete plan or edit for many-to-many persistence.
scale.2: The trajectory notices a many-to-many/save_m2m issue but only reproduces it or discusses it, with no correct localized implementation yet.
scale.3: The trajectory has localized the save() override and understands that ModelForm save semantics are missing, but the visible implementation is incomplete, unverified, or risks breaking commit=False/password behavior.
scale.4: The trajectory applies a mostly correct fix that saves many-to-many data after the object is saved and preserves password hashing, with only minor uncertainty around deferred commit=False behavior or validation coverage.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements ModelForm-compatible semantics for both commit=True and commit=False, preserves password hashing and return behavior, and provides focused validation demonstrating immediate and deferred many-to-many persistence.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Value-Aware construct_instance Transfer for Omitted Declared Default Fields
reference_golden_rubrics.description: When the narrow default-transfer activation is present, the trajectory should fix the save-time transfer from cleaned_data to the model object for a declared field with a model default whose submitted value was omitted. A strong implementation is value-aware: it keeps the model default when the omitted field cleans to an empty value, but saves the cleaned value when clean() or field cleaning produced a meaningful non-empty value. It should preserve existing ModelForm behavior for editable fields, AutoField skipping, fields/exclude filtering, Boolean/checkbox semantics, and FileField deferral. Equivalent implementations are acceptable; do not require one exact textual patch.

activation_evidence: The visible task is about a model default persisting even though the form’s cleaned_data contains a derived value for the same participating field.
The field is part of normal ModelForm construction, not merely an arbitrary extra cleaned_data key or a field excluded from the form field set.
The observed call path reaches construct_instance or equivalent save-time field assignment logic.
primary_visible_evidence: The trajectory localizes the problem to construct_instance and the condition combining f.has_default() with widget.value_omitted_from_data().
The fix distinguishes meaningful cleaned values from empty cleaned values instead of relying only on key presence in cleaned_data.
The behavior after saving is that derived non-empty cleaned_data overrides the default, while omitted empty input still leaves the model default intact.
Related behaviors for checkboxes, optional fields, FileFields, and fields/exclude constraints are preserved or at least not visibly broken.
non_success_requirements: Do not require _post_clean, full_clean, raw data mutation, global widget changes, or changes to model defaults.
Do not give high implementation credit for a reproduction alone.
Do not score an excluded-field or undeclared-key cleaned_data scenario as the target behavior.
metadata.uncertainty_rule: If the visible edit does not show whether empty cleaned values are distinguished from meaningful values, give partial credit rather than assuming the implementation is correct from a single passing reproduction.

scale.1: No localization to construct_instance or save-time field transfer, or the trajectory works mainly in an unrelated validation layer.
scale.2: The trajectory notices the default/omitted-data interaction or reproduces it, but has no correct localized implementation.
scale.3: The trajectory edits construct_instance or equivalent logic, but the fix is too broad, such as removing the default-skipping branch or checking only key presence in cleaned_data so empty values may overwrite defaults.
scale.4: The trajectory implements a mostly correct value-aware transfer for omitted declared fields, with only minor uncertainty around edge behavior or validation coverage.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements the value-aware semantics, preserves related ModelForm behaviors, and validates both the derived non-empty override case and the omitted-empty default-preservation case.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Misframing Default Transfer as Undeclared cleaned_data or Validation Rewrite
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories or rubrics that treat the default-transfer problem as a requirement to save arbitrary cleaned_data keys, fields excluded from normal ModelForm construction, or values injected outside the declared form/model field path. Also penalize fixes that require or primarily reward _post_clean, full_clean, validation-exclusion changes, raw submitted data mutation, global widget behavior changes, or model default edits when the needed behavior is value-aware construct_instance transfer.

contradictory_visible_evidence: The proposed criterion says fields excluded from the form field set must be copied from cleaned_data to the model object as the main target behavior.
The fix still skips every omitted field with a model default regardless of the actual cleaned value.
The fix lets omitted empty cleaned values overwrite defaults by only checking f.name in cleaned_data or by removing the default-skip logic entirely.
The trajectory makes validation-stage rewrites a success requirement even though the visible problem is save-time transfer.
metadata.judge_mapping: For this negative rubric, low scores mean no such misframing is visible; high scores mean the implementation or judging criterion would rank the wrong behavior above the value-aware declared-field fix.

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw; the trajectory keeps the target to declared omitted fields and save-time value-aware transfer.
scale.2: Minor ambiguity in wording, but the visible implementation likely still targets the correct declared-field/default interaction.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory overemphasizes cleaned_data key presence or validation-stage changes without proving empty-value default preservation.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the implementation or criterion would reward excluded-field copying, _post_clean rewrites, or broad key-presence logic over the intended behavior.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the central solution is to save arbitrary cleaned_data keys or remove default preservation, causing omitted empty values to overwrite model defaults.

experiences.title: Disambiguate Non-Unique Composite Index Deletion
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django schema/migration task involves deleting a legacy composite index that shares columns with a unique constraint, especially when introspection can report unique constraints as indexes.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django schema editor or migration operations when the reported failure is that removing an index_together entry on fields also present in unique_together, UniqueConstraint, or an equivalent uniqueness declaration causes constraint lookup to find more than one database object. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or modified the schema deletion path, backend constraint introspection, or a focused reproduction of the duplicate match. It is less useful for unrelated index creation, migration autodetector-only changes, generic environment setup, or tasks whose main requirement is avoiding index recreation when moving declarations to Meta.indexes rather than fixing the crash during deletion. The activation boundary remains deletion of the ordinary non-unique index; lessons about primary-key or field-level unique colliders are used only to judge whether the same-column filtering logic is complete rather than subtype-specific.
experiences.experience:
For this cluster, the useful rubric focuses on the semantic boundary between deleting an ordinary composite index and deleting a uniqueness-bearing constraint. The important observable evidence is that the agent recognizes a unique constraint may also satisfy index=True in database introspection, so an index_together deletion lookup using only index=True can match both the non-unique index and a unique constraint on the same columns. A good rubric should reward trajectories that narrow the ordinary index deletion predicate to target non-unique indexes, preserve the existing unique-constraint deletion path, and validate that removing index_together leaves the uniqueness declaration intact.

Small reusable lesson: do not give full credit for a fix that excludes only one special collider, such as primary-key-backed constraints, if other same-column uniqueness objects could still match the broad lookup. The decisive distinction is comprehensive type filtering versus subtype-only filtering. For ordinary index deletion, strong evidence is a predicate equivalent to index=True plus unique=False, or another backend-correct way to isolate the non-unique index. A primary_key=False-only edit, a name-suffix heuristic, or validation that covers only a primary-key collision should be treated as incomplete when the visible lookup could still match field-level unique=True, unique_together, UniqueConstraint, or equivalent unique objects reported as indexes. Conversely, do not penalize equivalent implementations that use a different call shape but prove the same target/non-target separation through introspection or focused schema-editor reproduction. Preserve uncertainty when the visible edit or validation scope is incomplete; do not assume either comprehensive coverage or a narrow primary-key-only fix without evidence.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Comprehensive Non-Unique Index Deletion Disambiguation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that deleting a legacy composite index targets only the non-unique index when uniqueness-bearing constraints exist on the same columns. Strong evidence includes identifying the schema editor composed-index deletion path, explaining that unique constraints may also be reported as indexes by introspection, applying or proposing a filter equivalent to index=True and unique=False for ordinary index deletion, and checking that the uniqueness declaration remains intact. Full-credit evidence must show comprehensive exclusion of unique colliders, not merely exclusion of a primary-key subtype or reliance on generated name patterns.

metadata.primary_failure_mode: constraint lookup for ordinary index deletion matches both unique and non-unique database objects on the same columns
metadata.decisive_observable_distinction: broad non-unique-index predicate versus subtype-only filtering such as primary_key=False
key_positive_evidence: inspects schema editor composed-index deletion or equivalent migration database operation path
recognizes unique constraints can have index metadata in introspection
narrows ordinary index deletion to non-unique constraints/indexes using unique=False or an equivalent backend-correct predicate
preserves unique_together, UniqueConstraint, field-level unique, and primary-key uniqueness semantics where applicable
validates that removing the ordinary index leaves the uniqueness object intact
avoid_as_primary_evidence: relying only on generated constraint name suffixes
excluding only primary-key constraints while leaving other unique colliders eligible to match
generic migration autodetector changes without schema deletion disambiguation
validation unrelated to the duplicate constraint lookup behavior
treating declaration move/recreation optimization as required for the crash fix

scale.1: 1: No evidence that the trajectory distinguishes ordinary composite index deletion from uniqueness-bearing constraint deletion; it may only inspect files, run unrelated validation, or discuss migrations generically.
scale.2: 2: Weak evidence: the trajectory locates relevant schema or migration code and mentions duplicate constraints, but does not identify that unique constraints can also match an index lookup or proposes only a subtype-specific exclusion such as primary_key=False.
scale.3: 3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory understands that the same columns have both unique and non-unique database objects and considers filtering by constraint type, but the implementation or validation is incomplete or could still affect unique constraint deletion.
scale.4: 4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans a fix that excludes unique constraints when deleting ordinary composite indexes and checks at least one focused reproduction or equivalent introspection path.
scale.5: 5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory directly targets the index_together deletion lookup with a non-unique index predicate, explains the introspection reason, verifies that the ordinary index is removed while the uniqueness object remains, and confirms related composed-index deletion semantics are not regressed.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Subtype-Only or Name-Based Filtering Leaves Ambiguous Matches
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that claim to fix the duplicate-match crash while leaving the ordinary index deletion lookup broad enough to match other unique objects. This includes edits that only add primary_key=False, only handle a primary-key collision in validation, or rely on suffix/name conventions instead of constraint semantics. The negative signal is strongest when visible evidence shows the lookup still lacks unique=False or an equivalent non-unique-index discriminator; preserve uncertainty if the relevant filtering or validation scope cannot be seen.

metadata.primary_failure_mode: implementation disambiguates one special unique subtype but not all uniqueness-bearing objects that can satisfy the lookup
key_negative_evidence: adds only primary_key=False to constraint filtering for an ordinary index deletion path
validates only a primary-key collision while claiming complete same-column disambiguation
does not address field-level unique=True, unique_together, UniqueConstraint, or equivalent unique colliders when they remain eligible under the lookup
uses generated constraint names or suffixes as the main discriminator
changes unrelated migration declaration logic without isolating the database object to delete
metadata.uncertainty_handling: If the visible material is truncated or the backend-specific equivalent predicate cannot be determined, avoid assuming either a comprehensive fix or a narrow subtype-only fix.

scale.1: 1: No evidence of subtype-only or name-based disambiguation; the trajectory either uses a semantic non-unique predicate or the relevant edit is not visible.
scale.2: 2: Minor concern: the trajectory mentions a special collider such as a primary key, but also appears to understand that unique constraints broadly must be excluded.
scale.3: 3: Moderate concern: the trajectory proposes a partial discriminator or narrow validation, and it is unclear whether other unique colliders would still match.
scale.4: 4: Strong concern: the visible edit or plan excludes only primary-key constraints, relies on names, or otherwise leaves field-level/declared unique constraints eligible to match the ordinary index lookup.
scale.5: 5: Severe concern: the trajectory explicitly treats primary-key-only exclusion or name matching as a complete fix despite evidence that other uniqueness-bearing objects share the lookup columns and flags.

experiences.title: Do not reward label-decoding intent without a complete, applyable local patch artifact
experiences.description: Retrieve when a scikit-learn trajectory for HistGradientBoosting early-stopping target encoding shows investigation, planned decoding, or tests against a different installed sklearn, but the current local source diff is not clearly verified, the agent may be drifting to unrelated files, or the final submitted artifact is only source excerpts, test output, prose, or raw source lines from grep/cat rather than a diff-formatted patch.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/scikit-learn source-tree tasks where the reported bug is a target-representation mismatch during scorer-based early stopping: classifier targets are internally encoded, while predictions/scorers operate on original class labels. The label-decoding idea is a valid semantic target when the trajectory is at final-review stage and the visible local diff shows the scorer path decoding both training-subset and validation targets while preserving loss/regressor behavior. It is misleading when the visible trajectory is still early exploration, only states the intended fix, relies on successful runs from a separately installed sklearn wheel, cannot import the local checkout, later edits unrelated model-selection/build files, or ends with a final artifact that is not a complete, applyable patch. A final submission of raw source lines obtained via grep or cat of a source file is not a patch even when those lines contain the correct edit; the submitted content must carry diff formatting (diff --git headers, ---/+++ file-path markers, @@ hunk headers with +/- line markers) to count as a complete code delta. For the scorer path, both training-subset and validation target coverage must be verified at the code-structure level in the actual patch, not just in the agent's reasoning or validation output.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly identified the central semantic fix: scorer-based early stopping for classifiers should pass targets in the same label space as predictions, without changing loss-based scoring or regressors. The problem was that the criterion was too solution-shaped and too broad for the visible stage of the trajectories. It gave partial or high credit to trajectories that merely reasoned about the fix, had unverified/truncated source edits, ran reproductions against an installed modern sklearn instead of the checkout under repair, or later drifted into unrelated files. For future rubric generation, keep the label-space criterion only when there is visible evidence of a current local edit in the early-stopping scorer path. Otherwise generate a stage-aware criterion that penalizes lack of verified local diff/current method inspection, reliance on the wrong installed package as validation, or unrelated final edits. Additionally, the final submitted artifact must be a complete, applyable code delta in diff format or explicitly accepted equivalent; source-file excerpts, generated code, test output, prose summaries, and raw source lines from grep or cat output are not equivalent even when they reveal apparently correct local code or the working tree contains the correct edit elsewhere in the trace. The decisive observable for artifact integrity is whether the final submitted content carries diff formatting: a diff --git header, ---/+++ file-path markers, and @@ hunk headers with +/- line markers. A trajectory that runs grep or cat mid-trajectory for inspection but then submits a git diff or patch-file output at the finalization step is valid; only the final submitted content is judged. A truncated diff that still begins with diff --git and shows @@/+/- markers remains a valid patch submission. Give artifact-integrity dominant weight: a branch with a missing, non-applyable, or non-diff-formatted final patch should be capped below branches that submit a complete plausible patch in diff format. Do not let validation breadth, number of test modules, or test-runner choice dominate final deliverable correctness. For conditional fixes like the scorer path, verify both the training-subset and validation target paths at the code-structure level in the actual patch, not just in reasoning or validation output. Avoid the tempting criterion 'agent understands it should decode y via classes_' as the main predictor; prioritize observable evidence: a complete submitted patch in diff format containing the current diff or method body in the target scorer path, both train and validation scorer calls covered at the structure level, loss/regressor paths left alone, and no unrelated changes replacing the intended fix.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unverified, Drifted, or Incomplete Final Patch Artifact
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this scikit-learn early-stopping target-encoding bug when the visible work does not establish that the local source checkout currently contains the intended scorer-path fix, especially if the agent only describes the decoding idea, inspects truncated output, validates by running a separately installed sklearn version, cannot import/build the local package, drifts into unrelated files instead of maintaining a focused change in the histogram gradient boosting early-stopping scorer logic, or ends with a final artifact that is only source excerpts, test output, prose, or raw source lines from grep/cat rather than a diff-formatted patch.

metadata.task_family: scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting classifier early-stopping scorer target encoding
prioritize_visible_evidence: a complete, applyable final submitted patch in diff format (containing diff --git headers, ---/+++ file-path markers, and @@ hunk headers with +/- line markers), not just excerpts, prose, or raw source lines from grep/cat
current local diff or full method inspection in the early-stopping scorer path within the submitted artifact
coverage of both training-subset and validation scorer targets verified at the code-structure level in the actual patch
explicit preservation of loss-based scoring and regressor behavior in the submitted change
awareness that installed sklearn runs do not validate the patched checkout
absence of unrelated file changes as the only final work
avoid_overcrediting: plans or comments that mention decoding without a verified local edit in the final artifact
successful reproducer output from a different installed sklearn package
stale earlier-summary claims not confirmed by recent diff or final submission
source-file excerpts, generated code, test output, or prose summaries treated as equivalent to a complete patch
raw source lines from grep or cat output treated as a valid patch submission even when the working tree contains the correct edit elsewhere in the trace
broad environment/build exploration or validation breadth with no complete submitted code delta in diff format
validation breadth, number of test modules, or test-runner choice dominating artifact integrity

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory submits a complete, applyable patch in diff format with a current, focused local source change in the early-stopping scorer path, or is still explicitly in early exploration without claiming validation; no unrelated drift is visible.
scale.2: Minor concern: the agent has a plausible local edit or clear plan but has not fully inspected the current diff/method body or the final artifact is not yet a complete patch in diff format, while avoiding misleading validation claims and unrelated edits.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory mainly demonstrates understanding of the label-decoding fix or has truncated/unverified edit evidence, and validation is blocked or ambiguous; the final artifact may contain excerpts or raw source lines but not a complete applyable diff.
scale.4: Clear concern: the agent treats runs against an installed sklearn or stale summaries as validation of the local patch, or recent steps fail to confirm that both scorer targets are fixed in the local checkout; the final submission is excerpts, test output, prose, or raw source lines from grep/cat rather than a complete patch in diff format.
scale.5: Severe concern: the visible or final-directed work has drifted to unrelated files or changes, or there is no verified local scorer-path edit despite claims that the bug has been fixed, or the final submitted artifact is not a complete, applyable code delta in diff format—including submissions of raw source lines from grep or cat that show correct code but lack diff markers.

experiences.title: Contract-Level Behavioral Test Evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an agent claims validation through added tests, changed expected outputs, or ad hoc scripts for a behavior-specific bug or feature; judge whether those tests assert the actual user-visible contract — including the exact set of produced values when the fix changes what is yielded or returned, and the exact per-branch or per-mode value/position assignments when the fix controls which specific values are selected per condition — rather than merely exercising code paths, confirming aggregate statistics match, or matching per-branch counts without verifying which specific values are assigned to each branch.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent trajectories across Python, Go, and TypeScript repositories after the agent has identified a fix and is using tests or manual scripts as confidence evidence. It is most relevant for tasks involving parsing metadata, fallback ordering, event-driven UI updates, set/membership semantics, deterministic selection, API parameter precedence, per-branch or per-mode value selection, or yield/return logic where a patch can look plausible while missing a boundary condition. It is less decisive during early exploration, when no implementation exists yet, or for very small localized source fixes whose correctness is directly visible from the changed line and no durable test has been added.
